statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether women in general go from first use of alcohol or other drugs to dependence, or to treatment, faster than men (the idea called 'telescoping'): the faster course was described mostly in people in treatment and self-help groups, from ages they recalled years later; the general-population survey read here for alcohol did not find the full pattern; and in a US general-population survey of cannabis use disorder, read in full, the recalled time from first use to the disorder was 0.40 years shorter in women, among people who already had the disorder and without adjustment for age, not the 2.5 years a critique reports. In two pooled US national household surveys (NLAES, 1991–1992, response 90%, and NESARC, 2001–2002, response 81%; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18 to 57; every age recalled at a single interview), women had their first drink later than men (on average at 19.0 against 17.8 years; the gap narrowed from 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943 to 0.4 years in those born 1974–1983). Among the 38,309 lifetime drinkers (more than 12 drinks ever), men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence than women in every birth cohort (hazard ratios 1.36 to 1.79, adjusted for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink, and, according to the table's footnote though not the Methods, for age). The authors read these hazards, the survival curves and a significant interaction of cohort, gender and time (its estimates not shown) as men becoming dependent faster, especially in younger cohorts. In the editors' reading, a hazard among all drinkers combines the chance of ever becoming dependent with the speed of getting there, and because the average times below were similar, the higher hazard in men mostly reflects that more men became dependent (in the table's unweighted counts, 23.7% of male and 16.2% of female lifetime drinkers; editors' arithmetic). Among the people who did become dependent, the group whose timing treatment-sample studies measure, the average time from first drink to dependence was about the same in women and men (5.6 against 5.8 years; unadjusted); it was shorter in women born 1964–1973 (3.7 against 4.2 years) and, not marked significant, in those born 1954–1963 (5.5 against 6.4), and longer, not significantly, in women of the other three cohorts. Among people with dependence, men also had a higher hazard of first alcohol treatment, significantly in two of five birth cohorts (1.55 and 1.42) (Keyes et al., 2010). The authors conclude that telescoping is not evident in the general population, although their Discussion's statement that women were faster on neither measure goes further than their own table. As described in a historical critique, the idea goes back to a 1952 WHO committee report and to stage models built from the recalled drinking histories of 98 men in Alcoholics Anonymous, with 15 women's answers set aside; the phrase 'telescoped development' was first used in 1958; the 1989 study usually credited with defining the term asked 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups to recall four landmark ages, and the interval from first alcohol-related problem to first treatment was 4.3 years shorter on average in the women; 75 of 103 articles citing that study used it as background without testing it; and the critique's authors recommend dropping the term (Marks & Clark, 2018). The same critique describes a US general-population survey (NESARC, by its reference title; 1,217 women and 3,297 men) as finding the time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, without giving its timing measure or adjustment (Marks & Clark, 2018); read in full, the survey shows a much smaller difference, and the critique misreports both the difference and the sample. In NESARC 2001–2002 (43,093 US adults interviewed once, response 81%), the comparison was restricted to the 2,080 men and 1,217 women (3,297 in all) who had ever had DSM-IV cannabis abuse or dependence: they had first used cannabis at the same average age (16.71 against 16.73 years) and the disorder had begun at similar ages (19.34 against 18.98 years, not significant), and the recalled time from first use to the disorder was 2.64 years in men and 2.24 in women, a difference of 0.40 years, about 5 months (p = 0.026). The comparison was adjusted neither for current age, although the women with the disorder were younger, nor for anything else; it was one of more than 50 outcome rows compared without multiplicity correction, with several tests for some rows (editors' count on the study card); and it describes speed among people who developed the disorder, not who develops it: the authors cite another analysis of the same survey in which 11.8% of men and 5.4% of women had ever had the disorder. The authors present the 0.40 years as evidence of telescoping outside treatment (Khan et al., 2013). A narrative review lists faster progression in women for alcohol, cannabis, cocaine (in people in the justice system) and prescription opioids, but not heroin, found mainly in women already in treatment, and, following an earlier review, explains the difference from population surveys by who is sampled: women in treatment likely have more severe disorders (McHugh et al., 2018; its cannabis citation points to a general-population paper on alcohol dependence). The same group's earlier review states as established that women advance faster from use to regular use to first treatment for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence, citing six studies, among them treatment samples and one population survey (Dawson, 1996) that the review itself describes elsewhere as showing no earlier treatment entry for women (Greenfield et al., 2007). The treatment-sample study that the papers above describe in opposite ways, read in full, compared people entering a US alcohol treatment trial (Project MATCH, 1991–1993, nine sites; 379 women and 1,210 men with all four landmark ages, recalled at entry; women and men compared within study arm and fifth of current age, nothing else adjusted for): women recalled first getting drunk regularly, first alcohol problems and first difficulty stopping drinking 2.5 to 3.9 years later than men (getting drunk regularly at 26.6 against 22.7 years on average) but reached their worst period of drinking at the same age (35.2 against 35.0 years). The recalled intervals were shorter in women from getting drunk regularly to first problems (0.9 against 2.3 years) and from loss of control to the worst period (5.5 against 7.8 years), not from first problems to loss of control (2.3 against 2.2 years), and, among the 735 people for whom the trial was their first treatment, from getting drunk regularly to treatment (11.6 against 15.8 years). Gender explained 1% to 4% of the variance; the differences were small or absent in the youngest fifth of participants (average age 26.6; getting drunk regularly at 18.8 against 18.0 years) and grew with age; and only 53% of participants reported the landmarks in the order the intervals assume. The reported age interactions concern landmark ages and time to first treatment, not every shorter successive-landmark interval. Trial-entry ages were similar for women and men in the full 1,589-person analysis sample (38 to 42 years on average), but sex-specific entry ages are not reported for the 735-person first-treatment subgroup. If they were similar there too, a later start would itself shorten the interval ending at treatment. The 3.9-year onset gap comes from the full sample and the 4.2-year interval gap from that subgroup, so comparing them is approximate (editors’ cross-sample comparison), and in the editors' approximate reading of the paper's figure the gaps in time to treatment by age group (about 0.8 to 7.7 years) track the gaps in the age of getting drunk regularly (0.8 to 7.1 years). The authors call telescoping relatively robust in people seeking treatment and recommend alerting women in general that they are more likely to develop alcohol problems rapidly (Randall et al., 1999); the papers that cite the study as showing telescoping, and the critique that counts it among studies with fewer telescoping effects, are each partly right. One of the treatment samples the earlier review cites (Greenfield et al., 2007), read in full, compared 156 women and 115 men entering inpatient or outpatient treatment for current DSM-III-R cocaine, opioid, cannabis or alcohol dependence at two Connecticut centres (362 of 855 consecutive patients recruited, paid; years not given; every timing recalled after entering treatment): women and men recalled starting regular use at ages that did not differ significantly (for example opioids 23.7 against 22.3 years), but the women recalled fewer years from the start of regular use to their current treatment for opioids (58 women, 35 men; F = 4.74, P = 0.03), cannabis (20 and 18; F = 7.28, P = 0.01) and regular drinking (41 and 42; F = 4.87, P = 0.03), roughly 4 to 5 years fewer by the editors' approximate reading of the bar chart, the only place the means appear, and not for cocaine (96 and 71; about 7.8 against 8.8 years); drug and alcohol severity at entry did not differ, while psychiatric and employment problems were greater in women. Where the review describes faster progression from use to first treatment, this study measured from the start of regular use to the current treatment, which for some patients was not their first (Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004, pp. 266–268; Greenfield et al., 2007, Introduction). The paper describes the interval both as time elapsed and as pretreatment years of regular use without saying how it was computed, and it adjusted every comparison for current age; computed as elapsed time, a shorter interval at the same current age would mean a later start, which the paper reports as absent, unless the interval analyses held covariates that the onset analyses did not (the paper lists previous treatments and other dependence diagnoses for them) (editors' reading on the study card). The authors sum up that their observations suggest an accelerated progression to treatment entry in women, which probably reflects a telescoped course, note that their cocaine result conflicts with earlier treatment-sample studies, and list recall, the many eligible patients who declined and the larger share of women among inpatients as limitations (Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Do women go from first use to problems faster than men? This has not been shown for women in general. The idea, called 'telescoping', came mostly from small groups of people in treatment or in Alcoholics Anonymous, who had to remember years later when each step happened, and its stages were first drawn from men's stories. In two big US surveys of adults in the general population, women had their first drink later than men, and fewer women than men became dependent on alcohol. Among the people who did become dependent, women got there about as fast as men, on average about 6 years after their first drink, and a little faster in one age group. The survey's authors read their results as men getting there faster; the editors think this mostly shows that more men became dependent. In a big US survey, among people who had had a cannabis use disorder, women and men had started cannabis at the same age, about 17, and the women's disorder began on average about 5 months sooner after their first use (2.2 against 2.6 years); a review reported this as 2.5 years, which is wrong. In a US alcohol treatment study, women started getting drunk regularly about 4 years later than men but reached their worst drinking at the same age, about 35, so the steps in between looked shorter; the differences were small and several varied with age. Similar trial-entry ages were reported for the whole sample; ages for the first-treatment subgroup were not given, so explaining its shorter intervals by a later start remains conditional. In a second US treatment study, of people starting treatment for drugs or alcohol, women said they had used opioids, cannabis or alcohol regularly for roughly 4 to 5 fewer years than men before their current treatment, though not cocaine; the study does not say how it counted these years, and its result is hard to square with its finding that women and men started regular use at about the same ages. A review suggests that the women who reach treatment may have more severe problems, which would explain why a faster course shows up in treatment. All these studies relied on memory. See the contested question.
population: Adults in two pooled US national household surveys (NLAES 1991–1992 and NESARC 2001–2002; US-born, aged 18 to 57; 53,238 people, 38,309 of whom were lifetime drinkers, with more than 12 drinks ever) for alcohol; US adults with a lifetime cannabis use disorder in NESARC 2001–2002 (2,080 men, 1,217 women); people entering a US alcohol treatment trial (Project MATCH, 1991–1993; 1,210 men, 379 women); people entering treatment for current cocaine, opioid, cannabis or alcohol dependence at two US centres in Connecticut (115 men, 156 women; years not given); and, for other drugs and other treatment and self-help samples, studies described in a historical critique and two narrative reviews
exposure: Being a woman (the studies compare by gender and do not separate sex from gender)
comparator: Men in the same samples
outcome: Time from first use, or from early drinking landmarks, to later landmarks, dependence or use disorder, and first treatment ('telescoping'), or, in one treatment sample, from the start of regular use to the current treatment; every step recalled at one interview or in questionnaires
magnitude: Not estimable as a general difference in speed. General-population surveys, alcohol (Keyes et al., 2010): age at first drink, women 19.0 vs men 17.8 years (gap 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943, 0.4 in those born 1974–1983; editors' subtraction); hazard of dependence among all lifetime drinkers (more than 12 drinks), men vs women, 1.56 (95% CI 1.35–1.79), 1.36 (1.23–1.50), 1.46 (1.33–1.62), 1.79 (1.58–2.02) and 1.71 (1.34–2.20) for people born 1974–1983, 1964–1973, 1954–1963, 1944–1953 and 1934–1943 (a mixture of the chance of dependence and its speed, read by the authors as faster progression in men; whether age was adjusted for is stated inconsistently); share of lifetime drinkers with a time to dependence in the unweighted Table 1 counts, men 23.7% vs women 16.2% (4,631 of 19,549 and 3,121 of 19,263; editors' arithmetic; these counts total 7,752, against 8,564 people with dependence in the hazard analysis); mean time from first drink to dependence among people who became dependent (unadjusted), women 5.6 vs men 5.8 years (ratio 1.04, not significant), born 1964–1973 3.7 vs 4.2 years (p = 0.02), born 1954–1963 5.5 vs 6.4 years (not marked significant; t about 2.4 from the printed means and standard errors, an editors' approximation on the study card), and longer in women in the other three cohorts (3.1 vs 2.8, 8.6 vs 7.9 and 11.8 vs 10.4 years; none marked significant); hazard of first treatment among people with dependence, men vs women, 1.16 (0.77–1.76), 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1.20 (0.91–1.58) and 1.38 (0.84–2.26) in the same cohort order; mean time from dependence to first treatment among people treated, born 1934–1943, women 19.4 vs men 23.5 years (the overall means, 6.1 vs 7.0, cannot be reconciled with the cohort rows and are not used). Treatment and self-help samples, second-hand (Marks & Clark, 2018): the 1989 study credited with defining the term, 33 women and 105 men, first problem to first treatment 4.3 years shorter in women, first drink about 2 and first intoxication about 3 years later in women, same age at treatment entry; Iowa treatment centres (3,132 men, 395 women), treatment about 2 years after a first attempt to quit in women, about 3 in men; 75 of 103 citing articles used the 1989 study as background. General-population survey of cannabis use disorder as described by Marks & Clark (2018): first use to the disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, in 1,217 women and 3,297 men; read in full (Khan et al., 2013; NESARC 2001–2002; 2,080 men and 1,217 women with lifetime DSM-IV cannabis abuse or dependence, 3,297 in all), men vs women, weighted means (SE): age at first use 16.71 (0.10) vs 16.73 (0.12), p = 0.88; age at onset of the disorder 19.34 (0.13) vs 18.98 (0.16), p = 0.10; time from first use to onset 2.64 (0.10) vs 2.24 (0.13) years, F = 5.20, p = 0.026, a difference of 0.40 years (approximate 95% CI 0.08 to 0.72, editors' calculation on the study card), unadjusted, among people with the disorder; lifetime disorder in the whole survey, cited by the authors from another analysis, 11.8% of men vs 5.4% of women. Treatment sample, read in full (Randall et al., 1999; Project MATCH 1991–1993; 379 women, 1,210 men; compared within study arm and fifth of current age), women vs men, mean (SD) recalled age at getting drunk regularly 26.6 (10.35) vs 22.7 (8.96), first problems 27.5 (10.75) vs 25.0 (9.87), loss of control 29.8 (11.28) vs 27.2 (9.95), worst problems 35.2 (10.89) vs 35.0 (10.93); intervals, drunk regularly to first problems 0.9 (5.53) vs 2.3 (7.04), first problems to loss of control 2.3 (6.12) vs 2.2 (7.08), loss of control to worst problems 5.5 (8.31) vs 7.8 (8.67) years; drunk regularly to first treatment, 735 people in their first treatment (numbers of women and men not reported), 11.6 (9.01) vs 15.8 (9.67) years, F(1, 715) = 44.5; gender ω² .01 to .04; youngest fifth of current age, drunk regularly 18.8 vs 18.0 years, oldest fifth 37.8 vs 30.7. Second treatment sample, read in full (Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004; two Connecticut centres; 156 women, 115 men; current DSM-III-R dependence; years not given), women vs men: recalled age at the start of regular use, mean (SD), cocaine 22.7 (5.5) vs 23.4 (6.8), opioids 23.7 (6.2) vs 22.3 (6.8), cannabis 15.6 (4.4) vs 14.1 (2.1), alcohol 20.3 (7.1) vs 18.0 (6.4), no difference significant (no statistics given); years from the start of regular use to the current treatment, shorter in women for opioids (58 and 35 people; F = 4.74, P = 0.03), cannabis (20 and 18; F = 7.28, P = 0.01) and regular drinking (41 and 42; F = 4.87, P = 0.03), regular intoxication P = 0.09, cocaine not different (96 and 71); means shown only as bars, read approximately by the editors (about ±0.3 year): opioids 8.1 vs 12.0, cannabis 12.8 vs 17.7, regular drinking 14.1 vs 18.7, regular intoxication 13.8 vs 17.8, cocaine 7.8 vs 8.8 years; current age and treatment setting entered every comparison, and the interval comparisons also previous treatments and other lifetime dependence diagnoses; severity scores at entry on the ASI, a standard interview scored 0 to 1, drug 0.19 vs 0.17 and alcohol 0.18 vs 0.23 (not different), psychiatric 0.36 vs 0.26 (P = 0.006), employment 0.79 vs 0.66 (P = 0.001).

risk_of_bias.note: Every timing was recalled at a single interview or in questionnaires, years or decades later (card sc_keyes_2010: JBI, moderate); treatment samples select people by having reached treatment. Of the two read in full, one (card sc_randall_1999: JBI, high for this question) reported similar entry ages for the full sample, not specifically for the first-treatment subgroup, so explaining the subgroup’s shorter treatment intervals by the later start remains conditional, and its effects were small; the other (card sc_hernandez_avila_2004: ROBINS-E, high) recruited 362 of 855 consecutive patients, timed the interval to the current treatment rather than the first, shows its means only as bars, and reports shorter intervals in women together with no difference in the age at which regular use began, which with current age held constant in both comparisons would be the same comparison if the interval were the age at treatment minus the age at onset (the paper does not say how it was computed). The other treatment samples are known here only through reviews that did not appraise them (cards sc_marks_2018, sc_mchugh_2018, sc_greenfield_2007); the cannabis survey (card sc_khan_2013: JBI, moderate) compared only people with the disorder, without adjustment for age, among more than 50 outcome rows with uncorrected comparisons; in the survey analysis the hazards among all drinkers mix the chance of dependence with its speed, the averages among people who became dependent are unadjusted and depend on age at interview, whether age was adjusted for is stated inconsistently, and several table and text values disagree.

inconsistency.note: Treatment samples point towards a faster course in women, though in the Connecticut sample only for opioids, cannabis and alcohol, not cocaine, which its authors note conflicts with earlier cocaine studies; the general-population cannabis survey points towards a slightly shorter course (0.40 years) among people with the disorder, while the general-population alcohol analysis does not find the full pattern; within the survey paper, the hazards (read by the authors as men faster) and the averages among people who became dependent (no difference overall; women faster in one cohort) differ; a review, following an earlier one, explains the difference by sample, which is plausible but untested.

indirectness.note: The general-population analyses read concern alcohol (US-born adults aged 18 to 57 interviewed in 1991–1992 and 2001–2002) and cannabis (US adults with the disorder in 2001–2002, from one of the same surveys); the two treatment samples read in full concern alcohol in the USA in 1991–1993 and cocaine, opioids, cannabis and alcohol at two US centres (years not given; the interval there ends at the current treatment, not necessarily the first); the evidence from other treatment samples, and for prescription opioids and for cocaine in people in the justice system, is second-hand (narrative reviews; METHODS §6.3).

imprecision.note: The survey estimates are precise (at least 4,603 people per cohort); the small treatment samples (33 women in the 1989 study) are part of the second-hand evidence already rated down; the alcohol treatment sample read in full has 379 women (66 to 85 per fifth of current age) and does not report how many of the 735 in its treatment comparison were women, and in the Connecticut treatment sample the cannabis comparison rests on 20 women and 18 men and the means can be read only approximately from a bar chart; the cannabis survey difference has an approximate 95% CI of 0.08 to 0.72 years (editors' calculation on the study card).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; that 75 of 103 papers citing the 1989 study used it without testing it concerns citation, not publication.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low, the floor. Counted once: McHugh et al. (2018) updates Greenfield et al. (2007) by the same group and reuses its search; both reviews and the critique describe overlapping treatment-sample studies and the same general-population analysis (Keyes et al., 2010), so they add no independent data; the survey analysis pools NLAES, which Greenfield et al. also cite through Dawson (1996), and NESARC, which is also the source of the cannabis analysis (Khan et al., 2013), so the two survey analyses share respondents, for different drugs; the treatment study now read (Randall et al., 1999) is the one Keyes et al., McHugh et al., Greenfield et al. and Marks & Clark cite, so their descriptions of it add nothing independent. Greenfield et al. (2007) also cite the Connecticut treatment sample (Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004), now read, so their description of it adds nothing independent. Each figure is labelled with its quantity: hazards among all drinkers (chance and speed together, read by the authors as speed) or averages among people who reached the step (speed only); that the hazards mostly reflect the chance of becoming dependent is the editors' reading, resting on the similar average times and on Table 1's unweighted counts, and the claim gives the authors' reading beside it. Reading Randall et al. (1999) and Khan et al. (2013) in full weakened the yes side without removing it: the treatment-sample differences are small (gender explained 1% to 4% of the variance), small or absent in the youngest participants and, for the first-treatment interval, may partly reflect a later start if that subgroup had similar entry ages; the cannabis difference is 0.40 years among people who already had the disorder, unadjusted for age, with no difference in the age at which the disorder began, and the critique's 2.5 years misreports it. Reading Hernandez-Avila et al. (2004) in full adds a second treatment sample in the same direction for opioids, cannabis and alcohol, not for cocaine, with the limits of treatment samples and recall and some of its own: the interval runs to the current treatment, not necessarily the first; the means appear only as bars; and its shorter intervals are hard to reconcile with its report that women and men began regular use at similar ages, at the same current age. It corrects the earlier review's description of it in one respect (the current, not the first, treatment) and agrees with it in others (alcohol, opioids and cannabis; similar severity at entry). The certainty stays very low. Status contested: credible evidence points both ways (treatment samples, and a small difference among people with the disorder in a general-population cannabis survey, against the general-population alcohol survey), with a published critique of the concept, so the six-part debate box applies.

debate.question: Do women go from first use of alcohol or other drugs to dependence, or to treatment, faster than men, as studies of people in treatment report (Randall et al., 1999; Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004), or does the faster course seen there come from who reaches treatment and from how the timing was remembered (Marks & Clark, 2018; McHugh et al., 2018)?
debate.evidence_yes: The faster course was described mostly in people in treatment. In the 1989 study usually credited with defining the term, 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups recalled their landmark ages: the women had started drinking about 2 years later and had first been drunk about 3 years later, entered treatment at the same age, and went from their first alcohol-related problem to their first treatment 4.3 years faster on average; in an earlier Iowa treatment sample (3,132 men and 395 women), women reached treatment about 2 years after a first attempt to quit and men about 3 (as described by Marks & Clark, 2018). In the treatment sample most often cited, read in full (Project MATCH, 1991–1993; 379 women and 1,210 men entering alcohol treatment), women recalled shorter intervals from getting drunk regularly to first problems (0.9 against 2.3 years) and from loss of control to their worst period of drinking (5.5 against 7.8 years), and, among people in their first treatment, from getting drunk regularly to treatment (11.6 against 15.8 years); the authors call telescoping relatively robust in people seeking treatment (Randall et al., 1999). In a second treatment sample read in full (156 women and 115 men entering treatment for drug or alcohol dependence at two Connecticut centres), women recalled fewer years from the start of regular use to their current treatment for opioids, cannabis and regular drinking (roughly 4 to 5 years fewer, by the editors' approximate reading of the paper's bar chart), though not for cocaine, after adjustment for current age, and arrived with similar drug and alcohol severity; the authors say their observations suggest an accelerated progression to treatment entry that probably reflects a telescoped course (Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004). Outside treatment, in a US general-population survey (NESARC 2001–2002), among the 2,080 men and 1,217 women who had ever had a cannabis use disorder, the recalled time from first use to the disorder was shorter in women (2.24 against 2.64 years, p = 0.026), which the authors present as telescoping (Khan et al., 2013; a narrative review's citation for cannabis points to a different paper). A narrative review lists faster progression in women for alcohol, cannabis, cocaine (in people in the justice system) and prescription opioids (McHugh et al., 2018), and the same group's earlier review states faster progression to first treatment as established for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence (Greenfield et al., 2007). In the general-population alcohol surveys, among the people who did become dependent, women born 1964–1973 got there faster than men (on average 3.7 against 4.2 years), the printed figures suggest the same for women born 1954–1963 (5.5 against 6.4 years, not marked significant; an editors' approximation on the study card), and among people who were treated, women born 1934–1943 reached treatment sooner after dependence began (19.4 against 23.5 years) (Keyes et al., 2010).
debate.evidence_no: In the general-population analysis read for alcohol, two pooled US national surveys (1991–1992 and 2001–2002; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18 to 57), women started drinking later than men, but among the lifetime drinkers men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence in every birth cohort (1.36 to 1.79) and, among people with dependence, a higher hazard of first treatment (significant in two of five cohorts, 1.55 and 1.42), after adjustment for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink (and, by the table's footnote, age); the authors read the dependence hazards as men progressing faster, especially in younger cohorts. Among people who became dependent, the average time from first drink to dependence was about the same in women and men (5.6 against 5.8 years) and, in three of five cohorts, longer in women, not significantly; the authors conclude that telescoping is not evident in the general population (Keyes et al., 2010). A narrative review, following an earlier one, explains the gap between treatment samples and population surveys by who is sampled, since women who reach treatment likely have more severe disorders, and reports that telescoping was not found for heroin (McHugh et al., 2018). The historical critique shows that the stages that define telescoping were drawn from the recalled histories of men in Alcoholics Anonymous (98 men analysed, 15 women's answers set aside), that the 1989 study was small and drawn from treatment and self-help settings, and that 75 of 103 papers citing it used it as background without testing it; it argues that, with women as the reference group, men's longer course might have been called magnification, and recommends discarding the term (Marks & Clark, 2018). Read in full, the two studies most cited for the yes side show less than their citations suggest. In the treatment sample, gender explained 1% to 4% of the variance, the differences were small or absent in the youngest fifth of participants, women reached their worst period of drinking at the same age as men (35.2 against 35.0 years), and both sexes entered the trial at about the same age in the full sample; entry ages were not reported for the first-treatment subgroup, so a later start explains its shorter treatment interval only if those entry ages were also similar (Randall et al., 1999). In the cannabis survey, women and men had started cannabis at the same age (16.73 against 16.71 years) and developed the disorder at similar ages (18.98 against 19.34 years, not significant); the 0.40-year difference was not adjusted for age although the women were younger, describes only people who developed the disorder, and appears in the critique as 2.5 years (Khan et al., 2013; Marks & Clark, 2018). In the second treatment sample, the interval ran to the current treatment, which for some patients was not their first; 362 of 855 consecutive patients took part; cocaine showed no difference; the means appear only as bars; and the shorter intervals are hard to reconcile with the paper's report that women and men began regular use at similar ages, since both kinds of comparison were made at the same current age, unless the interval analyses used other covariates (Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004).
debate.neither_can_show: Every timing in these studies was recalled, often decades later, at a single interview or in a questionnaire; none was recorded as it happened, and no study read tested whether women and men remember timing differently (the surveys' recall check, which the authors read as showing limited recall bias, tested only whether dependence beginning at 25 or later was reported less often by members of the same birth cohorts interviewed 10 years later; Keyes et al., 2010). Treatment samples time only people who reached treatment, so a group that reaches treatment soon after its problems begin will look fast whatever its course in the population, and when women and men are recruited at treatment entry at similar ages, a later start in women by itself shortens every interval that ends at treatment (as in Randall et al., 1999); an interval that ends at the current treatment also depends on earlier treatment histories (Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004). Comparisons restricted to people who developed a disorder, as in the cannabis survey, show speed among them, not who develops it (Khan et al., 2013). In the general-population surveys, hazards among all drinkers combine the chance of ever becoming dependent with the speed of getting there, so on their own they cannot say who is faster; the averages among people who became dependent come closer to speed but are unadjusted and depend on age at interview, and the youngest cohort, interviewed only as young adults, could contribute only early steps (Keyes et al., 2010). People who died before the surveys, or were older than 57, are missing. None of these designs separates sex (biology) from gender (roles, access to treatment, stigma), which the critique asks studies to be designed from the outset to test (Marks & Clark, 2018); the general-population evidence read is for alcohol and cannabis in the USA only.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The faster course in women was described mostly in treatment and self-help samples, from recalled ages (Marks & Clark, 2018; McHugh et al., 2018), and the idea grew out of stage models built from men's recalled histories (Marks & Clark, 2018). In the general-population survey read for alcohol in the USA (Keyes et al., 2010), women were less likely than men to become dependent and, once dependent, had a lower hazard of reaching treatment (significantly in two of five birth cohorts), and those who did become dependent got there about as fast as men on average, faster in one birth cohort; the authors read the same data as men progressing faster, a reading that rests on hazards that mix the chance of dependence with its speed and on an interaction whose estimates are not shown. So the evidence read here does not show that women in general move faster from first use to dependence; whether women who do develop dependence move faster, and whether this holds for other drugs, is open. Read in full, the two studies that bear most directly on the yes side show less than their citations suggest: in the alcohol treatment sample, women's shorter recalled intervals were small overall, small or absent in the youngest participants, and may partly reflect a later start if the first-treatment subgroup, whose entry ages were not reported by sex, also entered at similar ages (Randall et al., 1999); in the cannabis survey, the difference was 0.40 years among people who had developed the disorder, unadjusted for age, with no difference in the age at first use or at onset of the disorder, not the 2.5 years a critique reports (Khan et al., 2013; Marks & Clark, 2018). A third study read in full, a second treatment sample, points the same way for opioids, cannabis and alcohol but not cocaine, measures the time to the current rather than the first treatment, and reports shorter intervals alongside similar ages at the start of regular use, which is hard to reconcile at the same current age (Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004).
debate.what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young women and men followed from before first use, with use, dependence criteria and treatment recorded as they happen (repeated interviews or linked records), as the authors of a treatment-sample study also call for (Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004), analysed with methods that separate the chance of ever becoming dependent from the speed of progression among those who do (for example mixture-cure or competing-risks models), with sex (including hormonal status) and gender (roles, access to treatment) measured separately and the study designed from the outset to compare them (Marks & Clark, 2018); and a systematic review of telescoping studies, drug by drug, that separates treatment from general-population samples and recalled from prospectively recorded timing.

statement: In US national household surveys, women with alcohol dependence compared with men with alcohol dependence were less likely, or slower, to reach alcohol treatment in the years after their problems began, while for drug use disorders, and for treatment in the past year, no gender difference was described; treatment was uncommon for both. Some studies described by a review found that the women who did reach treatment got there sooner after first use or onset, which concerns speed among people treated, not who gets treatment. In two pooled general-population surveys (NLAES, 1991–1992, and NESARC, 2001–2002; 8,564 US-born adults aged 18 to 57 with alcohol dependence, not counting 258 first treated before dependence began; ages at onset and at first treatment recalled at a single interview), the hazard of first alcohol treatment was higher in men than in women in all five birth cohorts, significantly in people born 1954–1963 (hazard ratio 1.42, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.73) and 1964–1973 (1.55, 1.22 to 1.96), with intervals including no difference in the other three, and over all cohorts together the difference was significant (F = 22.7, p < 0.001); the models adjusted for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink, and, according to the table's footnote though not the Methods, for age; about a quarter (24.6%) of people with dependence had ever had any alcohol treatment; among people who were treated, women born 1934–1943 reached treatment sooner after dependence began (19.4 against 23.5 years) (Keyes et al., 2010). As described by a narrative review, an earlier analysis of the 1991–1992 survey (Dawson, 1996; 7,359 people with alcohol abuse or dependence; onset and treatment reported after the fact; adjustment not described) found that 23% of men and 15.1% of women had ever been treated (counting a doctor, counsellor, Alcoholics Anonymous, another professional or a treatment facility), with no gender difference in the first 8 years after onset, men 13% to 20% more likely to start treatment between 8 and 25 years after onset, and no difference among the most severely dependent; past-year alcohol treatment among people with alcohol dependence was 12.5% in women and 12.1% in men in a 1999 household survey, and gender was not associated with past-year use of substance use services in the 2002 national survey (Greenfield et al., 2007, second-hand). Women were a smaller share of people in US alcohol treatment than of people with alcohol use disorders (men to women 3.3 to 1 in treatment facilities against 2.7 to 1 in the population in 1991), and women with drinking problems more often sought help in mental-health and other non-specialist services; barriers described for women include childcare, pregnancy and fear of losing custody or of prosecution, stigma and co-occurring mental-health problems (Greenfield et al., 2007). A later review reports, from the 2015 national survey, that 10.4% of women and 11.1% of men who needed treatment for an alcohol or drug use disorder received it, that under-treatment was most marked among women with alcohol use disorder, that gender was not associated with past-year treatment use for illicit drug use disorders, and that some studies found women reached treatment sooner after first use and after onset; it adds that women with alcohol use disorder more often named stigma as a barrier in two population surveys, while other surveys found few gender differences in barriers, perhaps because they did not ask about pregnancy, childcare or family attitudes (McHugh et al., 2018, second-hand). The two analyses of the 1991–1992 survey share data and are not independent; all timing and treatment were self-reported, years later; 'treatment' was defined differently across studies; and the figures are from the USA. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team (two analyses that share a survey).
plain: Are women less likely than men to get treatment? For alcohol, somewhat. In US surveys, men with alcohol dependence reached treatment more often or sooner than women in some age groups. In one 1992 survey, as a review describes it, 23 in 100 men and 15 in 100 women with alcohol problems had ever been treated, and the gap appeared only 8 or more years after the problems began. Some studies found that the women who did get treatment got there sooner after their problems began. For drug problems, and for treatment in the past year, the reviews describe no difference. In 2015, about 10 in 100 women and 11 in 100 men who needed treatment for alcohol or drugs got it. Women more often went to mental-health services. Reviews list barriers such as childcare and fear of losing custody, but several surveys found few differences between women and men in the barriers they named, apart from stigma. People reported all of this themselves, years later, and the figures are from the US.
population: US adults with alcohol dependence in national household surveys (NLAES 1991–1992 and NESARC 2001–2002 pooled; 8,564 US-born, aged 18 to 57) or with alcohol abuse or dependence (NLAES, as described); for drug use disorders and for 2015, US national surveys as described in two narrative reviews
exposure: Being a woman
comparator: Men with the same disorders in the same surveys
outcome: Ever receiving treatment, time to first treatment, and treatment in the past year (self-reported)
magnitude: Keyes et al. (2010), hazard of first alcohol treatment among people with dependence, men vs women (Cox, adjusted; age is listed among the controls in Table 2 but said in the Methods to have been dropped; 258 people first treated before dependence began excluded; pooled gender effect F = 22.7, p < 0.001): born 1974–1983 1.16 (95% CI 0.77–1.76), 1964–1973 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1954–1963 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1944–1953 1.20 (0.91–1.58), 1934–1943 1.38 (0.84–2.26); 24.6% of people with dependence ever treated (possibly weighted; 3,056 of 8,564 unweighted, about 36%, editors' arithmetic on the study card); among people treated, born 1934–1943, mean time from dependence to first treatment women 19.4 vs men 23.5 years. Second-hand: NLAES 1992 (Dawson, 1996), ever treated men 23% vs women 15.1%, cumulative probability by 30 years after onset .424 vs .356, no difference up to 8 years, men 13–20% more likely between 8 and 25 years, men-to-women ratio 1.75:1 with one symptom and 1.24:1 with 15 symptoms; past-year alcohol treatment among people with alcohol dependence (1999 household survey, 32,628 people) women 12.5% vs men 12.1%; men to women in US alcohol treatment 3.3:1 against 2.7:1 for alcohol use disorders in the population (1991), and 2.3:1 in facilities (2002) against 1.9:1 for past-year alcohol dependence and 1.5:1 for illicit drug dependence (2003) (Greenfield et al., 2007); 2015 national survey, treatment received among people needing it, women 10.4% vs men 11.1%; some studies find women reach treatment sooner after first use and after onset (no figures given) (McHugh et al., 2018).

risk_of_bias.note: Ages at onset and at first treatment were recalled at a single interview and 'treatment' is not defined (card sc_keyes_2010: JBI, moderate; analysed numbers and some table values disagree, and whether age was adjusted for is stated inconsistently); the 1992 lifetime figures and the past-year figures are known only from narrative reviews that did not appraise them (cards sc_greenfield_2007, sc_mchugh_2018).

inconsistency.note: The figures differ by time window in the way the review describes: lifetime treatment differs from about 8 years after onset, while past-year treatment and drug use disorders show no difference; an offered explanation, not a conflict. Studies that time only people who reached treatment, some of which found women sooner (as described), measure speed among people treated, a different quantity from the hazards and lifetime shares.

indirectness.note: The primary data read are for alcohol dependence in the USA in 1991–2002; everything for drug use disorders and for 2015 is second-hand (narrative reviews; METHODS §6.3).

imprecision.note: Large national samples; three of the five cohort hazard ratios include no difference, which the claim states.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to national surveys.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: very low. Counted once: Keyes et al. pooled the 1991–1992 survey that Dawson (1996) analysed, so the two lifetime findings share data (status replicated by the same team: shared sample, METHODS §6.4); the 2015 figures come from a review by the group that wrote the 2007 review. The hazard ratios among people with dependence mix the chance of ever reaching treatment with how soon, so the claim says less likely, or slower; among people who were treated, women reached treatment sooner in one cohort, and a review describes some studies in which women reached treatment sooner after first use and onset; that is about speed among people treated, not about who gets treatment. The size of the gap depends on the time since onset and on what counts as treatment, as the reviews say.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether women and men who enter treatment for alcohol or other drug use disorders differ in how long they stay or how well they do: as summarized by two narrative reviews from one research group, most large studies found no gender difference in retention, completion or outcome; where differences appeared, the 2007 review found that they generally favoured women, while most of the differences the 2018 update lists, for quitting smoking and for particular medicines, went against women; the reviews' figures are second-hand. A review of 280 articles published from 1975 to 2005 (11.8% of them randomized trials; the studies were not appraised) describes large multi-programme data sets with very few gender differences in retention (among 10,010 patients in 96 programmes, men were 20% less likely than women to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care; in a national study of 4,689 adults, gender was not associated with completion after adjustment), small clinical studies that disagreed (five found women more likely to drop out, two less likely), and outcome studies that mostly found no difference and, where they found one, mostly favoured women (in one study of older adults in outpatient alcohol treatment, 79.3% of women and 54% of men were abstinent at 6 months, a difference that disappeared after adjustment for length of stay, although the women still reported no heavy-drinking days in the past month against an average of four among the men) (Greenfield et al., 2007). The group's 2018 update describes no gender difference in outcome in large randomized trials (COMBINE, 1,226 people with alcohol dependence, 31% women; a prescription-opioid trial, 653 people, 40% women), none in retention across 24 NIDA Clinical Trials Network trials (more than 11,000 people), and none in completion across more than 1.7 million US treatment episodes, except that women less often completed detoxification; behavioural treatments and mutual-help groups showed no clear difference between women and men. The exceptions it lists mostly go against women: worse results in quitting smoking, nicotine replacement working better in men, and worse responses in women to disulfiram for cocaine dependence and to buspirone for cannabis and cocaine dependence (where buspirone did no better than placebo in either sex); one smoking medicine, varenicline, worked better in women in one meta-analysis and gave women more benefit than other aids in another, naltrexone findings for alcohol were mixed, and the effect of disulfiram for alcohol dependence in women is unknown because women were, for example, 1.2% of trial participants (McHugh et al., 2018). Comparisons of women-only with mixed-gender treatment were few and mixed. Of the randomized comparisons described in the 2007 review, one found no difference in early dropout, one found better retention in a women-only day programme, and in the one that compared alcohol and drug outcomes the women-only day programme did not differ from two community mixed-gender programmes and had lower abstinence than a hospital programme that cost twice as much per week; the review, relaying the conclusion of that trial's authors, says that women may be equally well served by good programmes of either kind and that changing a programme to women-only does not by itself change outcomes (Greenfield et al., 2007). The 2018 update describes comparisons in which women in women-only programmes did better (across 43 programmes, despite greater severity; and on later crime and incarceration, designs not described), randomized trials it cites as supporting programmes designed for particular groups of women (women with children, with co-occurring psychiatric disorders or in the criminal justice system), and two trials of the group's own women's group therapy: better than mixed-gender group counselling at 6 months in a small first trial, and as effective, not more, in a larger one (McHugh et al., 2018). These comparisons are between women and men who had already entered treatment; within trials, women and men were compared as subgroups, not assigned at random; outcomes were defined in many different ways; a non-significant difference is not evidence that outcomes are the same; and several of the analyses are the reviewers' own. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Once in treatment, do women do as well as men? Most large studies found no difference: women and men stayed in treatment about as long and had similar results. Where differences did appear, the older review found that women mostly did better, while the newer one listed more results in which women did worse, mainly in quitting smoking and with some medicines. Programmes for women only gave mixed results: in the one trial that compared results, a women-only programme showed no difference from two mixed ones and did less well than a costlier hospital programme, and some other studies favoured women-only programmes. All of this comes from two reviews by one research group, which did not check the quality of the studies, and finding no difference is not proof that results are the same.
population: Women and men who had entered treatment for alcohol or other drug use disorders, mostly in the USA, in studies described by two narrative reviews (1975–2005 and 2007–2017)
exposure: Being a woman (an observed characteristic, not assigned at random, even within trials)
comparator: Men in the same programmes or trials
outcome: Retention, completion and substance use outcomes, as each study defined them
magnitude: Second-hand, none pooled, mostly without intervals. Greenfield et al. (2007): 280 articles 1975–2005, 11.8% randomized trials; small clinical retention studies, five with more dropout in women, two with less, one mixed; 10,010 patients in 96 programmes, men 20% less likely to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care; 26,047 patients in 87 Los Angeles programmes, women more often completed where differences appeared; 4,689 adults (1,239 women), gender not associated with completion after adjustment; older adults, abstinence in the past 30 days at 6 months 79.3% of women vs 54% of men, not significant after adjustment for length of stay, heavy-drinking days in the past month none in women vs an average of four in men; randomized comparison of outcomes in women-only against mixed-gender day programmes, women-only no different from two community programmes, lower total abstinence than a hospital programme costing twice as much per week. McHugh et al. (2018): COMBINE (n = 1,226, 31% women) and a prescription-opioid trial (n = 653, 40% women), no gender difference in outcome; 24 Clinical Trials Network trials (n > 11,000), no difference in retention; more than 1.7 million treatment episodes, no difference in completion except detoxification (women less often); smoking cessation worse in women; nicotine replacement better in men; varenicline better in women in one meta-analysis and, in another of 32 trials (n = 14,389, 51% women), comparable against placebo with more benefit for women relative to other aids; disulfiram for cocaine dependence and buspirone for cannabis and cocaine dependence worse in women; naltrexone for alcohol mixed; women 1.2% of participants in the disulfiram trials for alcohol cited as an example; women in women-only programmes better on drug use across 43 programmes (observational).

risk_of_bias.note: Not appraisable: neither review appraised the studies it describes (cards sc_greenfield_2007: some concerns; sc_mchugh_2018: high); within trials, women and men are compared as subgroups, not by random assignment; several analyses are the reviewers' own.

inconsistency.note: The large studies agree on no difference in retention, completion and overall outcome. The differences found point both ways and differ by era and treatment (programmes and psychosocial treatment in the 2007 review, mostly favouring women where present; quitting smoking and particular medicines in the 2018 update, mostly against women), which the claim states; small clinical studies of retention split five to two against women.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: every anchor is a narrative review's account (METHODS §6.3); people who had entered treatment, mostly in US programmes; outcome definitions vary from 30-day abstinence to completion.

imprecision.note: Intervals are not given for most comparisons, so a non-significant difference cannot be shown to be small (METHODS §6.3, absence of evidence).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from two narrative reviews.

grade.reasoning: The studies described are mostly observational, and even in the trials gender is an observed subgroup, so the evidence starts low; down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision: very low, the floor. Rests only on narrative reviews: stays at draft, its figures are second-hand, and it is not for the at-a-glance box (METHODS §6.3). Counted once: McHugh et al. (2018) updates Greenfield et al. (2007) with the same search terms and authors. Status replicated: as described, several independent large data sets and trials (multi-programme data sets, the Alcohol and Drug Services Study, COMBINE, a prescription-opioid trial, 24 Clinical Trials Network trials, 1.7 million treatment episodes) agree on no difference in retention, completion and overall outcome; the specific differences point both ways and differ by era and treatment, which the claim states rather than summarizing them as favouring women; the relation is insufficient evidence because no difference was shown to be small.

statement: In people born from 1950 to 1993 and adopted in Sweden outside their biological family (adoptions by relatives or by a biological parent's partner excluded), with register information on both adoptive parents and at least one biological parent, both what was passed on from their biological parents and features of the adoptive home they grew up in were associated with a later register record of drug problems; the study estimated no heritability percentage. Of 18,115 adoptees followed in national registers to 2009 (a record meant a diagnosis of a drug use disorder or drug psychosis in hospital, outpatient, primary-care or death records; a conviction under two crime-register codes for crimes related to drug abuse, convictions only for alcohol-related crimes or only for drug trafficking or possession not counting; or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives, hypnotics or opioids; alcohol and tobacco excluded; the study calls this 'drug abuse'), 4.5% had a record, against 2.9% of everyone in Sweden born in the same years. Adoptees whose biological parent had a record, though they were not raised by that parent, had one in 8.6% of cases against 4.2% when neither biological parent had (odds ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.66 to 2.62), and in 11.9% when both had; records were also shared with biological siblings raised apart (full siblings, odds ratio 1.84, 1.28 to 2.64; half siblings, 1.41, 1.19 to 1.67). In the adoptive home, records were shared with adoptive siblings, who were not biologically related to the adoptee: 6.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees with a record had one, against 3.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees without (odds ratio 1.95, 1.43 to 2.65), and the adoptive mother's divorce and an adoptive parent's death were also associated with a record; adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with a record had one in 6.8% of cases against 4.5%, an imprecise estimate that included no difference (1.55, 0.86 to 2.80), with only 1.0% of adoptive parents affected. On the scale of absolute risk, an adverse adoptive home added more risk for adoptees whose biological relatives' records put them at higher risk, an interaction the paper does not report on the odds scale; at the lowest level of the biological-relative index the added risk could not be told apart from none (Kendler et al., 2012). An adoption study separates the family that passes on genes from the family that raises a child, but what passes from biological parents includes the pregnancy, care before placement (up to about 3 in 10 adoptees may have joined their adoptive family after age 5, by a census-based estimate) and how agencies matched children to homes (modest, by the authors' judgment), as well as genes. The authors report that children usually spent the time before placement in a nursery or foster home rather than with their biological parents, and that later placement did not go with a higher risk (odds ratio 0.96 per year before adjustment, 1.00 after); their argument against effects in the womb rests on 9.9% with an affected biological father against 8.2% with an affected mother, overlapping intervals without a test. As summarized, without figures, by a narrative review, twin studies find that genes and both shared and individual environment influence whether people start using tobacco, alcohol or cannabis, that genes matter more for regular use and dependence, and that the environment twins share is no longer detectable for regular use or dependence in adulthood though it is in adolescence (the adoptive-sibling association above, if it reflects the shared home, does not fit this summary well); single genetic variants have small effects that replicate poorly, scores combining many variants explained less than 1% of the variation in alcohol dependence, and the size of genetic influence has been reported to differ between environments (Prom-Wormley et al., 2017, second-hand). A heritability, where one is given, is a ratio: the share of the differences between people in one population, for a trait measured at a particular time or age, that goes with differences in their genes. It is therefore not the share of any one person's risk, or of a trait, that comes from genes; a high heritability does not mean that genes fix the outcome or that the environment cannot change it (human height has a heritability of about 0.8, yet average height has risen over generations); and it says nothing about why groups differ or why levels change over time. Because it depends on how much the genes and the environments vary, it can change when environments change, with age and with how the trait is measured, and in theory a figure from one population does not predict another, though the heritabilities of similar traits are often similar across populations; for a diagnosis, the figure is always smaller on the observed yes-or-no scale than on an assumed underlying scale of liability, and much smaller when the condition is rare (by the review's formula; editors' calculation); and the classical twin design estimates only three variance components and overstates heritability when identical twins share more of their environment than non-identical twins do, or when genes and environments are correlated (Visscher et al., 2008, a conceptual review by geneticists that discusses no drug-use figure). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Do genes and the home you grow up in shape drug problems? In a large Swedish study of adopted children, both were linked to drug problems. Children whose birth parent had a drug problem in official records had one themselves about twice as often (about 9 in 100, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did), even though other parents raised them. Drug problems were also shared within adoptive families, between children not related by birth: when an adopted child had one, about 6 in 100 of their adoptive brothers and sisters did too, against 3 in 100 when the adopted child did not. Divorce or a parent's death in the adoptive family also went with more drug problems. The study did not work out a percentage due to genes, and what comes from birth parents also includes the pregnancy and the time before adoption. A percentage due to genes, where studies give one, describes differences between people in one place and time; it does not say how much of one person's risk comes from genes, it does not mean that the environment cannot change things, and it can change when living conditions change.
population: People born 1950–1993 and adopted in Sweden outside their biological family (adoptions by relatives or by a biological parent's partner excluded), with register information on both adoptive parents and at least one biological parent, who first lived with their adoptive parents by age 10 by a census-based estimate (18,115 adoptees; national registers to 2009); twin studies summarized without figures by a narrative review
exposure: A register record of drug problems in biological parents or in biological siblings not raised with the adoptee (what passes from biological relatives: genes, pregnancy, care before placement), and in adoptive siblings or parents, or disruption of the adoptive home (the rearing environment)
comparator: Adoptees whose biological, or adoptive, relatives had no such record
outcome: A register record of drug problems (the study's 'drug abuse': drug use disorder or drug psychosis diagnoses; convictions under two crime-register codes for crimes related to drug abuse, with alcohol-only, trafficking and possession convictions excluded; or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives, hypnotics or opioids; alcohol and tobacco excluded)
magnitude: Kendler et al. (2012): adoptees with a record 4.5% (95% CI 4.2–4.8; 820 people) vs 2.9% nationally for the same birth years. Biological parent with vs without a record 8.6% vs 4.2%, OR 2.09 (1.66–2.62); none, one or both biological parents 4.2%, 8.2%, 11.9%; biological father 9.9% (7.2–12.1), mother 8.2% (6.3–10.5). Biological full siblings raised apart, record in 10.7% of the full siblings of adoptees with a record vs 6.1% of those of adoptees without, OR 1.84 (1.28–2.64); half siblings 7.4% vs 5.3%, OR 1.41 (1.19–1.67). Adoptive siblings of adoptees with vs without a record 6.2% vs 3.2%, OR 1.95 (1.43–2.65); adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with vs without a record 6.8% vs 4.5%, OR 1.55 (0.86–2.80). Multivariable: adoptive mother's divorce OR 1.31 (1.03–1.68), adoptive parent's death 1.37 (1.08–1.73). Interaction on the probability scale 0.0005 per decile × decile (0.0001–0.0008): each decile of the adoptive-home index added about 0.15 percentage points of risk at the lowest decile of the biological-relative index (the main effect with the interaction term, 0.0015, −0.0006 to 0.0036, an interval that includes no added risk) and about 0.6 at the highest (editors' calculation on the study card, recomputed with deciles coded 0 to 9). Later placement: odds ratio 0.96 per year before adjustment, 1.00 after. No heritability estimated. As summarized by Prom-Wormley et al. (2017): polygenic scores explained less than 1% of the variance in alcohol dependence; no twin heritability figure for any drug use disorder is given.

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the associations as worded (card sc_kendler_2012: ROBINS-E, some concerns): the national adoption design and a register outcome recorded independently of the study make the familial associations unlikely to be artefacts; the remaining concerns (pregnancy and care before placement, selective placement) bear on what the biological-parent association means, which the claim states, rather than on whether it exists. Families with criminal or psychiatric records may be more visible to police and services, which could inflate some associations.

inconsistency.note: One study; the biological and adoptive associations are consistent across kinds of relative.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: Swedish adoptees born 1950–1993 with a biological parent in the registers (the paper does not say 'born in Sweden' or 'domestic adoptions') and a broad register construct, both stated; the gap to diagnosed use disorders, to other countries and to later cohorts is stated, not assumed away.

imprecision.note: Large cohort; the adoptive-parent estimate is imprecise (0.86 to 2.80), which the claim states; the sibling intervals may be too narrow if several siblings of one adoptee were counted as independent pairs (card reporting issue).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a single registry study.

grade.reasoning: Observational (a national register adoption cohort): starts low; not downgraded. Strict reading: counting the broad register outcome and the possibly too narrow sibling intervals as risk of bias would give very low. The gradient with the number of affected biological parents (4.2%, 8.2%, 11.9%) is not used as a dose–response upgrade: it concerns the biological side only, cannot separate genes from the pregnancy and care before placement, and the claim's weaker link, the adoptive home, shows no gradient (the adoptive-parent estimate is imprecise). No heritability percentage was estimated, the extreme-decile odds ratios in the paper overstate the contrast by one step and are not used (card reporting issue), and the gene-environment interaction holds on the probability scale only as reported, with the added risk at the lowest biological-relative level not distinguishable from none. The narrative review gives no figures for drug use disorders and is used for context only (second-hand). What a heritability does and does not mean now rests on Visscher et al. (2008), a conceptual narrative review by quantitative geneticists, used for definitions only: it discusses no drug-use figure, its numerical examples (height, IQ, livestock, schizophrenia and depression) are second-hand illustrations, two of its worked examples do not match its own formulas (card reporting issues), and it does not change the rating. Status single study.

statement: In one pre-registered online experiment with adults who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative, the words used to describe a person's difficulty changed some of the attitudes readers reported, but not others, and changed what they did in a pretend money task only slightly. 1,613 adults (largest age group 18 to 25; 55.9% women; 77.1% White; recruited through university research-participation schemes, Prolific and social media; country of residence not stated) were each randomly assigned to read one short story about a person called Alex. When Alex's serious trouble at home and work was said to come from increasing drug use rather than from a health concern (819 against 741 readers), readers reported wanting more social distance from Alex (standardized difference d 0.87), saw Alex as more dangerous (d 0.78) and gave higher public-stigma scores (d 0.95; means 50.6 against 42.2): two of these differences are large by the usual standard and the third (danger) is just below it. They agreed less that the condition had genetic or disease causes (d −0.35), and their hope for Alex's recovery was the same within the study's equivalence bounds (d −0.06). In a pretend task in which readers could give or take small sums of money for Alex's answers, readers of the drug-use story took slightly more money (62.05 against 53.96 pence; d 0.14, interval 0.02 to 0.26), a difference the study could not show to be larger than its 0.20 threshold for a meaningful effect, and gave the same amount within the equivalence bounds (d −0.03). Among readers of the drug-use story, calling the condition a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than a 'problem' (392 against 423) made readers agree more that it had genetic or disease causes (d 0.54; the study calls this subscale blame). With the brain-disease label, social distance (d −0.20, interval −0.36 to −0.03) and public stigma (−0.18, −0.34 to −0.02) were slightly lower, and the differences in danger (−0.11) and hope (−0.07) were smaller; all four were inconclusive, so the study could not tell whether any of them was more than trivial, and the label did not reliably change the money given or taken. Framing Alex's treatment as likely to succeed rather than uncertain (the two versions also differed in whether Alex was in a treatment programme or had seen a doctor) gave inconclusive differences on every attitude measure and on money given, and the same money taken (Pennington et al., 2023). The study measured attitudes reported after one made-up story, not how people who use drugs are actually treated by the public, health workers or services; people with a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis, or a close relative with one, could not take part; in the drug-use version four questionnaire items named opioids, so that comparison changed the questions as well as the story; the intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals; and it did not compare person-first words with labels for the person. Words for the person were tested in one earlier, smaller experiment: of 728 people at talks on substance use at two mental-health conferences in 2008 (location not stated), described by the authors as mental health care providers, 516 (mean age 51; 64.5% with a doctoral-level degree; 34.8% with a professional focus on alcohol or drug problems) completed one of two versions of a story about a man in court-ordered treatment who had positive drug and breath tests; those whose version called him 'a substance abuser' agreed slightly more with a mixed set of statements about blame, punishment, expected violence and religious or other non-medical responses than those whose version said he had 'a substance use disorder' (2.92 against 2.82 on a 1–6 scale; d about 0.2), and did not differ detectably in willingness to have him as an employee, neighbour, co-worker or friend, or in statements about treatment and biological causes (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010). That study calls itself randomized, but the two versions were handed out alternately; 29% of those handed a form did not complete it; its printed p = .02 matches an unstated one-sided test (two-sided about .04, above the authors' own threshold of .025); and it could not rule out differences of about the same size in social contact or in the treatment and biological-cause statements. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Do words about drug use change how others see a person? In one experiment, 1,613 adults online each read one short story about a person called Alex, with the wording chosen at random. When Alex's trouble was said to come from drug use rather than a health concern, readers clearly wanted to keep more distance from Alex, saw Alex as more dangerous and gave higher stigma scores. In a pretend money task they also took slightly more money from Alex, a small difference the study could not call meaningful. Calling it a 'brain disease' instead of a 'problem' made readers think more that it came from genes or illness. Readers also kept slightly less distance, but the study could not tell whether this or the label's other effects mattered. Readers rated a made-up story; people with a drug or mental health diagnosis, or a close relative with one, could not take part; and the study did not test words for the person, such as person-first words. An older, smaller study did: about 500 mental health workers at two conferences agreed slightly more that a man deserved blame and punishment when he was called 'a substance abuser' than when he was said to have 'a substance use disorder', a small difference that may not be reliable.
population: Adults recruited online (university research-participation schemes, Prolific, social media; country of residence not stated; largest age group 18–25) who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative; 1,613 randomized; and 516 attendees of talks on substance use at two mental-health conferences in 2008, described by the authors as mental health care providers (mean age 51; 64.5% with doctoral-level degrees; 34.8% with a professional focus on alcohol or drug problems; Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010)
exposure: Reading a short story in which a person's difficulty was described as drug use (against a health concern); within the drug-use story, as a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' (against a 'problem'); and treatment framed as likely to succeed, with Alex in a treatment programme (against uncertain, with Alex having seen a doctor); in the second study, a man in court-ordered treatment described as 'a substance abuser' (against as having 'a substance use disorder')
comparator: Readers assigned to the other wording (at random in the pre-registered study; by alternation of the forms in Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010)
outcome: Self-reported social distance, perceived danger, hope for recovery, genetic or disease attribution (the study's blame subscale), need for continued care and public stigma; rewards and punishments in a pretend money task; agreement with a mixed set of blame, punishment, expected-violence and non-medical statements, willingness for social contact, and treatment and biological-cause statements (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010)
magnitude: Pennington et al. (2023), Cohen's d with intervals printed as 99% that match 98% intervals (card reporting issue): drug use vs health concern (819 vs 741): social distance 0.87 (0.74 to 0.99), perceived danger 0.78 (0.66 to 0.90), public stigma 0.95 (0.82 to 1.07; means 50.59 vs 42.15), blame subscale (genetic or disease attribution) −0.35 (−0.47 to −0.23), all meaningful by the study's rule; prognostic optimism −0.06 (equivalent); continued care 0.09 (inconclusive); reward −0.03 (equivalent; 248.11 vs 249.72 pence); punishment 0.14 (0.02 to 0.26; inconclusive: the interval does not include zero but reaches below the 0.20 bound; 62.05 vs 53.96 pence). 'Chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem' (392 vs 423, drug-use arm): blame subscale 0.54 (0.38 to 0.71; means 8.61 vs 7.22), meaningful; continued care 0.01 (equivalent); social distance −0.20 (−0.36 to −0.03), prognostic optimism −0.07, danger −0.11, public stigma −0.18 (−0.34 to −0.02; means 49.62 vs 51.20) and reward 0.15, all inconclusive; punishment 0.007 (equivalent). Treatment framed as likely to succeed vs uncertain (383 vs 362): every self-report measure and reward inconclusive (for example public stigma 0.31, 0.14 to 0.48, higher with the uncertain framing), punishment equivalent. Detectable equivalence bounds ±0.28 and ±0.30 for the label and treatment comparisons. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), label version vs 'substance use disorder' version: 'perpetrator-punishment' subscale 2.92 (SD 0.57) vs 2.82 (SD 0.58) on a 1–6 scale, t = 2.05, 504 df, p printed as .02 (one-sided by the editors' calculation; two-sided about .041), d printed as 0.20 (about 0.17 to 0.18 recomputed; approximate 95% CI 0.01 to 0.36, editors' calculation); 'social threat' (willingness for social contact) and 'victim-treatment' (treatment, genetic and chemical-imbalance causes, severity) subscales, no difference (ps > .59).
