risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2, some concerns (card sc_pennington_2023): people who failed a manipulation check were left out of that analysis (3.3% to 12%, not given by condition); attitudes reported right after an explicit story are open to demand effects; for the drug-use against health-concern comparison the questionnaire wording also differed (four items named opioids).

inconsistency.note: One study. The authors say two earlier vignette studies agree that drug problems are among the most stigmatized conditions, but as the paper describes them only Rundle et al. (2021) compared a substance use disorder with other conditions; Kelly et al. (2021) had no comparison condition. The two disagree on the brain-disease label, partly because they used different measures.

indirectness.note: A young online convenience sample without substance use or psychiatric diagnoses in themselves or close relatives, one hypothetical story, and self-reported attitudes and a pretend money task instead of how people who use drugs are treated; the words tested describe the condition, not the person; the one comparison of a label for the person with person-first wording (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010) used one story about a man under court supervision and attendees of talks on substance use at mental-health conferences, mostly doctoral-level.

imprecision.note: The drug-use contrasts are precise (for example d 0.87, 0.74 to 0.99); the label effects that are inconclusive are stated as such, not as no effect.

publication_bias.note: Registered report accepted before the results; all outcomes reported.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. The verb increases rests on random assignment within the experiment; the rating concerns how far the result carries to other people, other words and real treatment. The intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals (all 24, recomputed from Table 1) and one p value is printed as below .01 when it is about .011 (card reporting issues); the study's classifications do not change. Three differences classed as inconclusive have printed intervals that do not include zero (money taken with the drug-use story; social distance and public stigma with the brain-disease label; at 99% the public-stigma interval would reach zero), and the statement gives them as small differences rather than as no change. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), now read, adds the comparison of a label for the person with person-first wording, in one story and one sample of conference attendees: allocation by alternation and 29% non-completion give it a high risk of bias (card sc_kelly_2010: RoB 2 high), its small difference (d about 0.2, approximate 95% CI 0.01 to 0.36, editors' calculation) relies on an unstated one-sided test, and taken alone it would be rated very low; the displayed rating is set by the pre-registered study. Each contrast rests on one study and neither repeats the other, so the status stays single study. Status single study.

statement: Official records can miss a death altogether, or count it as a drug poisoning without identifying a particular drug. These are different gaps: the US statistical corrections described here address missing drug categories within deaths already counted as drug poisonings, not deaths missing from the overall overdose total. Comparisons in Sweden and New Mexico also found records that met one source's definition but not the other's, in both directions; the size and meaning of a gap depend on place, years and the reference used. In US coded death records for 1999–2015, 23.1% of 568,699 drug poisoning deaths of all intents had only unspecified-drug coding (26.0% in 2008, 17.2% in 2015; Ruhm, 2018). In overlapping national records, 97,159 of 438,607 unintentional overdose deaths had only unspecified-drug coding (22%; Buchanich et al., 2018), and 9,429 of 38,329 overdose deaths in 2010 had only that code (Slavova et al., 2015). These records do not establish which deaths had toxicology or whether an individual drug was absent from the original certificate text. By 2023, the share without a drug or drug-class code was 4.0%, down from 12.3% in 2017 (Garnett et al., 2026, editors' arithmetic); identifying a drug class still need not identify an individual drug. Ruhm's model used deaths with a specified drug category to estimate opioid involvement among deaths with only unspecified drugs, conditional on demographic and other covariates. The paper reports opioid counts 21% to 35% higher by year, including 33,091 to an estimated 39,999 in 2015; the maximum from its table is 35.7% by editors' arithmetic, so the printed range is approximate (Ruhm, 2018). A simpler reallocation within each state and year added about 70,000 potential unintentional opioid-related deaths over 1999–2015, 5,662 in 2015 (editors' table sum), with Pennsylvania's estimated 2015 rate changing from 9.90 to 20.12 per 100,000 (Buchanich et al., 2018). Neither correction checked the added drug assignments against toxicology or case files, and each can only add opioid assignments. A scoping review's national range largely cites Ruhm analyses of overlapping national files, with different periods and methods, not independent national replications (Gutkind et al., 2025). Certificate-text searches can separate names that a broad code merges but cannot supply a drug never written down (Ossiander, 2014; Garnett et al., 2026). A review reports South Carolina's rate with prescription-type opioid codes rising from 4.7 to 9.3 per 100,000 between 2013 and 2014 as certificates listing specific drugs rose from 57.7% to 94.4% after a new name-collection process. The authors attribute this mainly to recording, citing personal correspondence, rather than separately measuring the contribution of changing drug exposure. The codes include synthetic opioids such as illicit fentanyl and do not show that a drug was prescribed (Slavova et al., 2019, second-hand). In Stockholm in 1985–1996, the certificate selection included 761 of 1,212 deaths in an individually assessed inventory. The inventory used a broad personal-history or illicit-drug definition, whatever the cause of death, including 151 hospital deaths, mainly HIV-related; a missing inventory case is therefore not automatically a missed drug poisoning. The certificate selection also held 419 deaths absent from the inventory, of which 30 were found to be inventory omissions. The authors described some other certificate-only deaths involving drowning, alcohol or medicines; they did not describe every remaining case. Totals were close despite roughly a third of cases differing in each direction, and the inventory itself was incomplete (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In New Mexico in 1995–1998, 37 deaths classified as poisonings by the medical investigator were coded as natural deaths in vital statistics, typically with poisoning only in Part II of the certificate. Conversely, 15 deaths treated as natural by the investigator had non-dependent drug-use coding in vital statistics. The explanation involving use or abuse wording is inferred from the paper's coding rule, not from presented text for all 15 certificates. This poisoning category includes alcohol and carbon monoxide as well as drugs; neither source was an independent reference standard (Landen et al., 2003). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, ONS counted a specific opioid when named in a cause-of-death field of the Record of Inquest. The voluntary NPSUM programme received reports from over 90% of coroners, but not every death. Among its heroin/morphine deaths, ambiguous causes with that opioid implicated by the consulting toxicologist accounted for 29% in 2011 and 36% in 2022 (endpoints, not the full range). Applying those shares to national counts without linking individual records gave 20,323 projected heroin/morphine deaths (95% interval 19,382–21,358), against 13,471 counted. Official counts were 61% to 68% of the projections across the opioids studied; 96.8% of programme opioid deaths had multiple drugs detected. The intervals cover sampling error in the programme's shares, not the assumption that its cases represent all deaths or the accuracy of causal attribution (Chen et al., 2025). Drug involvement is also different from a drug causing death. A death may appear under several drugs; in overlapping US records, at least 45% of unintentional opioid-coded deaths also had a non-opioid drug code, not necessarily a complete measure of multi-drug coding (Buchanich et al., 2018, editors' calculation). In England and Wales in 2000, researchers classified 802 of 1,037 accidental deaths reported by coroners to a drug-related register as direct overdose; that category was the default when recent drug use and no other explanation were recorded. Treating its 77% share as a ceiling would be the editors’ conditional interpretation, assuming the other classifications were correct, not the authors’ validated bound on true causes. Other classifications were acute physical events such as aspiration (74), toxicity with a medical condition (112), injuries (31) and acute infections (18). This was not a linked comparison with official overdose statistics (Webb et al., 2003). Definitions also exclude deaths: US overdose totals exclude chronic effects (Garnett et al., 2026), and Liverpool authors argue that definitions of the time excluded deaths from infections transmitted by injecting (Beynon et al., 2007, argument based on other studies). Non-opioid evidence is limited, not absent: a review reports larger gaps for cocaine and smaller ones for amphetamines in a Florida comparison of 2003–2017 (Gutkind et al., 2025, second-hand); the Swedish study also compares capture of deaths with amphetamine, cocaine or THC detected. Those are differences between sources, not validated rates of missed deaths caused by each drug. Most evidence here concerns historical US opioid records, not current counts everywhere. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do official counts miss drug deaths? Some deaths are left out of a list. Others are counted as overdoses, but the records do not say which drug was involved. In US records from 1999 to 2015, about 23 in 100 overdose deaths had only an unspecified-drug code. By 2023, about 4 in 100 had no drug or type-of-drug code. Models estimated more opioid involvement among deaths already counted as overdoses; they did not find deaths missing from the total, and their drug guesses were not checked against the case files. In Stockholm, two lists had similar totals but differed about which people belonged on them. One list also included deaths from other causes in people with a history of drug problems. In England and Wales, one estimate suggests the counts held about two thirds of deaths involving each opioid. It used a sample of reports without matching each death across the lists, so that estimate may be wrong. Most evidence concerns older US opioid deaths. There is no single missing-death rate for every drug and place.
population: Drug deaths in official death statistics: United States (national death records 1999–2015 and 2017–2023), the Stockholm area 1985–1996, New Mexico residents 1995–1998, England and Wales 2000 and 2011–2022, Washington State 2003–2010, Liverpool 2004–2005
exposure: Official counts built from death certificates and their ICD-10 codes, or from coroners' conclusions
comparator: Corrected counts (statistical imputation or reallocation of deaths naming no drug), an individually assessed inventory, the state medical investigator's records, a coroner-reported national register with toxicology (unlinked projection), or researchers' categorisation of register deaths
outcome: Drug deaths missing from, or wrongly included in, official counts, and the share of certificates naming no drug
magnitude: US unspecified-drug coding: 23.1% of 568,699 drug poisonings 1999–2015, 26.0% in 2008 and 17.2% in 2015 (Ruhm, 2018); 97,159/438,607 unintentional overdoses, 22.2% (Buchanich et al., 2018; editors' arithmetic); 9,429/38,329 overdoses in 2010, 24.6% (Slavova et al., 2015; editors' arithmetic). No drug or drug-class code: 12.3% in 2017, 4.0% in 2023 (Garnett et al., 2026; editors' subtraction). Model estimates, not added deaths in the all-drug total: Ruhm printed range 21–35% more opioid-involved deaths (Table 1 maximum 35.7%, editors' calculation); 2015, 33,091 to 39,999, no computed intervals. Buchanich reallocation about 70,000 potential opioid deaths 1999–2015, 5,662 in 2015 (editors' sum), Pennsylvania 9.90 to 20.12 per 100,000. Stockholm 1985–1996: 761/1,212 inventory deaths in the certificate selection, 419 certificate-only, 30 confirmed inventory omissions; inventory included 151 hospital deaths (Fugelstad et al., 2020). New Mexico 1995–1998, broad poisoning: 37 investigator poisonings coded natural, 15 investigator natural deaths coded non-dependent drug use (Landen et al., 2003). England/Wales 2011–2022 unlinked projections: heroin/morphine 13,471 counted versus 20,323 projected (95% interval 19,382–21,358); projections not counted 32.5% fentanyl to 39.1% methadone (editors' calculations). Intervals cover sampling error only (Chen et al., 2025). Register composition: direct overdose 802/1,037 (77.3%, editors’ calculation; a recorded default classification, not a validated upper bound on true causes), physical events 74, medical-condition groups 40+72=112 (editors' sum), injuries 31, infections 18 (Webb et al., 2003). Second-hand South Carolina rate 4.7 to 9.3 per 100,000 as named-drug certificates rose 57.7% to 94.4% (2013–2014; Slavova et al., 2019). Swedish presence-versus-certificate-selection capture, Table III period unstated: amphetamine 56%, cocaine 43%, THC 23%; not drug-specific causal miss rates (Fugelstad et al., 2020).

evidence.locator: Datasets and inventory definitions, Table I and Methods (pp. 3–4); Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory (p. 5); Discussion limitations and dataset differences (pp. 7–8)
evidence.extracted: Stockholm, 1985–1996: the inventory included deaths involving illicit drugs or non-prescribed morphine/methadone and deaths of people with a personal history of drug use problems, regardless of whether acute poisoning caused death. It contained 1,061 forensic and 151 hospital cases (1,212 total). NMR/Stockholm included 761 of the 1,212 inventory deaths and 734 of the 1,061 forensic cases. For the 151 hospital deaths, mainly in people with HIV who used drugs, the paper prints 28% captured; subtracting 734 from 761 gives 27, and 27/151 is 17.9%, so the printed percentage is not reconcilable from those counts. NMR/Stockholm also included 419 deaths absent from the inventory; 30 were confirmed inventory omissions, comprising 21 Stockholm residents who died elsewhere and nine administrative omissions. The paper describes 49 other deaths involving drowning, pharmaceutical drugs or alcohol, and seven with no cause found, without describing every remaining certificate-only death. The inventory is therefore neither complete nor an independent standard for true drug-caused deaths. Table I prints 1,181 NMR/Stockholm deaths, one more than 761+419=1,180. The paper also says Toxreg included 317 of 454 inventory deaths in 1994–1996, then says 43 of the 317 Toxreg cases were absent from the inventory because findings suggested medical treatment; these contradictory descriptions do not establish an unambiguous 317-overlap-plus-43 count. Independent arithmetic gives 1,212−761=451 inventory cases absent from NMR and 419−30=389 other NMR cases, but neither quantity is a validated number of missed or falsely attributed drug-poisoning deaths. Using inventory membership alone, 761/1,212=62.8% capture and 761/(761+419)=64.5% positive predictive value; the paper prints 64.5% as sensitivity and 62.8% as positive predictive value. These appear interchanged under those denominators, but the inconsistent totals and subsequent inventory omissions prevent treating the printed accuracy measures as validated causal accuracy estimates.

evidence.locator: Introduction, ONS cause-of-death fields (p. 1); Methods › Office for national statistics data, National programme on substance use mortality data and Data analysis, plus Results (p. 2); Fig. 1 and multiple-drug detection (p. 3); Table 1 and Strengths and weaknesses (pp. 3–4)
evidence.extracted: The National Programme on Substance Use Mortality (NPSUM) receives voluntary reports from over 90% of coroners in England and Wales, including causes of death and full toxicology reports. The consulting toxicologist evaluates detected substances for likely involvement; this is more than drug detection alone. For each opioid and year, the authors classified NPSUM cases according to whether that opioid was specifically named in a cause-of-death field or an ambiguous drug-related cause was given with the opioid implicated as causative by the consulting toxicologist. They divided ONS counts by the NPSUM named share to project national totals, without linking individual deaths. In 2011, 122 of 416 NPSUM heroin/morphine deaths had ambiguous causes (29.3%); the paper reports that 574 ONS deaths yielded a projected 813. Independent arithmetic using the exact printed counts gives 574/(294/416)=812.2 rather than 813, so 813 is retained as the paper’s reported estimate. In 2022, the paper reports 1,264 ONS deaths versus a projected 1,980 (36% of the projection uncounted). For 2011–2022, ONS count versus reported projection (rounded share of projection uncounted) was heroin/morphine 13,471 versus 20,323 (34%); methadone 5,752 versus 9,444 (39%); tramadol 2,455 versus 3,865 (36%); dihydrocodeine 1,201 versus 1,854 (35%); codeine 1,886 versus 2,859 (34%); fentanyl 599 versus 887 (32%). Multiple drugs were detected in 16,101 of 16,628 NPSUM opioid-related deaths (96.8%). The paper states that ONS identifies specific opioids from cause-of-death fields in the Record of Inquest; it does not explicitly describe searching or excluding a separate conclusion entry. Heroin and morphine are combined. Table 1 gives projected heroin/morphine 95% intervals of 813 (767–868) in 2011, 1,980 (1,894–2,074) in 2022 and 20,323 (19,382–21,358) over all years. The abstract instead gives 765–866 for 2011, and Results gives 1,895–2,075 for 2022; Table 1 values are used here. Applying the stated Wilson method to the printed 2011 NPSUM counts independently yields transformed endpoints 766.94–868.05, rounding to 767–868. Other annual NPSUM denominators and supplements were not supplied, so the 2022 and aggregate intervals were not independently regenerated. These intervals address sampling uncertainty in programme proportions, not representativeness, the unlinked projection or causal-attribution assumptions. Reports from over 90% of coroners do not imply complete case coverage, and the 29% and 36% endpoint shares do not give the full annual range.

evidence.locator: 2.1 The NP-SAD database and 2.2 Case identification (p. 68); 2.3 Case categorisation (pp. 68–69); 3.2 Causes of death (p. 69); Table 1 column headings (p. 70); final Discussion paragraph on negative findings (p. 73)
evidence.extracted: Among accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales to NP-SAD in 2000, two researchers independently identified and classified 1,037 cases, with a medical consultant confirming case identification and categories. Suicide verdicts, open verdicts with clear suicidal or homicidal intent, cases with no verdict and cases with insufficient information for a causal judgment were excluded. They classified 802 (77%) as direct acute overdose; other categories were traumatic accidents (31), toxicity with a non-drug-related medical condition (40), toxicity with a drug-related medical condition (72), acute infections (18), and acute non-traumatic physical events (74). In the last group, aspiration was mentioned in 42 direct-aspiration-asphyxia cases and 22 aspiration-pneumonia cases; not all 74 were aspiration deaths. Medical-condition and infection categories were separate from acute physical events. Independent arithmetic gives 802/1,037=77.3%, 40+72=112 medical-condition cases, and all six category counts sum to 1,037. Methods classified recent drug use with no evidence of another cause as accidental direct overdose by default. The authors do not call the 77% share an upper limit; that would be an editorial interpretation of their classification rule, not a reported finding or validated bound. The final Discussion says that when a substance was not reported it was unclear whether it was absent at post-mortem testing or had not been tested for, and that including negative findings would help. No linked comparison with official statistics or ICD-coded overdose totals was made. This describes classification within a broader drug-related register, not a measured false-positive rate for official overdose statistics.

risk_of_bias.note: The drug-category corrections assume, without validation against toxicology/case files, that unspecified deaths resemble specified deaths conditional on the chosen covariates or state/year (Ruhm and Buchanich cards: high). Chen is an unlinked projection, and its sampling intervals exclude representativeness and attribution assumptions (high). The Stockholm inventory uses a broader personal-history definition, is itself incomplete and contains inconsistent accuracy/count reporting (high); New Mexico has no independent reference (moderate). Differences between definitions are not automatically causal classification errors.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: studies consistently find incomplete drug attribution or disagreement between sources, while the comparisons that allow both directions also find cases included by only one source. Sizes concern different quantities and definitions; they are not one common missing-death rate.

indirectness.note: Question concerns official counts generally; most evidence is historical US opioid coding, with Stockholm 1985–1996, New Mexico 1995–1998 and England/Wales unlinked projections 2011–2022. US coding completeness improved by 2023. Non-opioid comparisons exist in the Swedish paper and second-hand Florida report, but do not establish validated causal miss rates for stimulants, cannabis or new psychoactive substances everywhere.

imprecision.note: Counts are large. Ruhm did not compute intervals; Chen did, but its Wilson intervals cover sampling error rather than the central model/representation assumptions. No extra downgrade beyond the methodological limitations already assigned under risk of bias.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to register comparisons.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim: starts low, never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); minus one risk of bias and one indirectness, floored at very low. Same-death comparisons in Stockholm and New Mexico describe discordance under different definitions in both directions, without an independent causal reference standard. US unspecified-code figures describe already-counted overdoses; corrected drug assignments are model estimates, not extra deaths in the total. Overlapping NVSS analyses and their summaries in Gutkind/Slavova reviews are counted once, not as independent replication. The reviews also supply explicitly second-hand Florida/composition context. Replicated describes the direction of incomplete attribution/source disagreement across independent settings, not a shared magnitude or proven true-cause error rate. Chen contributes a combined heroin/morphine projection, with sampling intervals and an untested representativeness assumption. Certainty and status unchanged; draft until independent checks.

statement: In the two studies read here that measured it, each at a single US centre, the cause expected or assigned without a full autopsy differed from the cause after it in a minority of deaths. At one centre, full autopsy with drug testing changed which deaths were put down to drugs in both directions: the autopsy found another cause in some deaths suspected to be drug deaths, and testing found drug deaths among deaths nobody suspected. At the other, pathologists given everything except the internal examination reached the autopsy pathologist's cause of death in most, but not all, of a selected set of deaths, and the study does not say in which direction they differed. Access to testing differs widely between US offices, and no study read here measured the effect on official counts. At a regional autopsy centre serving 33 counties of western North Carolina (population 2,354,038), which kept doing full autopsies on suspected drug deaths in 2016–2021 when other offices had moved to an external examination with toxicology, investigators suspected before autopsy that 2,719 of 2,956 adult deaths were drug-related, from drug equipment at the scene, a history of substance use disorder or earlier overdoses. After full autopsy and comprehensive toxicology, the assigned pathologist gave a cause unrelated to drugs in 265 of them (9.75%), for example a blood clot in the lungs, a burst stomach ulcer, a burst brain aneurysm with no stimulants in the body, or a bleed pressing on the brain in a homicide. Because the 265 include deaths whose toxicology found no drug, which an external examination with toxicology would presumably not have put down to drugs, 9.75% is an upper limit (editors' reading) for what such an examination would have put down to drugs wrongly, among the suspected deaths only; the paper does not give the split. In the other direction, toxicology showed a drug cause, with no significant findings at autopsy, in 115 of the 237 deaths not suspected (48.5%, editors' calculation). The assigned pathologist's conclusion was the yardstick, illicit drugs found were counted as at least contributing unless a catastrophic natural or traumatic cause was found, and intentional (suicidal) drug overdoses, deaths with obvious fatal injuries and people under 18 were left out. The authors also say that scene investigation, external examination and comprehensive toxicology gave a correct determination in a majority of cases, and they summarize another US study, not read here, in which toxicology found no drug and another cause was concluded in 11% to 13% of suspected drug deaths (Hancock et al., 2024). The other study read here, at the coroner/medical examiner office of Jefferson County, Alabama, took 60 deaths of 2017 from the 109 full autopsies by one pathologist that were left after homicides, suicides, undetermined deaths and accidents from vehicles, asphyxia, falls, fires, firearms and an envenomation were excluded; deaths with contributing factors were also excluded (number not given), and how the 60 were chosen is not stated: 38 were accidental drug-toxicity deaths and 22 natural deaths. Three other pathologists of the office, all co-authors, working separately from written accounts of the history and scene, the external examination and the toxicology, without internal-examination findings, matched the case file's cause of death in 71.6%, 66.6% and 80.0% of the 60 (mean 73%) and its manner of death in 85.0%, 70.0% and 85.0% (kappa against the case file 0.71, 0.46 and 0.69). They agreed with one another only moderately (kappa 0.53 to 0.61), so the design cannot say how much of the disagreement came from the missing internal examination rather than from differences between pathologists, and the paper does not report whether the disagreements would have added drug deaths or removed them. Its subgroup figures are printed for groups whose sizes do not fit the counts it gives (38 drug-toxicity and 22 natural deaths, or 43 with a drug history or paraphernalia and 17 without; only groups of 40 and 20 reproduce them, editors' check) and are not used here. The authors judge that the accuracy gained justifies full autopsy for their office and, in their view, the nation, without having set in advance what agreement would be enough (Dye et al., 2019). Hancock et al. (2024, p. 191) summarize this study as 75% to 80% correct on cause and manner; its results are 66.6% to 80.0% for cause and 70.0% to 85.0% for manner (Dye et al., 2019, p. 100), and 75% and 80% appear only in its Discussion, as what to expect when the investigation points to drug use, figures that cannot be traced to its results (p. 101). The National Association of Medical Examiners recommends an autopsy whenever intoxication is suspected (with possible deferral in selected delayed deaths after an overdose following review of hospital records) and comprehensive toxicology for eight kinds of death; it states that history, investigation and autopsy together are an insensitive guide to intoxication and that no peer-reviewed study has shown an external examination to be as accurate as an autopsy, and it cites one study of drug deaths, without a figure, for external examination being less accurate even when the scene strongly suggests an overdose (the Alabama study above, in which the position paper's first author was one of the three reviewing pathologists, and whose figures for such deaths are among those not used here); the position paper's figure of 20% to 30% wrong diagnoses without autopsy comes from general autopsy studies, some decades old, and a mortality data brief, not from studies of drug deaths (Davis et al., 2020, a position paper). Access to testing varies: in the 2018 census of US medical examiner and coroner offices, as the offices reported it, of 1,320 offices that answered, 82.6% had access to toxicology (5.9% in-house, 76.7% through outside laboratories), 11.2% said they had none and 6.2% that they did not need it (the authors note that some offices without access may have their deaths tested through an autopsy provider or a state office); 96.4% of offices serving 250,000 people or more had access, against 75.1% of those serving fewer than 25,000; a coroner or other non-physician was the role most often named as deciding which deaths were tested (by 64.7% of offices; more than one role could be named); and 53.9% of 1,326 offices used drug screening tests, 95.1% of 709 of these confirming them in a laboratory. These are shares of offices, not of deaths: the authors state that the number of suspected overdose deaths actually tested is not known (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025). In surveillance records of 55,430 drug poisoning deaths in nine US states in 2019–2021, a full or partial autopsy was recorded for about 67%, an opioid test for 79% and an alcohol test for 76%, with 'no' and 'unknown' counted together for the two tests (Lundberg et al., 2026). What is tested changes what is found: as a review reports, after routine testing for gabapentin began in Kentucky in July 2014, its share among drug overdose deaths rose from 2.9% in 2013 to 17% in 2014 (Slavova et al., 2019, second-hand), and a US consensus panel noted in 2013 that many immunoassays used for screening did not detect some opioids, such as oxycodone and hydromorphone, and that laboratories used no standard detection threshold (Goldberger et al., 2013). Of 48 of Kentucky's 120 elected coroners who answered a survey in 2016, after state laws of 2012 and 2015 required toxicology testing, 58% reported more toxicology testing requested and 35% reported more autopsies; these are the coroners' own reports, and no death records were examined (Quesinberry et al., 2019). In Norway in 2007–2009, deaths without an autopsy had higher odds of being counted by the cause-of-death register but not by the police register (adjusted odds ratio 2.66) (Amundsen, 2017), and in Stockholm a register built from forensic toxicology could not include deaths without a forensic examination, such as the 151 hospital deaths in a local reference inventory of drug deaths (Fugelstad et al., 2020). How often deaths certified without autopsy or testing are wrongly put down to drugs, or missed, has not been measured in official statistics. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do autopsies and drug tests change which deaths count as drug deaths? At one autopsy centre in North Carolina (2016 to 2021), investigators suspected that 2,719 deaths were drug deaths. After a full autopsy and drug tests, about 10 in 100 of them had another cause, such as a blood clot or a burst blood vessel in the brain. This is an upper limit for the suspected deaths, because it includes deaths where tests found no drug at all. Of 237 deaths nobody suspected, drug tests showed that about 49 in 100 were drug deaths. The authors say that most deaths would have been put down correctly from the scene, an outside examination of the body and full drug tests, without an autopsy. In a smaller study in Alabama, three doctors were told everything about 60 chosen deaths except what the autopsy found inside the body. Their cause of death matched the autopsy doctor's in 67 to 80 of every 100. They did not always agree with each other either, and the study does not say whether drug deaths would have been missed or added. Testing differs a lot: in 2018, about 11 in 100 US death investigation offices said they had no access to drug testing (some may send deaths elsewhere for testing), and small offices had it less often than big ones. Medical examiners' guidance says to do an autopsy whenever a drug death is suspected, but the error figure it gives comes mostly from autopsy studies of all kinds of deaths. This rests on two centres in two US states.
population: Adult deaths autopsied at one regional centre in western North Carolina, 2016–2021 (2,956, suicides and obvious injuries excluded); 60 selected accidental drug-toxicity and natural deaths autopsied at one Alabama office in 2017; US medical examiner and coroner offices in 2018 (1,320 answering); drug poisoning deaths in nine US states, 2019–2021; Kentucky's elected coroners in 2016
exposure: Full autopsy with comprehensive toxicology; access to and use of toxicology testing
comparator: Investigators' suspicion before autopsy (as a stand-in for external examination with toxicology); certification by other pathologists from the investigation, external examination and toxicology without internal-examination findings; offices without access to testing; testing before a change of practice
outcome: Deaths suspected to be drug deaths that full autopsy assigned to another cause, and unsuspected deaths found to be drug deaths; agreement between certification without and with internal-examination findings; how often testing is available and recorded
magnitude: North Carolina centre 2016–2021 (Hancock et al., 2024): suspected before autopsy 2,719 of 2,956; non-drug final cause in 265 (9.75%; editors' Wilson 95% interval 8.7% to 10.9%), an upper limit for external examination with toxicology among the suspected deaths only; not suspected 237, drug-related final cause shown by toxicology in 115 (48.5%, 42.2% to 54.9%, editors' calculation); printed sensitivity 95.52%, specificity 31.52%. Second-hand in the same paper (not read): 11% to 13% of suspected drug deaths with no drug found and another cause. Jefferson County, Alabama, 2017 (Dye et al., 2019): 60 selected deaths (38 accidental drug toxicity, 22 natural); three pathologists without internal-examination findings matched the case-file cause in 71.6%, 66.6% and 80.0% (43, 40 and 48 of 60; Wilson 95% intervals 59.2% to 81.5%, 54.1% to 77.3% and 68.2% to 88.2%, editors' calculation) and manner in 85.0%, 70.0% and 85.0% (kappa against the case file 0.71, 0.46 and 0.69); kappa between reviewers 0.54, 0.61 and 0.53; direction of disagreement not reported; subgroup figures not used (only groups of 40 and 20 reproduce them, not the 38/22 or 43/17 the paper describes; editors' check). risk_of_bias.note: The North Carolina comparison (card sc_hancock_2024: JBI moderate) uses the assigned pathologist's conclusion as the yardstick, which partly includes the investigation behind the suspicion and counts illicit drugs present as contributing, does not report how suspicion was classified or whether blind to the final cause, and mixes toxicology-negative deaths into its 265; the Alabama comparison (card sc_dye_2019: QUADAS-2 high) took 60 clear-cut deaths chosen by an unstated method and used as its reference the certification of one pathologist, who also designed the questions put to the reviewers; the census describes what offices reported, with misclassification the authors document (card sc_smiley_mcdonald_2025: moderate).

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: the two direct comparisons measure different things (suspicion before autopsy against the final cause in North Carolina; certification without internal-examination findings against the autopsy pathologist's in Alabama), so their sizes are not comparable, but both find that the cause expected or assigned without a full autopsy differed in a minority of deaths; the other sources describe testing practice and point the same way.

indirectness.note: Two US centres, adults only: in North Carolina a regional centre that kept full autopsies, with suicides and obvious injuries left out; in Alabama 60 selected accidental drug-toxicity and natural deaths, with written case accounts read in place of examining the body and toxicology available in every case. Testing access and practice from the US in 2018 and nine states in 2019–2021. Nothing measures the effect of autopsy or testing on national counts, or practice outside the US apart from two Nordic register notes.

imprecision.note: 2,956 deaths in North Carolina; the 9.75% has an editors' interval of 8.7% to 10.9%. The Alabama study's 60 deaths give each reviewer's agreement an interval of about 10 to 13 points either side (editors' calculation), which the claim reports as a range rather than a single figure; not downgraded.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim: starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: very low. The North Carolina series compares the same deaths before and after full autopsy and toxicology, the kind of comparison this question needs, and finds changes in both directions (another cause found at autopsy in suspected deaths; drug deaths found by testing among deaths not suspected); it is a single centre, and its 9.75% is an upper limit, among suspected deaths only, for what external examination with toxicology would misattribute. Papers of 12 November: the Alabama study (Dye et al., 2019), now read in the original, is a second, independent single-centre comparison, in which pathologists without internal-examination findings matched the autopsy pathologist's cause of death in 66.6% to 80.0% of 60 selected deaths; it cannot separate the missing internal examination from differences between pathologists, does not show direction, and its subgroup figures, which do not fit its group sizes, are not used. It leaves the certainty at very low, the lowest level. Status moves from single study to replicated: two independent centres find that the cause expected or assigned without a full autopsy differed in a minority of deaths, although they measure different comparisons and the finding that the differences run both ways rests on the North Carolina series alone. The figure Hancock et al. (2024) give second-hand for the Alabama study (75% to 80%) is replaced by its own results; the other study they summarize remains second-hand and is not counted. The position paper (Davis et al., 2020) is cited for its recommendations and the origin of its error figure, not as evidence of an error rate; the one drug-death study it cites is the Alabama study, in which its first author was a reviewer. The Kentucky survey records coroners' own reports; the gabapentin figure is second-hand from a review. Whether the type of official who investigates matters is a separate, contested answer.

statement: In one randomized online experiment with UK adults, details in a simulated news report of a drug death changed how much stigma readers said they felt towards the person who died, by small to moderate amounts, but hardly changed their stated support for harm-reduction policies. In June 2022, 1,248 adults on a UK online research panel (Prolific; mean age 45.7, 51.0% women) were each randomly assigned to read one of eight versions of a BBC-style news story about an inquest, adapted from a real BBC report of an ecstasy death in 2019; the versions differed in the person's gender (Jane or John), age together with use history (21 and had used the drug 'once or twice', or 43 and had used it regularly for 15 years) and drug (ecstasy or heroin). Stigma towards the person, on a new nine-item measure of blame, anger, pity, responsibility, control and wish for distance (range 9 to 81), was higher when the person was a man (mean 45.6 against 43.4 for a woman), when the person was older with long use (46.7 against 42.3) and when the drug was heroin (46.9 against 42.1): about 0.2, 0.4 and 0.4 standard deviations (editors' calculation), with the eight versions ranging from 38.6 (young woman, ecstasy) to 50.1 (older man, heroin). Support for six harm-reduction policies (such as drug checking, drug consumption rooms, take-home naloxone and opioid agonist treatment; range 6 to 30) was slightly higher after the older person's story (about 23.6 against 23.0, editors' calculation from the condition means, about 0.1 standard deviation; the paper prints the two means in reverse order), a difference seen in the ecstasy stories only (about 23.9 against 22.7, with none in the heroin stories, editors' calculation), and did not differ by drug or by gender. In exploratory, non-randomized analyses of 868 participants, stronger belief in a just world, less perspective-taking and more general stigma towards people with drug problems went with more stigma towards the person, and having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug death went with less (Sumnall et al., 2023). The study was not registered in advance, the stigma measure was new, the panel was matched to the UK population on sex, age and ethnicity only and over-represented people with degrees and people who prefer left-wing parties, the outcomes were self-reports measured once straight after one written story, and 'older' cannot be separated from 'longer use'. How real news coverage affects behaviour, policy or the people affected was not studied. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Does how the news describes a drug death change what readers think? In one UK study, 1,248 adults online each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random. Readers judged the person more harshly when the person who died was a man, was 43 and had used the drug for years rather than 21 and had used it once or twice, and when the drug was heroin rather than ecstasy. These were small to moderate differences. Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed. Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; the study did not look at what they did later, and it could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using drugs for longer.
population: UK adults on an online research panel (Prolific), June 2022; 1,248 randomized (mean age 45.7, 51.0% women; matched to the UK on sex, age and ethnicity)
exposure: Reading a simulated news report of a drug death in which the person who died was a man, was 43 with 15 years of regular use, or died after heroin
comparator: Versions of the same report in which the person was a woman, was 21 and had used the drug once or twice, or died after ecstasy (factorial randomization)
outcome: Self-reported stigma towards the person depicted (new nine-item measure) and stated support for six harm-reduction policies, measured once, straight after reading
magnitude: Sumnall et al. (2023), 2 × 2 × 2 factorial, n = 1,248 (degrees of freedom imply 1,238 analysed). evidence.extracted: The Results report higher harm-reduction support after the older rather than the younger person's story (F(1,1230)=4.5, p=.035), but print the means in the order 22.98 (SD 5.09) versus 23.57 (SD 4.78). A profile-plot discussion of the age-by-drug interaction describes higher support after the older rather than younger person in the ecstasy story, while printing F(1,1230)=4.8, p=.029 and means 22.7 (SD 5.4) versus 23.89 (SD 4.67). Independent editorial calculations using the rounded Table 1 cell summaries and header group sizes give harm-reduction means of 23.575 for older versus 22.974 for younger stories, 23.899 versus 22.652 within ecstasy stories, and 23.251 versus 23.299 within heroin stories. These support the authors' narrative direction and indicate that the two printed older-younger mean pairs are reversed. With a pooled within-cell SD of 4.927, approximate equal-marginal contrasts give F=4.63 for age, F=5.43 for age-by-drug and F=10.07 for age within ecstasy. The printed F=4.8 is therefore more consistent with the interaction than with the within-ecstasy age comparison in this reconstruction, but its exact identity cannot be established: the cell values are rounded, Table 1 header counts sum to 1248, and the reported residual degrees of freedom imply 1238 observations under the stated full eight-cell model. indirectness.note: An online panel matched to the UK on sex, age and ethnicity only, one simulated written story read once, and self-reported attitudes measured straight away, rather than real news, other countries or what readers did later.

imprecision.note: 1,248 randomized; the main stigma differences are clear (F 11.1 to 50.1), and the harm-reduction differences are stated as very small.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. The verb 'increases' rests on random assignment within the experiment and applies to stigma towards the depicted person; for support for harm-reduction policies the claim reports a very small difference by age with use history and no difference by drug or gender. The participant-trait associations come from non-randomized regressions on 868 participants and are reported as associations. Status single study; the authors report no earlier experiment on news depictions of drug deaths.

statement: In bodies examined after death, the measured concentration of a drug in blood can differ from the concentration at the moment of death, and from one blood vessel to another in the same body, by amounts that vary between drugs and between bodies and that, in the sources read, cannot yet be predicted for a given death. In four suspected overdose deaths chosen by forensic medicine authors in Dundee and Edmonton to illustrate the problem (tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and the sleeping medicine flurazepam; autopsy about 7 to 48 hours after death; office and period not stated), blood drawn separately from up to 11 systemic vessels of the same body differed 3.5- to 6.6-fold for each drug taken in the overdose and 1.6-fold for lidocaine, given in hospital (editors' calculation from the printed ranges), usually highest in central vessels near the lungs and liver and lowest in the subclavian or femoral veins, though in one case the lowest value was in the pulmonary artery; in the only person with a blood sample from life, taken in hospital about one hour before cardiac arrest (the reported intervals imply about two hours before death), every post-mortem sample, femoral blood included, held 1.8 to 7.9 times as much imipramine (editors' calculation). The authors attribute the differences mainly to drug diffusing out of organs after death, while allowing incomplete distribution in life as a contributor and calling the cause unresolved and probably multifactorial; the report describes one post-mortem sampling occasion per body, alongside the separate sample from life in case 4 and unabsorbed drug was still in the gut in three of the four, so part of the differences may have arisen before death (Pounder & Jones, 1990). A compilation of 10,993 results from 5,375 post-mortem cases for 50 compounds (published reports found by keyword searching, plus a Finnish national laboratory database for 2000 to 2018; cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids were left out) calculated within-case ratios where a published source gave both values, then medians for each drug; the medians across these drug-specific medians were 1.27 for other blood such as heart blood (576 results), 0.99 for muscle, 0.45 for the fluid of the eye (vitreous humour), 1.84 for brain, 2.03 for heart muscle, 5.06 for liver and 5.52 for bile, with more than tenfold ranges across the available drug-specific medians in all ten specimen types (other blood from 0.90 to 14.61, vitreous humour from 0.03 to 1.59, liver from 0.95 to 54.29, some of these values resting on few results; for other blood, morphine 1.26 and methamphetamine 1.50); no within-drug range or interval is given, and cause of death and time since death, which the sources did not always give, could not be taken into account (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019). A review of 87 publications selected from a two-database search in April 2025 reports that in animal experiments drug levels in heart blood rose within minutes of death; that in human bodies sampled more than once, femoral blood, the sample thought least open to change (Ferner, 2008), rose significantly after death for about a dozen drugs, among them fentanyl and methadone, and fell for others, among them 6-MAM (the marker of heroin) and THC; and that, in the studies that reported or estimated it, the reported mean time to the first sample was about 17 hours after death (range 1 to 292 hours), so change before then was not seen. That summary is accompanied by 12 citations, but the review does not supply the underlying interval values, weights or aggregation method. It gives no sizes and does not appraise the studies; it judges that a heart-to-femoral blood ratio other than 1 can indicate, if the two were equal at death, that change after death occurred but not how much, and that a ratio of 1 does not rule it out, and it concludes that evidence linking the change to specific variables is often lacking, drug properties explaining only part of it (Borra et al., 2026). A 2003 practitioners' review lists 99 entries (98 distinct labels), of which 82 have numeric parentheses, including an ambiguous nicotine/cotinine annotation; two are ranges and 16 labels, including THC, have no numeric value. It gives no case counts or per-value source attribution (for example morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3); for 17 of 24 shared labels its value exceeds 1.10 times the compilation's paired median for other blood. Other blood is not only heart blood, and the review's peripheral blood is not necessarily femoral; this comparison is descriptive, not a validated correction (editors' comparison; Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ketola & Kriikku, 2019), and a clinical pharmacologist's review adds that post-mortem whole blood is compared with plasma or serum values from living patients, and that the ratio between the two differs by drug even in life (Ferner, 2008). Change can run both ways: a level after death can be higher than in life, as in the one case with a hospital sample, which can make a drug look more involved in a death than it was, or it can fall after death, as reported for 6-MAM and THC, which can make a drug look less involved. The evidence consists of a selected case series, an unappraised compilation drawn mostly from published reports, some of them about poisonings, and narrative reviews, mostly about medicines; how often, and by how much, a level changes in an ordinary death is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Can the amount of a drug in the blood change after death? Yes. In four selected overdose deaths, levels in different blood vessels differed about 3 to 7 times for the drugs taken in overdose; a medicine given in hospital varied less. In one person tested in hospital before death, all later imipramine samples were about 2 to 8 times higher. A compilation found large differences between drugs and specimens. Its typical other-blood ratio was about a quarter above thigh blood, but that was a median across drug-specific medians, not an average of all deaths. Repeated tests after death found rises for some drugs and falls for others. The size and frequency of these changes in ordinary deaths remain unknown.
population: Bodies examined after death: four selected suspected overdose deaths at medico-legal autopsy (Pounder & Jones, 1990); 5,375 post-mortem cases from published reports and a Finnish laboratory database, 2000 to 2018 (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019); animal experiments and human bodies sampled more than once, as reviewed (Borra et al., 2026); narrative reviews (Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ferner, 2008)
exposure: Drug concentration measured after death in blood from different vessels and in other specimens, and at different times after death
comparator: Femoral (thigh vein) blood from the same body; a blood sample taken in life (one case); earlier samples from the same body
outcome: Size and direction of differences in measured drug concentration between sampling sites and over time after death
magnitude: Within one body (four selected overdoses, autopsy about 7 to 48 h after death): highest to lowest systemic-blood value 3.5- to 6.6-fold (excluding the separately reported portal values) per drug taken in the overdose (editors' calculation; doxepin 3.5, amobarbital 6.0, secobarbital 6.5, pentobarbital 6.2, clomipramine 5.4, flurazepam 6.6, imipramine 4.4; lidocaine given in hospital 1.6). One case with a sample from life: post-mortem imipramine 4.1–18.1 mg/L against 2.3 mg/L in hospital, 1.8- to 7.9-fold. Medians across drug-specific medians of paired within-case ratios (printed number of results): other blood 1.27 (576), muscle 0.99 (385), vitreous humour 0.45 (356), brain 1.84 (565), heart 2.03 (185), kidney 2.86 (401), lung 3.69 (187), spleen 4.25 (71), liver 5.06 (1,697), bile 5.52 (537); between drugs, liver 0.95–54.29, vitreous 0.03–1.59, other blood 0.90–14.61; other blood for morphine 1.26 (53), methamphetamine 1.50 (9). Human repeated sampling: first sample on average 17 h after death (range 1–292 h) where reported or estimated; rises in femoral blood for about 12 drugs, falls for 5 (no sizes). Narrative-review approximate heart-to-peripheral values without case counts or per-value sources (82 numeric-labelled entries among 98 distinct labels, including a nicotine/cotinine annotation; two ranges): morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5–2.3; more than 10% above the compilation's paired other-blood median for 17 of 24 drugs in both (editors' comparison). No within-drug intervals are given. The Table 3 N columns sum to 4,960 but include one oxazepam brain count without a printed ratio; the counts are results, not distinct deaths.

risk_of_bias.note: The site differences come from four overdose deaths chosen to illustrate the problem, with no denominator and no serial sampling (card sc_pounder_1990, JBI high); the ratios come from a compilation drawn mostly from published reports, some of them focused on poisonings, without study-level appraisal or uncertainty estimates (its number-weighted descriptive summaries do not supply study-level precision weighting or within-drug spread) (card sc_ketola_2019, AMSTAR 2 by analogy, critically low); the changes over time are relayed without sizes from a review that does not appraise its studies (card sc_borra_2026). Selection of striking cases could make the differences look larger than in ordinary deaths.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: every source points the same way (levels differ by site and change after death); the size varies by drug, which the claim states rather than hides.

indirectness.note: The question concerns deaths involving any drug, including drugs used outside medicine; the compilation excludes cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids, the case series concerns large overdoses of medicines with drug still in the gut, and part of the evidence on timing is from animals.

imprecision.note: Four cases; no ranges, percentiles or intervals for any compiled ratio; many drug–specimen ratios rest on one to three results.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for case series and compilations of case literature.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which reaches the floor: very low. Strict reading: that drug levels can differ between sampling sites and change after death is shown consistently by independent designs (a case series with a sample from life, a large compilation of paired values, repeated-sampling studies as reviewed) and on its own would be rated low; the sizes, and how often a change matters in an ordinary death, are very low. Status replicated: Pounder & Jones and the primary studies compiled by Ketola & Kriikku and reviewed by Borra et al. are independent and agree in direction. Counted once: Pounder & Jones is one of the compilation's doxepin sources; Ferner (2008) takes its heart-to-femoral ratios from Leikin & Watson (2003), so the narrative reviews' ratios are one source, used only as second-hand examples.

statement: Excited delirium is a disputed label for extreme agitation, sometimes with stimulant drugs present. The two reviews considered here do not establish whether the described state kills independently of restraint, or how much deaths given the label were caused by restraint, drugs or both. They report no validated diagnostic criteria or specific autopsy/laboratory marker, and discuss the label as a diagnosis of exclusion (Strömmer et al., 2020; Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026). The 2020 review says forensic-pathology publications almost exclusively use excited delirium and describe fatal cases, while clinical publications use both excited and agitated delirium for survivors as well as deaths. This describes source types, not a count of which professionals apply the label. The 2026 review also describes a checklist used with living people in policing and prehospital care. It favours acute behavioral disturbance, retains the older term when citing its sources, and recommends replacement where possible; Strömmer’s team instead proposes agitated delirium with a modifier for restraint and a homicide or undetermined manner in restrained fatal cases. These are the authors’ recommendations, not conclusions tested by the data. Strömmer’s pooled analysis selected 168 individually described cases from 61 English-language reports/series found to 23 April 2020. Of 120 labelled excited delirium, 92 died; of 48 labelled agitated delirium, 12 died (unadjusted odds ratio 9.9). Some force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths and 43 of 64 survivors; none in 2 deaths and 1 survivor, and unknown in 8 deaths and 20 survivors. Force covers manual actions, handcuffs, hog/hobble ties, electrical weapons, sedation and other measures; it does not mean every case involved prone compression. These categories overlap. Cocaine was noted in 55 of 104 deaths and 19 of 64 survivors, as classified from case reports without standardized toxicology assessment or drug concentrations (Strömmer et al., 2020). The authors argue that restraint and the label are intertwined, and find no reliable evidence for an independent lethal syndrome. Their own limitations acknowledge nonrandom publication, overrepresentation and better documentation of deaths, and missing drug and restraint details. The editors’ appraisal is that source type, selection and clustering can connect the label, death and recorded force; the univariate analysis does not adjust for them. Only 3 cases explicitly had no force, and 28 had force status unknown, so neither absence of an independently lethal condition nor a causal death risk from restraint can be established. Some printed tables are internally inconsistent: Table 4 gives 100% mortality to a cited study whose title specifies non-fatal encounters. No corrected group fatality rate is supplied here; the later exchange is not part of the 2020 source (Strömmer et al., 2020). The 2026 narrative systematic review searched 2010–2025 and describes cocaine, methamphetamine and phencyclidine as frequently detected, without proportions or concentrations. It favours ventilatory compromise with metabolic collapse during prone restraint, but also allows stress/stimulant-associated arrhythmia in some deaths. It also cites case reports of deaths attributed to excited delirium without overt restraint. Attribution in those reports is not proof that the state itself caused death; the primary reports were not read. It describes volunteer experiments without clinically significant hypoxia or major circulatory compromise, and low mortality in some operational cohorts, while explaining why these do not reproduce all real-world conditions (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026, secondary summaries). For certification and counting, the 2026 review cites 46 Ontario investigation reports with most deaths classified accidental or natural and reports undercounting of restraint-related deaths without quantifying it. Its sources and methods are heterogeneous; the complete included-study set and supplement are unavailable here. The two reviews are rated critically low and overlap because the 2026 review cites Strömmer. They cannot quantify drug-caused deaths or give a causal verdict for an individual. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: What is excited delirium, and why is it disputed? It is a label for extreme agitation, used with living people as well as after deaths. These reviews report no agreed validated criteria or specific autopsy sign. In 168 published cases, force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths, but force included sedation and electrical weapons as well as being held down. Only 3 cases explicitly had no force; many had missing information. A later review also cites deaths attributed to the label without overt restraint. That does not prove what caused them. The selected reports cannot show how often restraint, drugs or the agitated state caused death. See the contested question.
population: People described as in 'excited delirium' or 'agitated delirium' in published case reports and series (168 cases, to April 2020), and people who died in police or prison custody in studies from 2010 to 2025, as reviewed
exposure: Being given the 'excited delirium' label; physical restraint and other force; stimulant drugs noted in the case or found on toxicology
comparator: Cases labelled 'agitated delirium'; published cases who survived
outcome: Death, and the cause and manner of death given
magnitude: Selected individually described cases: 168 from 61 reports; 104 deaths, 64 survivors; excited 92/120 fatal versus agitated 12/48, unadjusted OR 9.9. Force: 94/104 deaths versus 43/64 survivors (editors subtraction from Table 2 none/unknown); none 2/1, unknown 8/20; total explicitly none 3, unknown 28. Police first 95/120 versus 16/48; handcuffs 80/120 versus 6/48; hog/hobble 46/120 versus 1/48. Cocaine noted 55/104 versus 19/64. These are selected-report associations, not causal effects or encounter rates. Secondary 2026 review: Finland 12/21,036 autopsies=0.06%; 229 deaths, 58% collapse within 1–5 min, at least 20% respiratory distress; Ontario 46 reports, most accidental/natural. No frequency of causal drug contribution. 2020 grouped rates are not repaired from unavailable later exchange.

risk_of_bias.note: Both reviews retain critically-low appraisals. Pooled cases are selected for publication; source type, case clustering, label and recording differ; analysis is univariate and several printed tables are inconsistent. The 2026 review does not identify the complete included set in its main article; primary studies and reviews may overlap, and a cited rapid-collapse source concerns litigation. Later exchange full texts and 2026 supplement are unavailable here.

inconsistency.note: The two reviews, and the evidence within them, are read in opposite ways: deaths labelled 'excited delirium' as restraint deaths, or as deaths from an agitated state and stimulant drugs in which restraint is incidental.

indirectness.note: Selected case/death reports are not a sample of all severe-agitation encounters. Clinical papers include both survivors and deaths. Force categories combine different actions and sedation; drug categories are taken from case descriptions without standardized concentrations. Volunteer data do not reproduce every real-world custodial circumstance.

imprecision.note: Only 3 pooled cases explicitly record no force, while 28 are unknown; no denominator of all encounters or count of causally drug-involved deaths. The 2 no-force deaths do not establish a mechanism.

publication_bias.note: Not separately rated; selection for publication is covered under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; unchanged two-level risk-of-bias and one-level inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision downgrades reach the very-low floor. Status remains contested with all six debate fields. The 2026 review cites Strömmer, so they are not independent replication. Authors’ terminology recommendations differ; the newer review retains the old term for source fidelity and says replace where possible. Professional-body positions, primary no-restraint cases and later exchange content are not independently verified here. Draft retained.

debate.question: Can the state labelled excited delirium cause death independently of restraint, or does the label conceal restraint-related deaths?
debate.evidence_yes: The 2026 review describes deaths attributed to the syndrome without overt restraint, and allows a stress-driven arrhythmic pathway with stimulant intoxication in some cases. The 2020 pooled set includes 2 deaths explicitly recorded without force, but its authors say their causes cannot be resolved. The 2026 review also relays healthy-volunteer and operational studies with no clinically important hypoxia or low mortality. These observations qualify a universal restraint explanation; none demonstrates an independent lethal syndrome. Cocaine was noted in 55 of 104 pooled deaths and 19 of 64 survivors, an unadjusted selected-case association rather than a drug effect (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026; Strömmer et al., 2020).
debate.evidence_no: The 2020 pooled reports link the excited label to death (92/120 versus 12/48 for agitated delirium), police as first authority (95/120 versus 16/48), handcuffs (80/120 versus 6/48) and hog/hobble ties (46/120 versus 1/48). Some force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths. The authors argue that this makes restraint a plausible explanation that the label can obscure. Their claim that previously published fatality figures under 10% and 8.3% trace to a source without mortality data is their citation-chain critique, not a newly verified primary finding here. The 2026 review describes rapid collapse after prone restraint in cited retrospective evidence: 58% of 229 deaths within 1–5 minutes, and breathing distress in at least 20%. At least one cited source concerns civil-litigation cases; the entire 229-case frame is not established from this review. It also reports non-specific biomarkers and favours a ventilatory/metabolic explanation (Strömmer et al., 2020; Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026).
debate.neither_can_show: The same presentation is labelled differently across source types. Forensic reports select deaths; clinical papers contain both survivors and deaths, not survivors alone. Publication, case selection, article clustering and documentation differ, and the pooled univariate analysis does not adjust for them. Force categories include sedation and electrical weapons as well as physical restraint, and missing force status is not absence of restraint. Drug categories do not provide a standardized concentration-based causal assessment. Volunteer findings do not reproduce every custodial setting, and selected death series cannot estimate the risk per encounter. Printed 2020 tables contain inconsistencies; later critiques/replies require their own full-source verification before their corrections or revised rates can be used. The 2026 supplement and several cited primary studies are unavailable. Neither review quantifies causal drug contributions or supplies an individual cause-of-death test.
debate.editors_reading: Editors’ reading (certainty: very low). The label describes a presentation; it does not by itself establish a cause. The evidence leaves both independently lethal agitation and restraint-related mechanisms unresolved at the population level. It does not justify treating stimulant detection as decisive or overlooking documented restraint. The 2 pooled deaths without force (Strömmer et al., 2020) and secondary reports without overt restraint (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026) qualify claims that every death requires restraint, but do not prove the state alone caused death. Equally, the high frequency of recorded force (Strömmer et al., 2020) does not establish the causal share of restraint. The 2026 review retains both physiological pathways and recommends independent investigation (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026); Strömmer recommends a terminology/manner change (Strömmer et al., 2020). These are attributed recommendations, not a causal verdict.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Prospective linked police, ambulance, hospital and death-investigation records covering all severe-agitation encounters, fatal or not, with an outcome-independent case definition. Record restraint type, position, duration, compression, devices, sedation, initial rhythm, temperature, blood gases and timed toxicology, with independent autopsy and transparent attribution criteria. Reanalyse published cases by source type and article clustering, and verify the later exchange and primary reports before using corrected rates.
