statement: In a US household survey, Australian twins and international survey analyses, a younger recalled start was associated with more lifetime drug problems or with dependence onset, and in a New Zealand birth cohort in which use was recorded at 13 and 15, not recalled, repeated drinking or drug use by age 15, mostly drinking, was associated with more alcohol or drug dependence at 32 after matching on childhood risk factors. The US analysis used DSM-IV diagnoses; the twins used modified drug-problem criteria and did not date when problems began. These designs do not establish that starting young itself causes later problems; a second analysis of the Australian twins found the link modest and much of it shared with genetic and family influences. In a 1992 US national household survey (NLAES; 42,862 adults interviewed once; about 92% of selected households and 97% of selected people took part), 6,447 people (15.6%, weighted) had used drugs from any of ten classes, other than as prescribed, at least 12 times; 18.6% of them had had lifetime DSM-IV drug dependence and 20.1% drug abuse without dependence. Lifetime dependence criteria were met by 33.6% of those who recalled first using drugs at 13 or younger, 26.8% at 14, 25.4% at 15, 17.7% at 16 and between 11.4% and 15.1% at 17 or older (13.6% at 21 or older); abuse without dependence was 28.9% for onset at 13 or younger and 13.6% at 20, with intervening rises as well as falls. After adjustment for age group, sex, race, family history of alcoholism, duration of drug use and current or former use, the odds of lifetime dependence were about 4% lower, and of abuse about 5% lower, for each later year of first use (coefficients −0.04 and −0.05, SE 0.01; the abstract gives the two the other way round). The age of first use was recalled in the same interview as the diagnoses; the drug first used and the drug of the disorder are not linked; family history of drug problems was not measured; conduct problems and other psychiatric disorders were not adjusted for, without establishing whether the survey measured them; current or former use, one of the adjustments, may itself follow from the disorder; and the only prospective study of age at first use and later drug problems the authors discuss, which followed 15-year-old boys for 13 years, found that age at first use did not predict drug-related problems at 30, a result they discount (men only, a single 3-year window, an aggregate measure). The authors call early onset a powerful predictor, but ask whether the delay itself or, more likely, a combination of other factors lowers the risk, and call for prospective studies (Grant & Dawson, 1998). In the young-adult cohort of the volunteer Australian Twin Register (born 1964–1971; telephone interviews in 1996–2000 at a median age of 30; both twins took part in 69% of pairs), in 311 same-sex pairs in which one twin recalled first using cannabis before 17 and the co-twin did not (136 identical and 175 fraternal pairs; 234 co-twins started later and 77 never used cannabis), the twin who started early more often met the study’s modified criteria for any illicit drug abuse or dependence (47.6% against 32.8%; conditional odds ratio 2.24, 95% CI 1.52 to 3.30), cannabis abuse or dependence (45.7% against 31.8%; 2.13, 1.45 to 3.13), alcohol dependence (42.8% against 29.6%; 2.17, 1.46 to 3.24) and use of other drug classes (2.57 to 5.15). Adjustment for differences between co-twins in early tobacco and alcohol use, conduct disorder, depression and social anxiety lowered the odds ratios by up to about a fifth (any drug abuse or dependence 1.98, 1.26 to 3.10; alcohol dependence 1.85, 1.21 to 2.83). The pair comparison controls shared rearing. Some other differences were assessed retrospectively, but peer affiliation and temperament are not described as measured covariates in this paper. This does not establish what the broader twin register measured. Identical and fraternal pairs were pooled, so the reported estimates control genetic differences only partly; separate identical-pair estimates were not printed, and 311 of the 407 discordant pairs counted in the paper's concordance analysis were analysed, without explanation. The authors read the results as consistent with a causal role and say that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from them alone (Lynskey et al., 2003). In the 17-survey WHO World Mental Health programme (2001–2005; ages recalled at one interview), pooled dependence models compared people who had used each drug. Drug dependence was not assessed in six of those surveys; the analyses therefore do not all cover 17 countries. A later start went with lower odds of dependence; the reported range across all dependence outcomes also includes alcohol and tobacco, and using more drug classes with higher odds, while starting drugs in an unusual order was largely unrelated to dependence (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). In the Dunedin birth cohort (New Zealand; 1,037 children born in 1972–1973, followed from age 3, with 96% of living members seen at 32), use was asked about at 13 and 15: 11.2% of members reported drinking or using drugs on several occasions in the past year at either age (alcohol 10% of members, cannabis 5%, inhalants or other drugs under 2%). Of the 927 adolescents analysed (the other 110 members are not accounted for), the 114 with such use, 65 of whom had used alcohol only, were matched three to one with 342 others on a score built from 13 childhood risk factors, among them conduct problems at 7 to 13, family history of alcohol or drug disorder, maltreatment and child and maternal IQ. At 32, 28.8% of the 114 against 14.7% of the 342 had past-year DSM-IV alcohol or drug dependence (odds ratio 2.25, 95% CI 1.35 to 3.73; a risk ratio of about 2.0, an editors' calculation: the paper's description of the early-exposed as about 2 to 3 times more likely to have the adult outcomes refers to odds ratios); among the 56 with no history of childhood conduct problems, 23.2% against 7.6% of 168 matched adolescents (odds ratio 3.64, 1.57 to 8.45). Peer drug use, puberty timing, early smoking and parenting practices such as monitoring were not among the matched factors; parenting entered only through a maltreatment measure that included rejecting mother–child interaction and harsh discipline (editors' reading of the 13 listed), and the exposure is repeated use by age 15, mostly drinking, not the age of first drug use. The authors read the results as supporting a causal link, while noting that matching cannot replace random assignment (Odgers et al., 2008). A second analysis of Australian twins (7,285 same-sex twins from two cohorts of the Australian Twin Registry, born 1964–1979 and interviewed once, at a mean age of 30.6; the earlier cohort is the one in the co-twin study above, and the two papers share authors) related recalled ages at first use of tobacco, alcohol and cannabis to lifetime counts of DSM-IV symptoms of nicotine dependence and of alcohol and cannabis use disorders. An earlier start went with more symptoms, but modestly (correlations −0.10 to −0.31 in men and −0.12 to −0.28 in women). In the twin models, much of the link was shared with genetic influences (genetic correlations .55 in men and .53 in women) and, in women, with family environment (.83); a correlation between influences unique to each twin remained (men .42, 95% CI .06 to .77; women .23, .04 to .42), carrying, by the editors' calculation from the printed paths, about a quarter of the correlation between the initiation and disorder factors in men and a tenth in women, and it shrank, by an amount not printed, when the model allowed correlated residuals. The authors read the remainder as consistent with a partly causal effect of starting early, state that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn (the data are cross-sectional, factors that differ between twins may confound, and one interview supplied both measures), and judge that delaying first use would likely reduce only a small part of the risk (Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Does starting drugs young go with drug problems later? The studies found a link, but do not show that starting young is the cause. In a 1992 US survey of adults who had used drugs at least 12 times, about 1 in 3 of those who started at 13 or younger had been dependent on drugs at some time, against about 1 in 7 of those who started at 21 or older. In Australian twins, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often met the study’s drug-problem criteria at some time in life than the twin who did not (about 48 in 100 against 33 in 100). In New Zealand, children followed from age 3 were asked about drinking and drugs at 13 and 15, not years later: at 32, 29 in 100 of those who had used several times by 15, mostly alcohol, were dependent on alcohol or drugs, against 15 in 100 of teenagers with similar childhood risks who had not. A larger study of Australian twins found the link modest and much of it shared with genes and family; its authors think delaying first use would lower the risk only a little. International surveys also linked a younger start with dependence. Except in New Zealand, adults had to remember when they started, and things that were not measured, such as friends, could explain part of the link.
population: US adults in a 1992 national household survey who had used drugs from any of ten classes, other than as prescribed, at least 12 times (6,447 of 42,862); Australian same-sex twins born 1964–1971 who differed in cannabis use before 17 (311 pairs), and 7,285 same-sex Australian twins born 1964–1979 (partly the same cohort); adolescents in the Dunedin birth cohort, New Zealand, born 1972–1973 (927 analysed: 114 with repeated use by age 15 and 342 matched); adults in 17 WHO World Mental Health surveys (2001–2005)
exposure: A younger recalled age at first drug use (per year, or by year of age); in the twins, first cannabis use before 17, or earlier recalled first use of tobacco, alcohol and cannabis; in the Dunedin cohort, use of alcohol or drugs on several occasions in the past year at 13 or 15, recorded at the time (mostly alcohol)
comparator: People who recalled starting later; in the twins, the co-twin who had not used cannabis before 17 (234 started later, 77 never), or the comparison of identical and fraternal twins; in the Dunedin cohort, adolescents without such use matched on 13 childhood risk factors
outcome: Lifetime DSM-IV drug dependence and drug abuse reported at the same adult interview (in the twins, also alcohol dependence and use of other drug classes, or lifetime symptom counts of nicotine dependence and of alcohol and cannabis use disorders); in the WHO surveys, onset of dependence; in the Dunedin cohort, past-year DSM-IV alcohol or drug dependence at 32
magnitude: Grant & Dawson (1998), people who had used drugs at least 12 times, weighted prevalence of lifetime DSM-IV drug dependence by recalled age at first drug use (SE): 13 or younger 33.6% (1.9); 14, 26.8% (2.4); 15, 25.4% (1.9); 16, 17.7% (1.3); 17, 15.1% (1.4); 18, 15.0% (1.5); 19, 13.4% (1.9); 20, 11.4% (1.8); 21 or older 13.6% (1.2); abuse without dependence 28.9% (1.9) at 13 or younger to 13.6% (2.0) at 20 (the 11.1% printed for 21 or older is lower than all four subgroup values and is not used); adjusted coefficient per later year of first use −0.04 (SE 0.01) for dependence and −0.05 (0.01) for abuse, odds ratios about 0.96 and 0.95 per year (editors' conversion on the study card); overall, lifetime dependence 18.6% (0.6) and abuse 20.1% (0.6). Lynskey et al. (2003), 311 pairs, twin who started cannabis before 17 vs co-twin, lifetime prevalence and conditional odds ratio (95% CI), unadjusted; adjusted: any drug abuse or dependence 47.6% vs 32.8%, 2.24 (1.52–3.30); 1.98 (1.26–3.10); cannabis abuse or dependence 45.7% vs 31.8%, 2.13 (1.45–3.13); 1.96 (1.25–3.09); alcohol dependence 42.8% vs 29.6%, 2.17 (1.46–3.24); 1.85 (1.21–2.83); use of sedatives 2.83, hallucinogens 5.15, cocaine or other stimulants 4.19, opioids 2.57 (unadjusted). Degenhardt, Dierker, et al. (2010): pooled dependence-onset models among people who had used each drug; drug dependence not assessed in six of the programme’s 17 surveys. Later onset was associated with lower odds. The 0.2–0.7 range across all outcomes includes alcohol and tobacco and is not a drug-dependence-only range; unit not stated. Odgers et al. (2008), Dunedin birth cohort, adolescents with repeated use by age 15 (n = 114) vs matched adolescents (n = 342), past-year DSM-IV alcohol or drug dependence at 32: 28.8% vs 14.7%, odds ratio 2.25 (95% CI 1.35–3.73); before matching vs 813 others, 28.8% vs 11.1%, 3.25 (2.04–5.18); after matching, risk ratio about 1.96 and risk difference about 14 percentage points (editors' calculation from the printed percentages; the odds ratio computed from them is 2.35, not the printed 2.25); no childhood conduct problems, 23.2% (n = 56) vs 7.6% (n = 168), 3.64 (1.57–8.45); conduct-problem history, 32.0% (n = 55) vs 15.3% (n = 165), 2.60 (1.24–5.46). Richmond-Rakerd et al. (2016), 7,285 twins: correlations between age at first use and symptom counts, men −0.10 to −0.31, women −0.12 to −0.28; correlations between the initiation and disorder factors, genetic men .55 (.38–.72), women .53 (.29–.76); shared environment women .83 (.45–1.00), men −.96 (−1.00 to 1.00, not significant); unique environment men .42 (.06–.77), women .23 (.04–.42), attenuated by an unreported amount when correlated residuals were allowed; implied factor correlation about .37 in men (genetic .31, shared −.04, unique .09) and .50 in women (.20, .25, .06) (editors' calculation from the standardized paths in Figures 4 and 5).

risk_of_bias.note: In both main studies the age of first use and the lifetime diagnostic or drug-problem information was collected at the same adult interview, years or decades later, so recall could change the size of the gradient; the survey sampled household survivors and adjusted for current or former use, which may follow from the disorder (card sc_grant_1998: ROBINS-E, high, chiefly for confounding); the twin analysis drew on a volunteer register with 69% pairwise response and used 311 of 407 discordant pairs without explanation (card sc_lynskey_2003: ROBINS-E, high, chiefly for confounding). The second twin analysis also rests on ages recalled at about 30, with both measures from one interview (card sc_richmond_rakerd_2016: ROBINS-E, high). The birth cohort recorded use at 13 and 15 and matched on 13 childhood factors, but peer drug use, parenting practices such as monitoring and puberty timing were not among them (parenting entered only through a maltreatment measure), 110 of 1,037 members are not in the analysis and missing data are not described (card sc_odgers_2008: ROBINS-E, high, chiefly for confounding).

inconsistency.note: The same direction in a national survey, two analyses of Australian twins (overlapping, counted once), an international survey programme whose drug-dependence models excluded six of 17 surveys, and a New Zealand birth cohort with use recorded at 13 and 15; the survey's per-year gradient is modest and flattens after 17, and the twin correlations between age at first use and symptoms are modest (−0.10 to −0.31). The one prospective study cited second-hand (Labouvie et al., 1997, young men only) found no prediction; noted, not counted.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: US adults in 1992 who had used drugs at least 12 times, Australian twins born 1964–1979 (early cannabis use; earlier first use of tobacco, alcohol and cannabis), available drug-dependence data from the 17-country WMH programme in 2001–2005, and a New Zealand birth cohort born in 1972–1973. US/WMH outcomes are interview-derived diagnoses; twin outcomes use modified drug criteria or symptom counts, and onset of problems was not dated. The birth cohort's exposure is repeated use by age 15, mostly drinking, and its outcome includes alcohol dependence; it is used for the direction of the association, not for the size of an age gradient.

imprecision.note: Large survey samples; the twin odds ratios for drug abuse or dependence, alcohol dependence and other drug use have intervals that exclude 1 (sedative abuse or dependence excepted, not used); the birth cohort's odds ratio for dependence after matching (2.25, 1.35 to 3.73) excludes 1 with 114 exposed adolescents; the WHO odds ratios have no stated unit and are used only for direction.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the within-pair odds ratios of about 2 shrink with adjustment and could be produced by differences between co-twins; in the birth cohort the matched risk ratio is about 2.0 (editors' calculation), at the threshold, with plausible confounders left out of the matching (peer drug use, parenting practices such as monitoring).

dose_response.note: Not applied: the survey's gradient is the exposure itself (age at first use), not an amount of drug, and it flattens after 17.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias (recall of onset and diagnoses at one interview in the survey and in both twin analyses, with selection in the survey and unexplained losses of discordant twin pairs; in the birth cohort, which recorded use at the time, plausible confounders left out of the matching and unexplained exclusions): very low. The papers of 12 November do not change the rating: the birth cohort (Odgers et al., 2008) removes adult recall of the exposure and points the same way, but its exposure is repeated use by age 15, mostly drinking, not the age of first drug use, so it supports the direction of the association, not the size of an age gradient; the second twin analysis (Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2016) shares twins and authors with the co-twin study and is counted with it (METHODS §6.3, overlapping evidence). The claim is worded as an association and rated as such; whether starting young causes drug use disorders is not rated: the survey cannot separate cause from shared liability, as its authors say; the co-twin comparison removes what twins share but not what differs between them, nor does it show identical pairs separately; the twin modelling places much of the association in shared genetic and, in women, family influences, and its remaining correlation within pairs, which its authors read as partly causal, also takes in confounders that differ between twins and shared reporting error, and shrank in a fuller model whose estimates are not printed; and the birth cohort's causal reading depends on no important confounder having been left out of the matching. Status replicated: four independent samples (NLAES 1992; the Australian Twin Register, analysed twice and counted once; the WHO survey programme, which does not include NLAES and whose drug-dependence analyses omit six of its 17 surveys; the Dunedin birth cohort) point the same way. The drug first used and the drug of the disorder are not linked in the survey, the co-twin study's exposure is cannabis, and the birth cohort's exposure is mostly drinking; the alcohol counterpart from the same survey (Grant & Dawson, 1997) is in the answer on drinking young.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether using cannabis makes people more likely to go on to other illegal drugs (the 'gateway' idea), or whether the usual order of first use, and the link between the two, come from a shared liability to use drugs and from which drugs people are offered first. In several observational samples, cannabis use usually came before other illegal drugs and was associated with more use of them. The order differed across countries, including some with moderate cannabis use; these patterns alone do not identify a cause. In New York State public high schools in 1971–1973 (5,468 students linked over 5 to 6 months, 66% of the students surveyed in the fall; students who could not be linked had used more drugs), 26% of the 558 students whose drug use had reached cannabis went on to another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, mostly pills (12 percentage points) or psychedelics (9), with heroin about 2, against 4% of 2,911 students who had used only legal drugs and 1% of 482 who had used none; 56% stayed at cannabis and 19% used only legal drugs in the interval. These percentages were weighted for the survey design and response, not adjusted for other characteristics. The paper calls cannabis a crucial step in both the abstract and the body, but also says a drug does not invariably lead to the next and that the stages are probably culturally determined (Kandel, 1975). In four US household surveys (1991–1994; 44,624 people aged 12 to 25; ages recalled in whole years; people compared within neighbourhood and survey year, with sex, race or ethnicity and age group adjusted for, plus age at first cannabis use in the cocaine models, but without individual-liability covariates in the described analysis), people who had used cannabis were more likely to have had a first chance to try cocaine (relative risk 4.6, 95% CI 3.8 to 5.6, without alcohol or tobacco use; 7.6, 6.9 to 8.4, with it; against people who had used none of the three) and, once offered, about 15 times as likely to start as people who had not used cannabis, regardless of alcohol or tobacco history (11.3 to 19.8), also when the 73% who reported starting at the same age as their first offer were left out (20.4, 10.2 to 40.7); this exclusion also removed people who accepted an unbidden offer at once, so it did not isolate active drug-seeking; about half of the people who had used cannabis started cocaine within 2 years of a first offer, against under 10% of the others many years later (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). In Australian twins born 1964–1971 (311 same-sex pairs in which one twin, but not the other, recalled first using cannabis before 17; interviewed at about 30), the twin who started early more often reported later use of other drugs (for example cocaine or other stimulants 47.9% against 26.4%, conditional odds ratio 4.19, 95% CI 2.60 to 6.75; hallucinogens 5.15; sedatives 2.83; opioids 2.57); the odds ratios stayed between 2.3 and 5.2 after adjustment for measured differences between the twins, and between 2.3 and 3.9 (unadjusted) in the 234 pairs in which both twins had used cannabis. The within-pair comparison accounts for shared rearing, but identical and fraternal pairs were pooled, so genetic confounding is controlled only partly. Separate identical-pair estimates were not printed; peer affiliation and temperament were not described as measured covariates in this paper, without establishing what the broader register measured; the authors call the results consistent with a causal role, perhaps through the social setting of cannabis use and access to other drugs, and say that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from them alone (Lynskey et al., 2003). In a New Zealand birth cohort (Christchurch, born 1977; cannabis and other illegal drug use reported for each year from 14–15 to 24–25 at interviews at 15, 16, 18, 21 and 25, so about 1991–2002; 953 to 1,025 people a year), at least 86% of those who used other illegal drugs had used cannabis a year or more before, and 98% by the same year; by 25, 42% had used other illegal drugs, and of them 82% had used hallucinogens (ecstasy, LSD), 20% cocaine and 9% opiates. In years when a person used cannabis more often, that same person more often used other illegal drugs in the same year, also after stable differences between people (as far as their effects stay the same with age) and 18 measured time-varying factors (among them friends' and partners' substance use and depression) were taken into account: log odds 0.93 per step of frequency (SE 0.07), about 2.5 times the odds at 19–20 (editors' calculation), against 1.45 before adjustment for covariates. The link weakened steeply with age: for weekly use against none, odds ratio 66.7 (95% CI 29.4 to 151.4) at 14–15, a model estimate when only 7 people used weekly that year, and 3.9 (2.2 to 7.0) at 24–25. Because both were measured over the same years, the models do not show which came first within a year; influences that change over time and were not measured are not removed, among them involvement in youth and drug culture, which the authors themselves name as a possible common cause; and some adjusted factors could lie on the path from cannabis to other drugs. Saying that causal conclusions from correlational designs are always open to uncertainty and debate, the authors believe their study provides 'relatively compelling evidence' suggesting that cannabis plays a causal role, while saying that which explanation, if any, applies is unclear and that omitted time-varying factors could lead to overestimation (Fergusson et al., 2006a). Three comments were published with the study. One argued that it is not really a test of the gateway idea, which concerns starting other drugs rather than using them in a given year, that fixed-effects models including the previous year's other drug use give inconsistent estimates, and that the order of use within each year was assumed rather than modelled (Kandel et al., 2006). One judged that the authors make a good case that the link is in some way causal and that it can no longer be dismissed as a product of residual confounding (Hall, 2006). One argued that the study makes any simple version of a shared-propensity account unlikely without eliminating it, because fixed effects cannot rule out influences whose effects change with age or interact with the measured factors (MacCoun, 2006). In their reply, the authors called the first objection sound and re-estimated their models with cannabis use taken from the preceding year, and without the previous year's other drug use: the coefficients stayed of similar size or grew (fixed effects 0.93 to 1.27, random effects 1.11 to 1.16, all P < 0.0001; the number of people and the covariates are not stated). This orders the years reported but not always the reports, since for 6 of the 10 pairs of consecutive years both years were reported at the same interview (editors' count from the interview schedule), and it does not address influences that change over time or whose effects change with age; answering MacCoun, the authors judged such influences possible but not very plausible, without testing them (Fergusson et al., 2006b). A simulation of US young people, calibrated to household surveys of 1982–1994, in which one shared liability brings forward both the chances to use and the use of all drugs and cannabis has no effect by design, reported a strong relative risk of using heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens (157 in the model, against 24 in the surveys). The survey ratio compares use of those drugs by 21 between people who had and had not used cannabis by 21, without requiring cannabis first; the model’s description also uses prior-initiation wording, so the two ratios may not measure exactly the same quantity. The model also produced an order in which those drugs rarely come first (11 per 1,000, against 16 in the surveys) and a rise with cannabis frequency, and adjusting for an imperfect measure of that liability left large associations; it shows that these patterns cannot by themselves identify a cause, but it was not compared with a model that includes one, and its authors think something like a gateway effect probably exists through contact with illegal markets (Morral et al., 2002). In the 17-country WHO programme (2001–2005; ages recalled at one interview), the order varied across countries alongside how common each drug was. Among people who had used other illegal drugs by 29, cannabis had not already been used at their first other-drug use in 11.4% in the USA and 12.7% in New Zealand, against 83.2% in Japan and 77.8% in Nigeria, where cannabis was rare; these definitions include people who never used cannabis. For Japan, Tables 2 and 4 display n entries 16 for other-drug use and 13 for not-already-cannabis histories; for Nigeria,8 and 7. The estimates are weighted cumulative/projected percentages, and the text does not explicitly define those n entries as unweighted observed counts. The percentages should not be rebuilt as simple fractions of those entries. The corresponding proportion was also high in South Africa (59.2%), where the authors call cannabis use moderate, and Mexico (48.4%). The observed correspondence does not show that prevalence caused the order. In pooled interaction models, the link of cannabis with later other drug use was weaker where cannabis was more common, while that of alcohol or tobacco with later other drug use was stronger where those were more common; the Netherlands–USA country contrast alone does not demonstrate that prevalence relationship; and starting in an unusual order was largely unrelated to later dependence (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). A narrative review by proponents of a shared liability argues that the order need not reflect causal steps and calls that liability empirically proven. It also argues that the cannabis-to-other-drug association itself is negligible after accounting for cannabis prevalence, citing a book rather than presenting new data for that assertion. It cites classical twin studies but the article body does not discuss discordant co-twin-control evidence (Vanyukov et al., 2012). No study read separated a causal effect, a shared liability and access to drugs in one design, and all their data were collected between 1971 and 2005. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does using cannabis lead to other drugs? This is not known. In many places studied, most people who used other illegal drugs had used cannabis first. This was not the order for everyone. Cannabis use was also linked to more use of other drugs: in New York schools in the early 1970s, about 1 in 4 students who had used cannabis tried another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, against 4 in 100 of those who had used only alcohol or tobacco. In a New Zealand group followed from birth, people used other illegal drugs more in the years they used cannabis more, most of all as young teenagers, and most of those who used other illegal drugs had used ecstasy or LSD. Both were asked about the same years. When the researchers later linked each year's other drug use to cannabis use in the year before, the link stayed, but both years were often asked about at the same interview. Experts who commented disagreed: one said hidden factors could no longer explain the link away; another said factors that change with age had not been ruled out. In Australian twins, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often used other drugs later than the other twin. The comparison accounts for growing up in the same home, but not all genetic or other differences between twins. A computer model showed that the same pattern appears if some people are simply more likely to use any drug and are offered cannabis first, with no effect of cannabis at all. Across surveys in 17 countries, the order varied. Some people had not used cannabis when they first used another illegal drug, including some who never used cannabis. This was common in some places with rare or moderate cannabis use; the displayed table counts for Japan and Nigeria were small, with their counting basis unclear. No study separated cause, shared risk and access to drugs. See the contested question.

risk_of_bias.note: No individual-liability covariates were included in the described analyses in the school panel or the surveys (cards sc_kandel_1975: ROBINS-E, very high, no confounder adjustment despite survey weighting and a third of the panel lost, more of them people who used drugs; sc_wagner_2002 and sc_degenhardt_2010a: high); the co-twin study cannot exclude factors that differ between co-twins and shows no identical-pair estimates (sc_lynskey_2003: high); the birth cohort's within-person models relate use within the same years, do not remove influences that change over time, such as drug-using social settings, and adjust for factors that could lie on the path (sc_fergusson_2006: high), and the authors' re-analysis in their reply takes cannabis use from the preceding year, but most pairs of consecutive years were reported at one interview, influences that change over time remain, and the number of people and the covariates are not stated (sc_fergusson_2006b); the simulation's assumptions are untested and it was not compared with a model that includes a gateway effect (sc_morral_2002: high); the review is an argued position without search or appraisal (sc_vanyukov_2012: high).

inconsistency.note: The strength of the link varies widely between countries (cannabis and later other illegal drugs at 18–29, odds ratio 7.4 in the Netherlands against 107.1 in the USA), non-cannabis-first histories also occur where cannabis use is moderate; they include never-cannabis use, and the designs address different parts of the causal question: a co-twin comparison finds a link beyond shared family factors, while a model with no effect of cannabis reproduces the population patterns. Within one cohort the link also weakened steeply with age (weekly use: odds ratio 66.7 at 14–15, 3.9 at 24–25), a difference by age rather than unexplained inconsistency.

indirectness.note: All data were collected between 1971 and 2005, mostly in the USA, Australia and New Zealand; the cross-national surveys show that the pattern varies across places and cohorts, so it may differ in other places and in later years, including where cannabis is sold legally (not studied in the papers read). In the New Zealand cohort, those who used other illegal drugs had mostly used hallucinogens such as ecstasy or LSD (82%), with cocaine 20% and opiates 9%.

imprecision.note: Large surveys and twin intervals that exclude 1; the Japan and Nigeria proportions have small displayed table counts (16 and 8 for other-drug use), whose count basis is not fully explained, and are used only to illustrate different histories; the simulation gives no intervals; the cohort's odds ratios at 14–15 are model estimates resting on few people (7 using weekly, 12 monthly).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence and a simulation start low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low, the floor. The claim concerns cause, so its relation is insufficient evidence; that cannabis use usually comes first and goes with a higher chance of using other illegal drugs is reported in it, not rated as a separate claim. The New Zealand birth cohort added on 12 November (Fergusson et al., 2006a) does not change the rating: its within-person models show that stable differences between people, as far as their effects stay the same with age, do not explain all of the link, but it relates use within the same years, cannot remove influences that change over time and is at high risk of bias for the causal question. Its gradient with cannabis frequency is not used to rate up for dose–response, because the simulation reproduces a rise with cannabis frequency with no effect of cannabis (Morral et al., 2002). The three comments published with that study and the authors' reply, added on 12 November (evening), do not change it either: the comments are arguments without data (Hall, 2006; Kandel et al., 2006; MacCoun, 2006), and the reply's re-analysis, in which the link held with cannabis use taken from the preceding year and without the lagged outcome, answers two specification objections but uses the same cohort and reports, most pairs of consecutive years having been reported at one interview, states neither its number of people nor its covariates, and does not address influences that change over time (Fergusson et al., 2006b). Counted once: Wagner & Anthony (1991–1994) and Morral et al. (1982–1994) draw on the same series of US household surveys; Vanyukov et al. add no data and cite Morral et al. and Degenhardt, Dierker, et al.; the WHO surveys include the US and New Zealand surveys whose earlier analyses the paper cites; the Christchurch cohort is a separate sample, and Fergusson et al. cite Lynskey et al. and Morral et al. without sharing their data; the reply's re-analysis uses the same Christchurch data and is counted with the original. Status contested: a co-twin comparison, a within-person cohort and survey analyses point to a link beyond shared family factors, stable differences between people and being offered, while a model and cross-national data show that a shared liability and access can produce the same patterns, and the comments published with the New Zealand study disagree on whether residual confounding has been answered (Hall, 2006; MacCoun, 2006), so the six-part debate box applies.

debate.question: Does using cannabis make people more likely to go on to other illegal drugs, as the authors of a New Zealand cohort study concluded (Fergusson et al., 2006a), or do the usual order and the link come from a shared liability to use drugs and from which drugs people are offered first, as a simulation showed can happen (Morral et al., 2002)?
debate.evidence_yes: In Australian twins born 1964–1971, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often went on to use other drugs than the co-twin who did not (conditional odds ratios 2.57 to 5.15; for example cocaine or other stimulants 47.9% against 26.4%), also after adjustment for measured differences between the twins (2.3 to 5.2) and in pairs in which both twins had used cannabis (2.3 to 3.9); the comparison accounts for shared rearing, with only partial genetic control when identical and fraternal pairs are pooled (Lynskey et al., 2003). In a New Zealand birth cohort followed from 14 to 25 (about 1991–2002), in years when a person used cannabis more often, the same person more often used other illegal drugs, after stable differences between people (as far as their effects stay the same with age) and 18 measured time-varying factors were taken into account (log odds 0.93 per step of frequency, about 2.5 times the odds at 19–20, editors' calculation), most strongly in early adolescence (weekly use against none: odds ratio 66.7 at 14–15, 3.9 at 24–25), and at least 86% of those who used other illegal drugs had used cannabis a year or more before; the authors, while saying that causal conclusions from correlational designs are always open to debate, believe this is fairly convincing evidence suggesting that cannabis plays a causal role (Fergusson et al., 2006a). In a re-analysis in the authors' reply, the link also held when cannabis use was taken from the preceding year and when the previous year's other drug use was left out of the model, with fixed-effects coefficients of 0.93 to 1.27 and random-effects coefficients of 1.11 to 1.16, all P < 0.0001 (Fergusson et al., 2006b). One commentator argued that, whatever its mechanism, the link can no longer be dismissed as a product of residual confounding (Hall, 2006). In US household surveys of 1991–1994, people who had used cannabis were more likely to be offered cocaine (relative risks 4.6 to 7.6) and, once offered, about 15 times as likely to start, also when people who reported starting at the same age as the offer were left out (20.4), with people compared within the same neighbourhood and survey year (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). Cannabis came before other illegal drugs for most people in most places studied; in 1971–1973 about a quarter of New York State students at the cannabis step went on to another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, against 4% of students who had used only legal drugs (Kandel, 1975); and in nearly every one of 17 countries, starting a drug earlier in the usual sequence went with much higher odds of starting a later one (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). Routes proposed but not tested include the social setting in which cannabis is used, lower perceived risk, and access to other drugs through people who sell cannabis (Lynskey et al., 2003; Morral et al., 2002).
debate.evidence_no: A simulation in which one shared liability, and the order in which drugs are offered, drive all first use, with no effect of cannabis by design, reproduced the patterns usually cited for a gateway: large printed relative risks (157 in the model and 24 in US surveys), whose exact comparability is unsettled because the survey counts use by 21 without requiring cannabis first while the model also uses prior-initiation wording, an order in which heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens rarely come first (11 against 16 per 1,000) and a rise with cannabis frequency; adjusting for an imperfect measure of that liability left large associations (an odds ratio of 297 fell only to 82 with an indicator correlated 0.8 with liability, corresponding to 64% variance in a simple linear reading (editors’ squared-correlation calculation)), so adjustment of the kind used in observational studies cannot rule a shared liability out (Morral et al., 2002). Across the WHO surveys the order varied alongside differences in prevalence: histories without cannabis already used were common in Japan and Nigeria, where cannabis was rare and the estimates rested on few people, and in South Africa, where use was moderate. These histories include never-cannabis use; the link of cannabis with later other drug use was weaker where cannabis was common; and starting out of order did not go with more dependence (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). In 1971–1973, most New York State students at the cannabis step did not move on within 5 to 6 months (56% stayed at cannabis, 19% used only legal drugs in the interval), the author wrote that the stages are probably culturally determined, and the percentages were survey-weighted without covariate adjustment (Kandel, 1975). In the New Zealand cohort, cannabis and other illegal drug use were related within the same year, so the models cannot show which came first; most of those who used other illegal drugs had used hallucinogens such as ecstasy or LSD (82%); the weekly-use odds ratio at 14–15 is a model estimate when only 7 people used weekly that year; and the authors themselves name involvement in youth and drug culture, which changes over time, as a possible common cause and say that omitted time-varying factors could inflate their estimates (Fergusson et al., 2006a). Commenting on that study, one group argued that it does not test the gateway idea, which concerns starting other drugs, and that the order of use within each year was assumed rather than modelled (Kandel et al., 2006); the authors accepted the first point as sound (Fergusson et al., 2006b). Another commentator argued that fixed effects cannot rule out influences whose effects change with age or interact with the measured factors, and that twin and animal evidence was not yet persuasive (MacCoun, 2006). The US survey analysis places part of the link at being offered cocaine, which fits access as well as an effect of cannabis, and measured no individual liability (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). Proponents of a shared liability argue that the order follows how available and common each drug is and that the stages are defined circularly (Vanyukov et al., 2012).
debate.neither_can_show: None of these studies randomly assigned cannabis use. The school panel and the household surveys (Kandel, 1975; Wagner & Anthony, 2002) rest on self-reports, mostly ages recalled years later in whole years, and did not include individual-liability covariates in the described analyses; the co-twin design (Lynskey et al., 2003) accounts for shared rearing but, with fraternal and identical twins pooled, not all genetic or other differences between them (friends, temperament, their own early behaviour), and the study read shows no separate results for identical twins; the within-person cohort (Fergusson et al., 2006a) adjusts for stable differences between people that were not measured, as far as their effects stay the same with age, but not influences that change over time; one commentator argued that fixed effects cannot rule out effects that change with age or interact with the measured factors, and the authors judged such influences possible but not very plausible, without testing them (Fergusson et al., 2006b; MacCoun, 2006); its original models relate use within the same years, and the re-analysis in the reply that takes cannabis use from the preceding year orders the years reported, not always the reports, since most pairs of consecutive years were reported at one interview (editors' count; Fergusson et al., 2006b); a simulation shows what a model can produce, not what happened (Morral et al., 2002). The cross-national comparison (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010) rests on differences between countries that also differ in law, drug markets and willingness to report use. None of the designs separates an effect of cannabis itself from the effect of buying it where other drugs are sold, and all the data were collected between 1971 and 2005.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). Several observational samples show cannabis usually coming first and an association with other-drug use (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010; Fergusson et al., 2006a; Kandel, 1975; Lynskey et al., 2003; Wagner & Anthony, 2002); histories without cannabis already used are also common in some countries with moderate use (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). The narrative review disputes the association itself, without presenting new data to establish its asserted negligible size (Vanyukov et al., 2012); that a shared liability and the order in which drugs are offered can produce this pattern without any effect of cannabis is shown by a model (Morral et al., 2002); that the link persists within twin pairs shows that the family background twins share does not explain all of it (Lynskey et al., 2003); and that it persists within the same people from year to year, most strongly in early adolescence, shows that stable differences between people, as far as their effects stay the same with age, do not explain all of it either (Fergusson et al., 2006a). In a re-analysis in the authors' reply, the link did not depend on measuring both drugs in the same year or on the model's lagged outcome, as far as reports of consecutive years, mostly given at one interview, can show (Fergusson et al., 2006b); whether confounding left after these controls explains the rest was argued both ways in published comments and has not been tested (Hall, 2006; MacCoun, 2006). The evidence read cannot say whether the remaining link is an effect of cannabis, of access to illegal markets and drug-using social settings, which change over time (Fergusson et al., 2006a; Morral et al., 2002), or of differences between twins, and in the one study that followed students over a few months, about 3 in 4 students at the cannabis step did not move on to another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months (Kandel, 1975).
debate.what_would_settle_it: A cohort followed from before any drug use that records offers and first use of each drug as they happen, not year by year as in the one cohort read (Fergusson et al., 2006a), analysed for first use rather than use in a given year and with methods suited to a lagged outcome, as one commentary proposed (Kandel et al., 2006), with liability measured beforehand (behaviour, family and friends' use) and the local availability of each drug, and with enough identical twin pairs who differ in cannabis use to give separate estimates, which the twin study read did not print (Lynskey et al., 2003); and natural experiments that change access to cannabis without changing access to other drugs, such as legal sales kept apart from illegal markets, with later use of other drugs measured, since contact with illegal markets is a route that several authors propose (Fergusson et al., 2006a; Morral et al., 2002); one commentator asserted, citing his own book, that Dutch retail sales of cannabis appear to have separated the soft and hard drug markets, while the study's authors replied that neither prohibition nor liberalization has been shown clearly to break the link between cannabis use and other illicit drug use (Fergusson et al., 2006b; MacCoun, 2006).

statement: As described in four reviews (two narrative reviews, and two systematic reviews of studies that sort people into groups by the drugs they report using, called latent class analyses), none of which pooled any figures and only one of which appraised the studies it describes, so that every figure here is second-hand, using more than one drug is common among people who use illegal drugs, how common depends on who was asked and how use was defined, and it makes the long-term effects of any one drug hard to study in people. Studies define it as using several drugs over a period (lifetime, or the past 1 to 12 months) or on the same occasion, the second being hard to capture in surveys and mostly studied in smaller high-risk samples, although the review also describes national survey work that measured same-occasion use; the historical DSM diagnosis of polysubstance dependence was dropped from DSM-5, and most population research records only how often each drug is used. Studies that group people by the drugs they use typically find a limited range (alcohol, tobacco, cannabis), a moderate range (adding amphetamine-type drugs) and an extended range (adding prescription drugs used non-medically and other illegal drugs). Limited-range use was reported by 18% of 12- to 17-year-olds (ever) and by 34% of teenagers before 16, in two samples; extended-range use by 2% of 12- to 17-year-olds and 13.5% of 18- to 29-year-olds in Australian national samples, two different age groups that the review calls panel designs; and up to 75% of people at underground raves used several drugs, on average five at the last rave. Classes with a wide range of use reported more psychological distress, anxiety and depression in the cited studies; several imaging studies and studies of inhibitory control and decision-making found no difference in performance from comparison groups, while another study reported large differences on standard tests outside the scanner and a metabolite study linked brain measures with memory performance. The studies differed on performance, but the review concludes that using several drugs is clearly associated with deficits in brain function and thinking; and the authors judged research on preventing and treating the use of several drugs underdeveloped (Connor et al., 2014). In the ecstasy research reviewed in 2006, the great majority of people who used it also used other drugs, most often alcohol, cannabis and stimulants: earlier studies found cannabis use in 90% to 100% of people who used ecstasy, and in one survey everyone new to ecstasy (1 to 9 pills in all) had smoked cannabis in the previous month, 32% on five or more occasions. Studies that compared people who use ecstasy with people who use no drugs therefore make it difficult to separate ecstasy from other drug effects; in studies with comparison groups who used other drugs but not ecstasy (samples described as up to 234, without resolving whether this counts only people using ecstasy or all comparison groups), raised psychological problems went with drug use in general rather than with ecstasy, though those comparison groups mostly used drugs more moderately; some earlier studies did not record other drugs; and findings on whether cannabis explains, adds to or offsets problems seen in people who use ecstasy pointed in different directions. The reviewers propose following large cohorts of young people who are not or not yet using drugs and may belong to risk groups, for years, with drug histories recorded and psychological and cognitive tests repeated (Gouzoulis-Mayfrank & Daumann, 2006). A systematic review of 23 studies that sorted adolescents aged 10 to 19 into such groups (published to June 2015; 19 from the US, most of them school or household surveys; 14 cross-sectional; all self-reported; nothing pooled) found 3 to 7 groups per study. A group with little or no use appeared in 19 studies (17% to 77% of each sample) and was the largest in most; a group using mainly alcohol appeared in 16 (15% to 80%); and every study found at least one group using several substances, most often alcohol, tobacco and cannabis together (12 of the 18 studies that measured all three; 6% to 29% of each sample), while groups that also used other drugs were smaller (alcohol, tobacco, cannabis and other drugs: 7 of 11 studies, 2% to 13%). The reviewers could not reproduce the limited, moderate and extended ranges described above in adolescent samples, partly because other drugs were often merged into one question; they count analyses that appear to share data as separate studies (for example two analyses of California pupils in grades 7, 9 and 11, with 419,698 and 418,702 pupils, and pairs from the Add Health and NLSY97 national surveys; editors' reading of the review's study table), and they rated 5 of the 23 studies at high risk of bias, mostly for missing information (Tomczyk et al., 2016). A systematic review of 137 studies that sorted adults into such groups (published to 2022; 55% from the US and 12% from Australia; 54 drew on local or national samples and the others on particular groups, among them people with a substance use disorder recruited in the community (27), sexual minorities (20), people in or entering treatment (19) and partygoers (8)) shows how much the groups found depend on how a study was done: 132 of the 137 used self-reports and 5 included urine, blood or other tests; about 7 in 10 used only yes-or-no questions, mostly about use in the past month or year; about a third did not ask about alcohol and about two thirds did not ask about tobacco (editors' arithmetic from the shares reported); studies found 2 to 8 groups, usually 3 or 4; and studies with larger samples, or that asked about more substances, found more groups (correlations .283 and .243, each accounting for under a tenth of the differences between studies, an editors' calculation). The reviewers warn that the names given to groups are the researchers' choice and can mislead. They appraised none of the studies, pooled nothing and do not summarize which groups recur, so the review cannot say which patterns are common among adults; like the adolescent review, it lists analyses that appear to use the same samples as separate studies, for example two analyses of apparently the same 552 people who used cocaine or heroin (LeComte et al., 2025; editors' reading of the review's study table). How often people who use cocaine also drink or use cannabis, and what that means for cocaine research, is in the answer on cocaine with alcohol and cannabis. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: How common is using several drugs, and why does it matter? It is common among people who use illegal drugs, according to four reviews whose figures are second-hand. In Australian surveys, 2 in 100 teenagers and about 13 in 100 young adults used a wide range of drugs; at underground raves, up to 75 in 100 people used several drugs, five on average at the last rave. In ecstasy studies, 90 to 100 in 100 people also used cannabis, and many also drank alcohol or used stimulants. In most of 23 studies of teenagers, the biggest group used little or nothing, but every study found a group using several substances, most often alcohol, tobacco and cannabis together (6 to 29 in 100 teenagers in each study); groups that also used other drugs were smaller (2 to 13 in 100). Studies of adults found 2 to 8 such groups, and bigger studies, or studies that asked about more drugs, found more, so the patterns found depend partly on how a study looks. Using several drugs makes it hard to know what one drug does over time: studies of people who use ecstasy may be measuring several drugs at once, and some older studies did not record the other drugs. The cocaine page has the figures for cocaine with alcohol and cannabis.
population: People in the samples two narrative reviews describe: national and student surveys (Australia, the USA, Brazil and elsewhere, mostly 2013), people at raves and clubs, treatment samples, and people who used ecstasy in the studies reviewed in 2006; adolescents aged 10 to 19 in 23 latent class studies published to June 2015 (19 from the US, mostly school and household surveys); and adults in 137 latent class studies published to 2022 (55% from the US; local and national samples and particular groups, such as people with a substance use disorder, sexual minorities, people in treatment and partygoers)
exposure: Using more than one drug, over a period or on the same occasion, as each source defined it
comparator: None for the proportions; for research on ecstasy, comparison groups who used no drugs, or other drugs but not ecstasy
outcome: How common using several drugs is, and its patterns, including the groups that latent class studies report and how those groups depend on the studies' methods; whether studies of one drug can separate its effects from those of the other drugs used
magnitude: As described, not pooled, no intervals. Connor et al. (2014): limited-range use 18% of 12–17-year-olds (lifetime) and 34% of teenagers before 16; extended-range use 2% at 12–17 and 13.5% at 18–29 (Australian national samples of different age groups; 13.2% in the review's annotation of one source); up to 75% of people at underground raves using several drugs, on average five at the last rave; a sedative-and-alcohol class with last-year prevalence 1.3% among young Australian adults. Gouzoulis-Mayfrank & Daumann (2006): cannabis use in 90–100% of people who used ecstasy in earlier studies; in one survey all people new to ecstasy (1–9 pills) had smoked cannabis in the previous month, 32% on five or more occasions; comparison studies with up to 234 people who used ecstasy. Tomczyk et al. (2016), 23 adolescent latent class studies (N 450 to 419,698 each; to June 2015), not pooled; shares of each sample in each group, as described: little or no use 17–77% (19 studies); mainly alcohol 15–80% (16 studies); alcohol and cannabis 8–20% (8 of 23 studies); alcohol and tobacco 1–23% (4 of 19); tobacco and cannabis 2–11% (2 of 19); alcohol, tobacco and cannabis 6–29% (12 of 18); alcohol, cannabis and other drugs 4–29% (4 of 15); alcohol, tobacco and other drugs 6–24% (3 of 11); alcohol, tobacco, cannabis and other drugs 2–13% (7 of 11); in five studies with frequency-sensitive questions, occasional several-substance groups 9–29% and frequent ones 7–18%. LeComte et al. (2025), 137 adult latent class studies (142 analyses; N 135 to 202,838, median 1,061; to 2022), not pooled: 2–8 groups per analysis (mean 3.85, median 4); substances asked about: stimulants in 91.97% of studies, cannabis 86.86%, opioids 73.32% (as printed), alcohol 67.15%, tobacco 32.85%; yes-or-no questions only in 71.53%; time frames past month 46.72%, past year 29.93%, lifetime 14.60% (some studies used several); larger samples and more indicators went with more groups (Spearman rho .283; Pearson r .243; unadjusted).

This appraisal is not a claim that all cited cognitive results were null.

risk_of_bias.note: Both narrative reviews lack reported systematic search methods or formal appraisal (cards sc_connor_2014 and sc_gouzoulis_mayfrank_2006: editors' checklist, high), each drawing partly on its authors' own studies; the two systematic reviews of latent class studies have critically low confidence by AMSTAR 2 (cards sc_tomczyk_2016 and sc_lecomte_2025: no protocol, or one that could not be checked; searches limited to peer-reviewed literature; no list of excluded studies; study quality not used in interpreting the results), one appraised its studies with an adapted Newcastle–Ottawa Scale and the other appraised none, and both count analyses of shared samples as separate studies; the primary studies cannot be appraised here (METHODS §6.3).

inconsistency.note: The figures differ widely by population (2% of 12- to 17-year-olds with extended-range use, up to 75% of people at underground raves using several drugs), as the claim states; in every sample of people who use illegal drugs that the reviews describe (people at raves, people who use ecstasy), using several drugs is common, and every one of 23 adolescent latent class studies found at least one group using several substances. Group sizes and solutions vary between latent class studies (for example 6% to 29% for the alcohol, tobacco and cannabis group; 2 to 8 groups in adult studies), partly with sample size and the substances asked about: variation by sample and method, stated in the claim, not inconsistency in direction.

indirectness.note: All figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3): mostly Australian and US samples around 2013, the ecstasy research reviewed in 2006, adolescent latent class studies to mid-2015 (19 of 23 from the US) and adult latent class studies to 2022 (55% from the US), many of the adult ones of particular groups.

imprecision.note: No intervals are given; the figures are presented as descriptions of the samples, or of the studies' methods, not as population estimates.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim resting on reviews: it starts low (the descriptive quantities used here come from observational survey samples), is rated down one level for risk of bias (two narrative reviews without appraisal and two systematic reviews of critically low confidence, one of which appraised none of its studies) and one for indirectness (every figure second-hand): very low. The papers of 12 November do not change the rating: the two systematic reviews pooled nothing, so their figures remain descriptions of samples reported by others; with them the claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews (METHODS §6.3), but its figures stay second-hand, as the statement says. The two narrative reviews come from different groups, in Queensland in 2014 and in Cologne in 2006, and describe different primary studies; the two systematic reviews cover adolescents (to mid-2015) and adults (to 2022), and each counts analyses that appear to draw on the same surveys or samples as separate studies, which the counts quoted here may inherit (METHODS §6.3, overlapping evidence). Those samples of people who use illegal drugs all show that using several drugs is common, and every adolescent latent class study found at least one group using several substances: status replicated, as a description of those samples, not of any population. The adolescent review could not reproduce the first review's three ranges of use, and the adult review shows that the groups found depend on sample size and on the substances asked about and cannot say which adult patterns are common; these qualify how patterns are described. The first review reports health and cognitive associations, with mixed cognitive findings and no design inventory; these are described, not rated as causal effects; its 2% and 13.5% compare different age groups in different samples, not the same people over time (card reporting issue). The cocaine figures (Liu et al., 2018) belong to the cocaine answer and are neither repeated nor counted here.

statement: How a death enters a count of drug deaths depends on the country, the register and the period, so figures from different sources do not count the same thing, and studies that matched the same deaths across two sources found that they overlapped only partly. In US national statistics for residents who died in the US, a drug overdose death is one whose underlying cause on the death certificate is coded to ICD-10 X40–X44 (unintentional), X60–X64 (suicide), X85 (assault) or Y10–Y14 (undetermined intent); deaths from long-term drug effects and from side effects of medicines taken as prescribed are left out. A drug counts as involved when the certifier, usually a medical examiner or coroner, wrote it in Part I, Part II or the injury description, unless the words around it say otherwise, and a death with several drugs is counted under each of them, so the 15 drug-specific counts for 2023 added up to 179,965 against 106,352 deaths (editors' arithmetic); the National Center for Health Statistics calls its drug counts minimums and says that the certificate cannot show which drug caused a death involving several (Garnett et al., 2026). ICD-10 codes put different drugs together (fentanyl and tramadol share one code; oxycodone, morphine and codeine share another): in Washington State in 2003–2010 one code covered 2,725 poisoning deaths; its most often named drugs or terms were oxycodone, morphine, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, codeine and opiate. These names overlapped within deaths and were not an exhaustive list; the certificate's words could separate names that the code grouped together (Ossiander, 2014). The certifier's words also decide whether and how a death is coded: a US consensus panel convened by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration notes that 'acute cocaine intoxication' is coded as a poisoning while 'cocaine use' or 'cocaine abuse' is coded as a mental and behavioural disorder (Goldberger et al., 2013), and 'drug overdose' with no drug named is coded as unspecified drugs (Slavova et al., 2015). The same panel separated deaths caused by a drug from deaths in which a drug was only detected (Goldberger et al., 2013). European registers differ again. Norway's Cause of Death Registry, under the European (EMCDDA, now EUDA) definition, counts only the underlying cause and the first contributing cause (Amundsen, 2017). In Sweden, a national selection counted a listed drug code anywhere on the certificate, the European selection only the underlying cause from a shorter list, and a forensic register any death in which an illegal drug, methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl was found at forensic examination, whatever the certified cause, at ages 10 to 60, with an exception at any age when both morphine and the heroin marker 6-monoacetylmorphine were found. The certificate selection had no age limit (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In England and Wales, the Office for National Statistics counts a death under a specific opioid only when a cause-of-death field in the coroner's Record of Inquest names it (Chen et al., 2025). Who decides differs as well: certifying physicians in Sweden and Norway, coroners in England and Wales, medical examiners or coroners in the US, and, for Norway's second register, local and central police (Fugelstad et al., 2020; Amundsen, 2017; Chen et al., 2025; Garnett et al., 2026). Matching the same deaths across two sources, the strongest evidence on this question, showed partial overlap in three countries. In Norway in 2007–2009, the Cause of Death Registry (822 deaths) and the police registry (562) together covered 929 people, of whom 455 (49%) were in both; 367 were only in the cause-of-death count, 74 police-registry deaths had a certified cause outside the European definition, and 33 had no match (39% of them not Norwegian citizens, the rest with missing or wrong identity numbers). The cause-of-death register covered Norwegian residents only; police covered unnatural deaths regardless of residence. Deaths only in the cause-of-death count were older, more often certified as dependence or suicide, more often had morphine or codeine, methadone, other synthetic opioids or stimulants rather than heroin as the first contributing-cause drug code, less often had an autopsy and more often occurred in hospitals or other institutions; autopsies were recorded for 715 of the 822, and the author states that neither source gives the correct figure, while judging the cause-of-death register more complete and broader and both sources probably too low (Amundsen, 2017). In Sweden in 1994–2012, the certificate-based selection and the forensic toxicology register shared 4,238 of the 9,707 deaths in either, with 2,210 only in the toxicology register and 3,259 only in the certificate selection; a separate table, whose period is not stated, reports that 96% of toxicology-register deaths whose main drug was heroin were also in the certificate selection, against 23% where it was cannabis (THC). The authors conclude that comparing numbers or rates of drug deaths between countries misleads, while comparing trends is meaningful where investigation and certification have not changed, although they analysed no other country (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In New Mexico in 1995–1998, where policy calls for full autopsy and toxicology of suspected drug or poison deaths, except in some tribal and federal jurisdictions unless invited (the actual share tested is not given), vital statistics and the medical investigator's records each held 1,046 of the 1,105 residents' poisoning deaths found in either, and 987 were in both. This was a broad poisoning category, including alcohol and carbon monoxide, not just drug poisoning. Of 59 deaths counted as poisonings only by vital statistics, 24 occurred in another state, 13 had never been reported to the medical investigator and 15 were natural deaths in the medical investigator's records (such as cirrhosis, sepsis or heart disease) that vital statistics coded as non-dependent drug use (the explanation involving use or abuse wording is the editors' inference from the paper's coding rule, not a reported reading of those individual certificates); of 59 counted only by the medical investigator, 37 had been coded as natural deaths, typically with poisoning written only in Part II of the certificate, and 17 as other injuries (Landen et al., 2003). In a coroner-fed UK register's wider drug-related category for Liverpool (70 deaths, from deaths in 2004 and inquests in January to June 2005), 25 were not deaths from drug toxicity and 15 were of people living elsewhere; these groups can overlap, and residence is a separate feature, not shown to result from the wider drug-related definition (Beynon et al., 2007). Around 2000 in England and Wales, as cited by Webb et al. (2003), coroners' verdicts of death from drug misuse numbered 605 (2000), the same register counted 1,296 drug-related deaths (2000) and the Office for National Statistics 2,943 deaths with drug poisoning as the underlying cause (1999). The linkage studies come from Norway, Sweden and one US state, the newest data are from 2012, and none comes from southern Europe. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: How is a death counted as a drug death? It depends on the country and the list. In the US count described here, drug poisoning must be the main cause on the death certificate. Drugs named in the cause-of-death or injury fields can each be counted, so one death can appear under several drugs. A Swedish list counted certain drugs found in tests, whatever the cause, mainly for people aged 10 to 60; its heroin-marker exception had no age limit. Doctors, coroners, medical examiners or police decide, depending on the place. The words they record affect the code. When researchers matched people across two lists, they did not fully agree: about half appeared on both in Norway, fewer than half in Sweden and about 9 in 10 in New Mexico. The New Mexico study counted other poisons too, such as alcohol and carbon monoxide. These are comparisons of three places, with different rules, and the newest linked data are from 2012.
population: Deaths counted as drug deaths in national and local registers: United States (national statistics 2017–2023; Washington State 2003–2010; New Mexico residents 1995–1998), Norway 2007–2009, Sweden 1994–2012, England and Wales around 2000, Liverpool 2004–2005
exposure: The definition and source used to count a death as a drug death: ICD-10 underlying-cause and drug codes, drugs named on the death certificate, drugs found in forensic toxicology, police selection or a coroner-fed register's own definition, and who decides
comparator: Other definitions and sources for the same population and period; in the linkage studies, the same deaths matched across two sources
outcome: Which deaths are counted as drug deaths, and how far two sources counting drug deaths in the same place and period agree on the individual deaths
magnitude: Definitions: US overdose deaths, ICD-10 underlying cause X40–X44, X60–X64, X85, Y10–Y14; drugs counted when mentioned in Part I, Part II or the injury description; 2023, 15 drug-specific counts sum to 179,965 for 106,352 deaths (1.69 times; 1.47 times in 2017; editors' arithmetic) (Garnett et al., 2026). Washington State 2003–2010: one code (T40.2) covered 2,725 poisoning deaths; six most common terms, not an exhaustive list, with overlapping mentions (Ossiander, 2014). Linkage: Norway 2007–2009, 929 people, 455 (49%) in both registers, 367 (40%) cause-of-death register only, 74 (8%) police register with a cause outside the European definition, 33 (4%) unmatched (Amundsen, 2017). Sweden 1994–2012: 4,238 of 9,707 in both the certificate selection and the toxicology register, 2,210 toxicology only, 3,259 certificate only; in a separate table with no stated period, capture of toxicology-register deaths by the certificate selection, heroin 96%, THC 23%; toxicology selection ages 10–60 except the heroin-marker cases at any age (Fugelstad et al., 2020). New Mexico 1995–1998, broad poisoning including alcohol and carbon monoxide: 1,046 in each source, 987 in both, 1,105 in either (94.7% and 89.3%); discordant deaths 59 each way (Landen et al., 2003). Liverpool 2004–2005: of 70 register deaths, 25 not from drug toxicity and 15 non-residents (overlapping categories) (Beynon et al., 2007). England and Wales, as cited: 605 coroners' verdicts (2000), 1,296 register deaths (2000), 2,943 ONS drug-poisoning deaths (1999) (Webb et al., 2003). No intervals; counts of linked records.

evidence.extracted: US National Vital Statistics System mortality files, 2017–2023, US residents who died in the US: an overdose death has an ICD-10 underlying cause of X40–X44 (unintentional), X60–X64 (suicide), X85 (homicide) or Y10–Y14 (undetermined intent), which reflect acute intoxication; deaths from chronic drug exposure (such as liver toxicity) and adverse effects of therapeutic or prophylactic doses are excluded. evidence.extracted: A US consensus panel convened and funded by SAMHSA defined a drug-caused death (certified as resulting from exposure to a drug, alone or with other substances, whatever the intent; parallel to the NCHS drug-induced category), a drug-poisoning death (acute exposure, the lay idea of an overdose; ICD-10 underlying cause X40–X44, X60–X64, X85 or Y10–Y14) and a drug-detected death (a drug found on post-mortem testing whatever its role, including natural and trauma deaths; no ICD-10 equivalent). Wording decides the code: 'acute cocaine intoxication', 'cocaine poisoning' or 'cocaine overdose' is coded as poisoning (X42 with T40.5), whereas 'cocaine use' or 'cocaine abuse' is coded to F14 (mental and behavioural disorders due to use of cocaine).

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded. The overlap counts come from matching complete registers on personal identity numbers (Norway, Sweden) or by hand with a case-by-case review of the discordant deaths (New Mexico) (cards sc_amundsen_2017, sc_fugelstad_2020, sc_landen_2003: JBI moderate, high and moderate). The reporting errors on those cards (a Swedish total printed as 6,648 and 6,448; one-death slips in New Mexico's union columns; a few cells of Norway's Table 1) change the overlaps by a few deaths, not their size, and the high rating of the Swedish card concerns its comparison with the Stockholm inventory, which this claim does not use. The definitions are taken from the bodies that apply them (NCHS, card sc_garnett_2026) or from the papers that describe their own registers. Complete-register linkage describes those records, not complete capture of all true drug-caused deaths; differing age, residence and cause definitions are not automatically errors.

inconsistency.note: The overlap ranges from about half (Norway: two different selecting bodies and definitions) to about nine in ten (New Mexico: two sources for the same poisoning deaths under similar definitions); the differences follow the definitions compared, as the claim says.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: each figure is given with its place, source and years, and no overlap figure is carried to other countries or to today. The claim states that the linkage data end in 2012 and that none comes from southern Europe.

imprecision.note: Counts of linked records from complete registers; no sampling.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to register comparisons.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim about how deaths are counted and how far sources agree: starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3). Not downgraded: three independent linkage studies in different countries and systems (Norway, Sweden, New Mexico) agree that sources counting drug deaths in the same place and period disagree on substantial numbers of individual deaths, in both directions, and each traces the disagreement to definitions, certificate wording, residency rules and reporting routes; comparisons of two sources for the same deaths are the strongest evidence on this question. The definitions are taken from the bodies that apply them. The consensus statement (Goldberger et al., 2013) and the Liverpool register study (Beynon et al., 2007) illustrate definitions and add no rate; the England and Wales counts quoted by Webb et al. (2003) come from other sources and different years and are given only as cited. Status replicated: independent studies in three countries point the same way. Whether official counts miss drug deaths, and by how much, is a separate answer.
