statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether the kind of official who investigates a death changes how drug deaths are counted. In the US, deaths in counties served by coroners were more often recorded as of undetermined intent than deaths in medical-examiner counties of the same states, and studies summarized second-hand found that certificates named no drug more often where coroners certify; but the one study of states that switched to medical examiner systems found no detectable improvement in how specifically poisoning deaths were coded, and across nine states taken together, without allowing for the state, the association with undetermined intent ran the other way; no study checked which records were right. A US consensus panel defines medical examiners as appointed, professionally trained forensic pathologists and coroners as elected or appointed officials whose qualifications vary widely (Goldberger et al., 2013); a later study describes medical examiners as typically appointed physicians and coroners as elected laypeople, with requirements varying by state, some states requiring coroners to be physicians (Lundberg et al., 2026). In Kentucky, for example, a coroner must be at least 24 years old and meet residence rules, no training in medicine or forensic pathology is required, and new coroners must complete 40 hours of basic training; of 48 coroners who answered a 2016 survey, 47 held another job, 28 as funeral directors (Quesinberry et al., 2019). In the 2018 census of US offices, about 80% were in coroner systems (a figure the authors quote from the Bureau of Justice Statistics report), coroners or other non-physicians were the role most often named as deciding which deaths were tested (64.7% of offices), and offices serving fewer than 25,000 people less often reported access to toxicology (75.1%, against 96.4% of offices serving 250,000 or more), a comparison by population served, not by type of office (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025). In surveillance records of 55,430 drug poisoning deaths in nine states in 2019–2021, deaths in coroner counties had higher odds of being recorded as of undetermined intent, rather than as an accident or a suicide, than deaths in medical-examiner counties of the same state and year (odds ratio 1.79, 95% CI 1.43 to 2.27; 1.52 to 1.61 after allowing for county characteristics, recorded investigation steps and the person's age, sex and race); without allowing for the state the odds were lower in coroner counties (0.32; 3.1% against 8.9% recorded as undetermined), which the authors attribute to Maryland, a state with a central medical examiner and many undetermined deaths, without showing a model that leaves Maryland out. The within-state comparison can draw only on states with both kinds of county, which excludes Indiana (coroners only) and North Carolina and Maryland (central medical examiners) (editors' inference from the authors' descriptions). An alcohol test was recorded for 58.6% of deaths in coroner counties against 84.5% in medical-examiner counties, while autopsies (about 68% and 67%) and opioid tests (about 80% and 79%) were recorded about equally often (editors' percentages), and whether a test was recorded was largely not associated with the classification, by the authors' account; the type of system was taken from a 2024 listing (Lundberg et al., 2026). A scoping review summarizes, second-hand, three studies that found more certificates naming no drug where coroners certify, one with odds ratios of 1.77 (2014) and 3.87 (2018) for an unclassified overdose death in coroner counties, and reports from another, a national analysis of 2008–2010, that the share of overdose deaths of undetermined manner varied by state but not by type of system (Gutkind et al., 2025); a commentary cites that analysis for the share of overdose certificates naming specific drugs, on average 92% in states with a central medical examiner, 73% in hybrid systems, 71% in local medical-examiner systems and 62% in coroner systems (Slavova et al., 2015, as cited); and a 2019 review reports that in 2016 the share of drug poisoning deaths recorded as of undetermined intent ranged from 1% in Connecticut and Massachusetts to 68% in Maryland, and suggests that office policies not aligned with professional recommendations may drive such differences (Slavova et al., 2019, as cited). Against this, seven states that switched to a medical examiner system in 1976–1996 (two of them from physician coroners or locally appointed physicians, two from justices of the peace), compared with seven states that did not, chosen for nearness and similar earlier trends, showed no detectable change in the share of poisoning deaths with a non-specific underlying-cause code (difference-in-differences −0.02 to −0.03, standard errors 0.04 to 0.06, so falls of 10 to 14 percentage points from a share near one half could not be ruled out, editors' calculation, with no stated allowance for repeated years of the same state), in data that ended in 1998 and included poisonings by substances other than drugs; the plots show differing descriptive levels and trajectories, including common sharp falls that the author attributes to the ICD-9 revision and a similar fall in Massachusetts before its system switch. They do not establish different causal reform effects in individual states; no formal state-specific effect comparison is reported (Zaychik, 2024). See the contested question. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does it matter whether a coroner or a medical examiner investigates? It is not clear. In the US, medical examiners are usually doctors appointed to the job; coroners are often elected, and in some states need no medical training. In nine US states (2019 to 2021), deaths in coroner areas were more often recorded without saying whether the death was an accident or a suicide than deaths in medical examiner areas of the same state. Other studies found that certificates named no drug more often where coroners work. But seven states that switched to medical examiners showed no clear change in how precisely poisoning deaths were recorded, although that study could not rule out a real improvement, and its data end in 1998. Nobody checked which records were right.
population: Drug poisoning deaths in US counties and states served by coroners or medical examiners: nine states, 2019–2021; seven states that switched systems in 1976–1996 and seven comparison states, 1968–1998; US offices in 2018; Kentucky's elected coroners in 2016
exposure: Death investigation by a coroner (elected or appointed, often without medical training) or a change from a coroner to a medical examiner system
comparator: Death investigation by a medical examiner (an appointed physician) in the same state and year; states that kept coroner or mixed systems
outcome: How specifically drug deaths were recorded: manner recorded as undetermined intent, certificates naming no drug, and non-specific poisoning codes
magnitude: Nine US states 2019–2021, undetermined intent in coroner against medical-examiner counties (Lundberg et al., 2026): within state and year, odds ratio 1.79 (1.43–2.27); adjusted 1.52 (1.20–1.95), 1.61 (1.26–2.06), 1.60 (1.25–2.05); pooled without state, 0.32 (0.29–0.35), 558 of 18,232 (3.1%) against 3,329 of 37,198 (8.9%); no within-state contrast in Indiana, North Carolina or Maryland (editors' inference). Alcohol test recorded 58.6% against 84.5% (editors' percentages). Second-hand: unclassified overdose deaths in coroner counties, odds ratios 1.77 (1.08–2.90) in 2014 and 3.87 (2.32–6.46) in 2018 (Gutkind et al., 2025); undetermined manner varied by state but not by system, 2008–2010 (Gutkind et al., 2025); certificates naming specific drugs 92% (central medical examiner), 73% (hybrid), 71% (local medical examiner), 62% (coroner) (Slavova et al., 2015); undetermined share of drug poisoning deaths in 2016, 1% to 68% (Slavova et al., 2019). Seven state switches 1976–1996 (Zaychik, 2024): difference-in-differences in the non-specific share −0.02 (SE 0.04), −0.03 (0.05), −0.02 (0.06); conditional editors’ normal 95% intervals from rounded SEs −0.10 to 0.06, −0.13 to 0.07, −0.14 to 0.10; the paper states no allowance for repeated state-years, and the effect of a different error model on interval width is not established. US offices 2018: about 80% in coroner systems (as quoted from the Bureau of Justice Statistics); toxicology access 75.1% (small) against 96.4% (large) (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025).

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias and one for inconsistency, which is below the floor: very low. Status contested: credible evidence points both ways, cross-sectional associations against the only before-and-after test and a reversed pooled estimate, so the six-part debate box applies. Counted once: the 92%, 73%, 71% and 62% figures appear in both reviews by the same first author (Slavova et al., 2015; 2019) and come from one earlier analysis (Warner et al., 2013, not read), which the scoping review (Gutkind et al., 2025) also summarizes; the scoping review is cited only for primary studies not read here, labelled second-hand. The Kentucky survey and the 2018 census describe who investigates and with what testing; they do not compare counts. Whether an autopsy or a drug test changes which deaths count as drug deaths is a separate answer.

debate.question: When a coroner rather than a medical examiner investigates, are drug deaths counted differently or less accurately, and would switching systems change the counts?
debate.evidence_yes: In surveillance records of 55,430 drug poisoning deaths in nine US states in 2019–2021, deaths in coroner counties had higher odds of being recorded as of undetermined intent than deaths in medical-examiner counties of the same state and year (odds ratio 1.79, 95% CI 1.43 to 2.27), and the estimate stayed between 1.52 and 1.61 after allowing for county size, poverty, unemployment, rurality, recorded autopsy and toxicology, suicide notes, investigator narratives and the person's age, sex and race; alcohol tests were recorded less often in coroner counties (58.6% against 84.5%), although whether a test was recorded was largely not associated with the classification (Lundberg et al., 2026). A scoping review summarizes three studies that found more certificates naming no drug where coroners certify, one with odds ratios of 1.77 (2014) and 3.87 (2018), with unclassified deaths falling faster in medical-examiner counties (72% against 43%, 2014–2018) and lower odds where the certifier is a pathologist, coroners must be trained or the system is centralized (Gutkind et al., 2025, second-hand). An earlier analysis cited in a commentary found that, on average, 92% of overdose certificates named specific drugs in states with a central medical examiner, 73% in hybrid systems, 71% in local medical-examiner systems and 62% in coroner systems (Slavova et al., 2015, as cited). Coroners in some states need no medical training (Kentucky; Quesinberry et al., 2019), and in 2018 about 80% of US offices were in coroner systems (as the authors quote from the Bureau of Justice Statistics), coroners or other non-physicians were the role most often named as deciding which deaths were tested, and small offices less often reported access to toxicology (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025).
debate.evidence_no: The only before-and-after test found no detectable improvement: in seven US states that switched to medical examiner systems in 1976–1996 (from coroners, justices of the peace or, in two, physicians), compared with seven comparison states that did not, the share of poisoning deaths with a non-specific underlying-cause code did not fall detectably more after the switch (difference-in-differences −0.02 to −0.03) (Zaychik, 2024). Across the nine states taken together, without allowing for the state, deaths in coroner counties were less often recorded as undetermined (3.1% against 8.9%; odds ratio 0.32), which the authors attribute to Maryland, a central medical-examiner state (Lundberg et al., 2026); in 2016 the share of drug poisoning deaths recorded as undetermined ranged from 1% in Connecticut and Massachusetts to 68% in Maryland, which a review tentatively puts down to office policies not aligned with professional recommendations (Slavova et al., 2019, as cited), so a medical-examiner system can record drug deaths very unspecifically. A national analysis of 2008–2010, summarized in a scoping review, found that the share of overdose deaths of undetermined manner varied by state but not by type of system (Gutkind et al., 2025, second-hand). In the nine-state data, autopsies and opioid tests were recorded about as often in coroner as in medical-examiner counties (editors' percentages; Lundberg et al., 2026).
debate.neither_can_show: No study checked, against an independent review of the same deaths, which recorded intent or drug was correct, so 'undetermined' or 'no drug named' measures how specifically deaths were recorded, not how many were missed or wrongly attributed. Comparisons between counties cannot separate the type of office from what usually comes with it (budget, staff, caseload, access to toxicology, rurality, state law), some of which is part of what a system is; the nine-state study took each county's system from a 2024 listing for deaths in 2019–2021, combined two surveillance systems by manner of death, and could compare kinds of county within a state only where a state had both (not in Indiana, North Carolina or Maryland). The before-and-after study had seven switches, all before 1999, two of them from systems that already used physicians; it used underlying-cause codes that mix drug and non-drug poisonings, states no allowance for repeated years of the same state, and pools state pairs with differing descriptive levels and trajectories that do not establish heterogeneous causal effects, and was too imprecise to rule out falls of 10 to 14 percentage points. The 92% to 62% figures and the county odds ratios are second-hand and unadjusted or not appraised here.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the US studies read, deaths investigated in coroner-served areas tended to be recorded less specifically, with no drug named more often, by second-hand accounts (Gutkind et al., 2025; Slavova et al., 2015), and, within states, more often as of undetermined intent (Lundberg et al., 2026), than deaths investigated by medical examiners. Whether that is caused by the type of office, or by what often comes with it, such as officials without medical training and, in one study, fewer recorded alcohol tests (Goldberger et al., 2013; Lundberg et al., 2026; Quesinberry et al., 2019), is not known, and the only test of a change of system, with data before 1999, could neither show nor rule out an improvement (Zaychik, 2024). Maryland shows that a central medical-examiner system can also record many drug deaths as undetermined (Lundberg et al., 2026; Slavova et al., 2019), so rules and practice within a state matter as well as the title of the office. None of this shows how many drug deaths either system misses or wrongly counts.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Before-and-after studies of recent changes of system or of rules (such as toxicology mandates or certifier training) in the ICD-10 era, with drug-specific outcomes (the share of certificates naming each drug and the share recorded as undetermined), matched comparison areas, enough cases and standard errors that allow for repeated years of the same area; and linkage of certificates in both kinds of system with an independent review of the same deaths, blinded to the type of office, recording each office's budget, staffing and testing, to measure missed and wrongly attributed deaths in both directions.

statement: A drug concentration measured after death cannot on its own show that the drug caused the death: concentrations in deaths put down to a drug overlap with those in deaths from other causes and with the reference ranges of living patients taking the drug as a treatment, tolerance shifts the level a person can survive, and levels change after death (see the answer on whether levels change after death). In Finland, where police can order a medico-legal investigation of a sudden or unexplained death and the forensic pathologist decides whether to test for drugs (over 13% of all deaths), one laboratory measured femoral-blood levels in 57,903 deaths of all causes with full drug testing in 2000 to 2010, sampled on average five days after death; for 46 of 129 drugs the median level was above the therapeutic plasma range of a clinical reference list, by up to 100-fold for one drug (24-fold for the next), for 61 it was within that range and for 22 below it. The median for methadone (207 deaths) and for buprenorphine (671 deaths) lay within the treatment range although forensic pathologists certified 43% and 45% of those deaths as poisonings with that drug as the main finding, and the authors state that for strong opioids the level after death plays a somewhat limited part in judging the cause, as it partly does for amphetamine and other drugs to which tolerance develops; the medians mix poisonings with other deaths, leave out levels too low to measure, and compare whole blood with plasma ranges (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). Among deaths with MDMA or a related drug found at full autopsy in Sheffield, England (1992 to 2008), femoral-blood MDMA overlapped widely between deaths put down to MDMA (0.478 to 53.9 mg/L in 13 with a value) and deaths from injuries (0.035 to 4.81 mg/L in 24), although the median was about 7 times higher in the first group (editors' calculation; Milroy, 2011; see the answer on MDMA levels). A Michigan series published in 1977, as the 1996 narrative review describes it, found blood morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes, such as injuries or homicide, in 74% of deaths put down to heroin overdose (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand; see the answer on heroin 'overdoses'). A clinical pharmacologist's review adds, second-hand, that published 'lethal' ranges are wide and overlap (for example 40 to 8,500 µg/L quoted for MDMA and 60 to 3,100 µg/L for methadone), that amounts that would kill a person without tolerance are survived by people who use heroin regularly, and that a fatal level could only be defined by classing deaths as caused by the drug or not without knowing the measured levels and then comparing the two groups (Ferner, 2008), which none of the studies read here reports doing; a 2003 practitioners' review lists nine questions a toxicologist should answer before judging a drug's role, among them where the blood was taken, whether the drug changes after death, what is known of the person's tolerance and whether the autopsy findings fit (Leikin & Watson, 2003). Both directions follow: a level that looks high can lead to a death being put down to a drug that was only present, and an ordinary or low level does not rule a drug out. A study of whether drugs were present, not of their levels, shows that judging without a full autopsy also errs both ways: at one North Carolina centre that kept doing full autopsies on suspected drug deaths (2016 to 2021), 265 of 2,719 deaths that investigators suspected before autopsy to be drug deaths (9.75%) were given a final cause unrelated to drugs after full autopsy and toxicology (by the paper's definition, deaths with no drug found or with drugs present but another sufficient cause; the split is not reported; people under 18, obvious lethal injuries and suicidal drug overdoses were excluded), while 115 of the 237 deaths not suspected (48.5%, editors' calculation) were judged drug deaths; the pathologists counted any illicit drug found as at least contributing unless a catastrophic other cause was found (Hancock et al., 2024; see the answer on autopsy and toxicology testing). The earlier source extraction reports that the Finnish certifiers received the toxicology results; in the North Carolina study the final cause followed full autopsy and toxicology; the Sheffield and Michigan reports, as read here, do not say who decided the causes or whether the levels were known. None of the studies read here itself compares post-mortem levels with levels in living people who use the drugs outside treatment; the heroin review cites three comparisons with survivors of overdose, without figures. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Can a blood test after death show that a drug caused the death? Not on its own. In an English autopsy study, MDMA levels in deaths put down to MDMA overlapped with levels in people who died of injuries. A review reports similar findings for morphine in an older US study. Finnish data compare levels after death with treatment reference ranges, rather than testing living patients in the same study. At one US centre, full autopsy and toxicology led to a different final classification in both directions: some suspected drug deaths were judged unrelated to drugs, and some unsuspected deaths were judged drug-related. That study examined drug presence, not blood levels. The certifiers' knowledge and rules limit what these comparisons can show.
population: Deaths with drugs measured after death: 57,903 Finnish medico-legal autopsies of all causes with full drug testing, 2000–2010; Sheffield autopsies with MDMA or a related drug, 1992–2008 (13 deaths put down to MDMA and 24 injury deaths with a femoral-blood value); deaths put down to heroin overdose in a 1977 Michigan series (second-hand); 2,956 autopsies at one North Carolina centre, 2016–2021
exposure: Drug concentration measured in blood after death (femoral blood where stated)
comparator: Therapeutic plasma reference ranges for living patients; deaths with the same drug present but another cause; deaths not certified as poisoning by the drug; the final cause after full autopsy
outcome: Whether post-mortem drug concentrations separate deaths caused by a drug from other deaths
magnitude: Finland 2000–2010 (57,903 deaths; 129 drugs): median femoral concentration above the therapeutic plasma range for 46 drugs (printed 35%; 35.7%, editors' calculation), within for 61 (47%), below for 22 (17%); the older card proposes 48, 58 and 23 under a consistent rule, but that source-table reconstruction was not independently repeated by reader 405; largest ratio to the upper therapeutic limit 100 (hydroxychloroquine), next 24 (promazine). Methadone median 0.40 mg/L (therapeutic 0.1–0.5), 43% certified as poisonings with methadone as the main finding; buprenorphine 0.0012 mg/L (0.0005–0.005), 45%; morphine 0.07 mg/L (0.01–0.1), 4%. Sheffield 1992–2008: MDMA deaths 0.478–53.9 mg/L (median 3.49; n = 13), injury deaths 0.035–4.81 mg/L (median 0.483; n = 24); at least 7 of the 13 inside the injury range (editors' calculation). Michigan series published in 1977 (study years unstated; second-hand): 74% of heroin overdose deaths with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes. Quoted lethal ranges (second-hand): MDMA 40–8,500 µg/L, methadone 60–3,100 µg/L. North Carolina 2016–2021 (presence, not levels): 265/2,719 (9.75%) suspected drug deaths with a non-drug final cause; 115/237 (48.5%, editors' calculation) of deaths not suspected judged drug deaths. No intervals.

statement: In studies published from 2000 to 2011 in Australia, the UK, Ireland, North America and seven other European countries, mostly surveys in which health professionals reported their own attitudes, many professionals described negative attitudes towards patients with alcohol or drug problems, or regarded them less well than patients with other conditions, more often outside specialist drug and alcohol services, while several studies found moderate, neutral or positive attitudes; whether such attitudes make the care these patients receive worse was examined in only a few studies, whose results point different ways. A systematic review of 28 papers (at most 25 independent samples by the editors' count of the shared samples the review marks; 12 from Australia, 7 from the UK and 5 from the US; 20 quantitative, mostly questionnaires at one time point, five interview or focus-group studies, two implicit association tests and two using observation, categories that overlap) gave no count or pooled estimate of how common negative attitudes were. Among its examples: among 866 professionals in eight European countries (one of them Scotland), regard was lowest for patients with drug and alcohol problems compared with patients with depression or diabetes, and lowest among doctors outside specialist drug and alcohol services; in a vignette study, professionals held more stigmatizing views of active substance use disorder than of other mental illness; and five study summaries in the review's table describe attitudes as moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive, with a sixth reporting stigma below the criterion for negative stigma (editors' count). More contact or experience went with more positive or different attitudes; the review cites a few studies as showing better attitudes or perceived knowledge after training or education, but in a survey of 1,605 nurses education went with better attitudes only where colleagues gave at least moderate support, and none of these studies is described as following people over time. On consequences for care: clients of residential rehabilitation services in Sydney who perceived more discrimination by staff were less likely to complete treatment (a mixed-methods study of 92 clients, attributed in the review's text to the wrong paper by the same team); two qualitative studies suggested that clinicians may impose their beliefs on patients, and described district nurses making shorter, task-focused visits and, in the review's table only, harder access to care for these patients; among 2,864 patients with HIV, 17.1% of them currently injecting drugs, physicians' negative attitudes were not associated with patients' reports of problems with care, dissatisfaction, unmet needs or access; and the one included study that rated the quality of care from observed visits, 683 visits to nine psychiatric emergency services in California in 1985–1986, found better care for patients with substance use problems than for other patients on all four criteria, a result the review's text does not mention (van Boekel et al., 2013). The review searched three databases in English and Dutch, excluded studies from Asia, Africa and South America and studies of training, weighted all studies equally whatever their response rate (from 31% to 92% where its table gives a rate, and all took part in one study; its table gives none for 11 papers), and is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 by the study card; its abstract's statements that negative attitudes diminished patients' empowerment and treatment outcomes and made care more task-oriented rest on two qualitative studies. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Do health workers see and treat people who use drugs differently? In studies from 2000 to 2011, mostly surveys, many health workers said they felt negatively about patients with drug or alcohol problems, or less positive than about patients with other illnesses, more often outside specialist drug and alcohol services; some studies found neutral or positive views. Whether this changes care was studied only a few times, and the results differed: in one study, people who felt treated unfairly by staff were less likely to finish treatment; in another, doctors' views were not linked to what patients said about their care; and the one study that watched real visits, from the 1980s, found better care for these patients.
population: Health professionals (nurses, doctors, staff of drug, alcohol and mental-health services, mixed groups) and, in five papers, their patients, in 28 papers published 2000–2011 from Australia, the UK, the USA, Canada, Ireland and seven other European countries
exposure: Being a patient with an alcohol or drug use disorder (the patient group professionals were asked about or treated)
comparator: Patients with other conditions (for example depression, diabetes or other mental illness) where studies compared them; otherwise none
outcome: Professionals' self-reported attitudes, regard and implicit associations; patients' perceived discrimination, treatment completion and reports of care; observed quality of care
magnitude: No pooled estimate and no count of studies by direction. As reported by van Boekel et al. (2013): 28 papers (at most 25 independent samples, editors' count); regard lowest for patients with drug and alcohol problems among 866 professionals in 8 European countries (one of them Scotland); 5 of the study summaries describe moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive attitudes and a sixth stigma below the criterion for negative stigma (editors' count of Table 5); 5 papers link more experience or contact with more positive or different attitudes; response rates 31% to 100% where given, none in 11 papers (editors' count of Table 4). Consequences: perceived staff discrimination predicted not completing treatment (92 clients, Sydney); physicians' attitudes not associated with patients' reports of care (2,864 patients with HIV, 373 physicians; 23.2% of the patients had physicians with negative attitudes towards people who inject drugs); better care for patients with substance use problems on all 4 criteria in 683 observed emergency visits (California, 1985–1986).

risk_of_bias.note: A systematic review with critically low confidence on AMSTAR 2 (no protocol; three databases in English and Dutch, PsycINFO giving 10 records; no list of excluded studies; studies weighted equally whatever their design or response rate, from 31% to 100% where given; conclusions about consequences not tempered by the designs behind them; card sc_van_boekel_2013), whose primary studies are mostly self-reported attitudes from self-selected respondents.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: the statement gives no single summary answer; it reports that attitude findings and consequence findings point in different directions (status mixed), so the spread is part of what is described.

indirectness.note: Seen only through the review (METHODS §6.3, second-hand): none of the primary studies was read, and the review's own summaries are not always reliable (a finding cited to the wrong paper; text and table disagree on Brener et al., 2007; an observational study left out of the text). The statement is worded as what the review reports, for the countries and years covered, and says that care itself was rarely measured.

imprecision.note: Not applicable to a narrative description without pooled estimates.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review; not judged for a descriptive summary.

grade.reasoning: Observational studies (mostly cross-sectional surveys and qualitative studies) seen only through one systematic review: starts low; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness (second-hand, METHODS §6.3): very low, the lowest level (one downgrade alone would already give very low). Rated as worded: the statement describes what the included studies reported, not how common negative attitudes are (the review gives no count), and gives the evidence on care as a handful of studies pointing different ways, including the observational study finding better care that the review leaves out of its text and the null survey result it notes without weighing (card reporting issues). Not used: the abstract's statements that negative attitudes diminished empowerment and treatment outcomes (two qualitative studies), the review's statement that patients rated professionals with more positive attitudes more favourably (Brener et al., 2007), which its own table describes differently (card reporting issue), and the recommendation of training (cross-sectional associations, after studies of training were excluded). A causal claim, that health workers' attitudes worsen care, would be insufficient evidence. Status mixed: findings on attitudes and on consequences differ between studies without an explanation the review can settle. The review is systematic, not narrative, so the claim is not narrative-only.

statement: In people released from prison or jail in eight mostly high-income countries between 1980 and 2018, the death rate was highest in the first week after release (counted from day 2), and deaths coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning had the highest rate of any cause in that week, although most such deaths happened later. In 18 record-linkage cohorts of everyone released (1,471,526 people, 88.3% of them men, in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA; 75,427 deaths), the pooled crude death rate over the whole follow-up was 725 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 625 to 831). The analyses by time since release used the 16 cohorts, in seven countries, that could give deaths by day (New Zealand's only cohort and one from Washington State could not): the rate was 1,612 (1,048 to 2,287) in days 2 to 7 after release and 737 (636 to 844) more than a year after release, and the first week's rate was 1.5 times that of the second week (1.2 to 1.8), 2.0 times that of weeks 3–4 (1.5 to 2.6) and 2.2 times that of weeks 9–12 (1.6 to 3.0). The 'first week' starts on day 2 because, by the authors' reading of their data, deaths in custody may have been recorded in some cohorts as deaths on the day of release, probably inflating the release-day rate (4,036 per 100,000 person-years; 826, with an interval of 0 to 3,455, in the ten cohorts that could separate the two). Deaths whose underlying cause was coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning, of unintentional or undetermined intent, a single category that does not separate alcohol, other drugs or combinations and names no drug, had a rate of 657 (332 to 1,076) in days 2 to 7, above suicide (135) and heart and blood vessel disease (71), and of 146 (103 to 197) over the whole follow-up, where they were the leading cause (16,126 deaths, 21.4%); yet 14,671 of these 16,126 deaths (91.0%) happened more than 4 weeks after release (Borschmann et al., 2024; the paper does not say whether counted from the first release in the study period or from the latest one), since most of the time people were followed lies beyond the first weeks (the editors' explanation). The study compared periods after release with one another, not with the general population; rates differed greatly between cohorts (236 to 1,183 per 100,000 person-years over the whole follow-up) and regions (days 2 to 7: Europe 2,762, the USA 934); causes came from death registers, and the paper reports no check of how deaths were certified or coded across countries and decades; and it analysed only age and sex, with no information on what happened between release and death, so it says nothing about drug use, treatment in custody or tolerance and cannot show why deaths cluster soon after release. Whether, and how fast, tolerance falls during a break from opioids is a separate answer, which rests on reviews (see the answer on tolerance after a break from opioids). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Is the time just after leaving prison more dangerous? In one large study, the risk of dying was highest in days 2 to 7 after release. Researchers followed about 1.5 million people released from prison or jail in eight countries. In the 16 of 18 groups with day-by-day records, deaths in days 2 to 7 were about 1.5 to 2 times as common as in the weeks that followed. Poisoning by alcohol or other drugs was the most common recorded cause of death, in that first week and overall. Still, 91 in 100 of these poisoning deaths happened more than 4 weeks after release. The records did not say which drugs were involved, and the study had no information on drug use or tolerance, so it cannot say why the first week is riskier.
population: People released from incarceration (prison or jail) in 18 cohorts of everyone released in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA, 1980–2018 (1,471,526 people; 88.3% men); analyses by time since release in the 16 cohorts, in seven countries, that could give deaths by day

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the all-cause first-week pattern: complete release cohorts linked to death registers and analysed under one plan, with sensitivity analyses for deaths in custody that may have been recorded on the day of release and for time back in custody (720 against 725). The cause-specific figures are less certain: death certification, toxicology and the coding of drug deaths and of undetermined intent were not appraised across eight countries and four decades (card sc_borschmann_2024: AMSTAR 2 critically low), and three Western Australian cohorts overlap in place and time.

inconsistency.note: I² is 91% for days 2–7 and 99–100% over the whole follow-up, and cohort rates range from 236 to 1,183, but the first-week excess holds in the pooled rate ratios with moderate heterogeneity (I² 26% against week 2); the heterogeneity concerns the size of the rates, which the statement gives with their range.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded for these mostly high-income cohorts, mostly men; the statement says that the poisoning category names no drug and includes alcohol and deaths of undetermined intent. The analyses by time since release leave out New Zealand's only cohort and one Washington cohort (16 of the 18 cohorts, in seven countries), which the statement says.

imprecision.note: The days 2–7 intervals are wide (all causes 1,048 to 2,287; poisoning 332 to 1,076), but the rate ratios against later periods exclude 1 (1.5, 1.2 to 1.8).

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the study; an individual participant data consortium analysed under one plan is less exposed to selective publication.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (crude death rates by time since release): starts low; not downgraded and not upgraded (descriptive claims are never upgraded). The rating applies to the all-cause pattern; the poisoning figures, taken alone, would be rated very low for risk of bias (unappraised cause-of-death coding across countries and decades), and the statement labels them as coded causes that name no drug. The rates by time since release come from the 16 cohorts that could give deaths by day (Figure 2), which the statement says and which does not change the rating. Status single study: one individual participant data meta-analysis; the cohort-by-cohort results by time since release are in the appendix, which was not read, so the 18 cohorts are not counted as independent replications here, and earlier studies of deaths after release (for example Binswanger et al., 2007, whose Washington cohort is one of the 18) were not read. The first-week peak and the 91.0% share of poisoning deaths after 4 weeks hold together because most person-time lies beyond the first weeks (study card note; the editors' explanation in the statement). Nothing about tolerance was measured, and the claim does not attribute the early peak to it.

statement: In people with alcohol or drug problems followed for between about a year and several decades, a large share no longer met the criteria for the problem at a later interview, but how many depends on who was counted (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, or people who had already recovered), on how a problem, recovery ('remission') and treatment were defined, and on the length of the time window; how many recovered without treatment was measured only in studies of alcohol problems. Of 451 men interviewed from a random sample of 470 US Army enlisted men who returned from Vietnam in September 1971 (interviews 8 to 12 months after return), 43% had used narcotics there (about a third of the men had tried heroin) and 20% reported having been dependent on narcotics there (21% by the study's own criteria for dependence), against 10% who had used narcotics and 0.7% who reported dependence (1% by the criteria) since their return; of 134 men from the study's two samples who were still dependent when they left Vietnam, 50% used narcotics again after return and 14% were dependent again (the table's numbers add up to both samples together, with no weighting stated). The authors give a remission rate of 95% without saying which sample it describes; their figure, read approximately, shows that of the men first dependent in Vietnam, about 2% of 90 in the general sample and about 7% of 341 in a second sample (selected on a urine test at departure positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates) were dependent again. Remission there meant not being dependent again within about a year; many of the men counted as remitted still used narcotics, and a period of more-than-weekly narcotic use was more common after return than before Vietnam (3% against under 0.5%); men whose urine was positive at departure were to be held for detoxification and treatment, but how many men received drug treatment, before or after return, is not reported; and the authors leave open whether the men's backgrounds or the change from Vietnam to home explains the remission (Robins et al., 1975). In a US national survey of adults interviewed in 2001–2002 and again about three years later (34,653 re-interviewed), 422 of the 1,172 people who had met the criteria for alcohol dependence in the year before the first interview met them again in the year before the second (36%), so about 64% did not (1,172 = 422 + 750, an editors' sum; both shares are editors' calculations from unweighted counts in a survey that over-sampled young adults and Black and Hispanic people, so they are not national estimates); in the paper's own weighted analysis, persistence was 32.4% at ages 21–23 and 44.5% at ages 43–52. Not meeting the full criteria can include people with one or two symptoms left, and treatment between the interviews is not reported (Vergés et al., 2012). A meta-analysis of 21 studies of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders, published 2000–2015 and mostly from the US (20 cohorts followed for 3 to 50 years, mean 17, 15 of them recruited through treatment, and one national survey that estimated remission over a lifetime), found 54% (95% CI 42% to 66%) of the people followed to the end in remission at the last follow-up, and 35% (25% to 46%) of everyone enrolled when deaths and people lost to follow-up were counted as not remitted; without the lifetime survey, about 50% (editors' recalculation) and 31%. Among the people followed to the end, single studies ranged from about 20% to 96%, the top value being the lifetime survey, and this rate, unlike the rate among everyone enrolled, was higher in cohorts followed longer and in cohorts that kept fewer of their participants. For treatment, the review compared cohorts only by whether people were in treatment when they entered, which cannot show who recovered without treatment: 51% with treatment at entry against 62% without (p 0.42), the six without including the lifetime survey (about 49% without it, editors' recalculation). Treatment during follow-up was not analysed, the pooled figures mix very different follow-up times and so describe no particular time point, the review reports no appraisal of its cohorts, and its authors read the results as showing that for many people these disorders are long-lasting (Fleury et al., 2016). For alcohol problems, a review of 124 estimates of recovery without treatment from 27 published studies (1976–2018, 24 of them North American; 71 of the estimates, the lowest among them, calculated by the reviewers from the studies' data) found figures from 2.7% to 98.3%, largely because the studies counted different things: among people already recovered, the share never treated (78% in two Canadian population surveys when recovery included moderate drinking, 56% and 66% when it meant not drinking); among people with an alcohol problem who stayed untreated, the share who recovered (in the US national survey of 2001–2002, 12.4% when recovery meant not drinking and 32.6% when moderate drinking also counted; in a Dutch survey, 78% of people with an alcohol use disorder who stayed untreated for three years were in remission at follow-up, against 40% of those whose disorder was moderate or severe; in one US cohort of people who had had no treatment beyond a single detoxification or a visit to an information and referral centre, 36.0% were in remission at both the 1- and 3-year follow-ups, and 14.0% when it also had to hold 16 years later); and among everyone with an alcohol problem, the share who recovered without treatment, which gave the lowest figures (2.7% to 63.6% in the nine studies that allowed all three counts). Most studies used a window of about one year, the review did not appraise the studies, and these figures are second-hand (Mellor et al., 2019). So a high share of never-treated people among those who recovered and a much lower share of everyone with a problem recovering without treatment in a year can both be right. No source read here measured recovery without treatment for drugs other than alcohol; for the Vietnam veterans, how many were treated is not reported. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment? Many do, but the numbers depend on how studies count. Of US soldiers in Vietnam, 20 in 100 said they had been dependent on narcotics there; in the year after coming home, about 1 in 100 had been. How many had treatment was not counted. In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent three years later, though some still had a few. In 20 long studies, mostly of people who had been in treatment, and one survey, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen, on average 17 years later. For alcohol, studies of recovery without treatment give anything from about 3 to 98 in 100, mostly because they count different groups: among people who have recovered, many were never treated; among everyone with a drinking problem, fewer recover without treatment in a given year. Most of this is about alcohol or heroin.
population: US Army enlisted men returning from Vietnam in September 1971, interviewed 8 to 12 months later (451 in a random general sample; 898 in both samples) (Robins et al., 1975); US adults in a national household survey interviewed in 2001–2002 and 2004–2005 (34,653 re-interviewed; 1,172 of them with past-year alcohol dependence at the first interview, an editors' sum) (Vergés et al., 2012); 21 studies of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders published 2000–2015 (20 cohorts, 15 recruited through treatment, and one national survey's lifetime estimate) (Fleury et al., 2016); 27 studies of untreated remission from alcohol problems, 1976–2018, mostly North American (Mellor et al., 2019)
exposure: Having had an alcohol or drug problem (narcotic dependence in Vietnam, self-reported or by the study's own criteria; DSM-IV alcohol dependence; substance use disorders as each cohort diagnosed them; alcohol problems as each study defined them), with or without treatment as each study defined it
comparator: None (descriptive); the same people's earlier status; in the alcohol review, three different denominators (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, people already recovered)
outcome: No longer meeting the criteria for the problem (remission) at a later interview or at the last follow-up, as each study defined it (not dependent again within about a year; not meeting full DSM-IV criteria in the year before an interview about three years later; at least six months without meeting criteria; abstinence or moderate drinking), and the share of it without treatment
magnitude: Robins et al. (1975), general sample N=451, before / in / since Vietnam: narcotic use 11% / 43% / 10%; dependence self-reported 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%, by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%. Still dependent at departure (both samples pooled, no weighting stated, n=134): 50% used narcotics after return, 14% dependent again. A period of more-than-weekly narcotic use since return 3% vs under 0.5% before service. Men first dependent in Vietnam dependent again 8–10 months after return (Figure, approximate): about 2% (general sample, N=90) and about 7% (urine-positive sample, N=341). Stated remission rate 95% (no denominator). Vergés et al. (2012), NESARC 2001–2002 to 2004–2005: 422 of 1,172 with past-year alcohol dependence (36%) dependent again about three years later, about 64% (750) not (1,172 = 422 + 750, and both shares are editors' calculations, unweighted); weighted persistence 32.4% (ages 21–23) and 44.5% (43–52). Fleury et al. (2016), 21 studies (20 cohorts, follow-up 3–50 years, and one lifetime survey estimate entered as 95.7%): standard remission 54.4% (95% CI 42.1–66.2), studies 19.6–95.7%, I² 99.4%; conservative 35.0% (25.2–46.4), I² 99.5%; without the lifetime survey, standard about 50.1% (42.5–57.6; editors' recalculation from Fig. 4, matching the lowest printed leave-one-out value) and conservative 30.9% (26.1–36.1, printed); treatment at baseline 51.1% vs not 62.4% (standard rate, p 0.421; about 48–49% for the five cohorts without treatment at baseline other than the lifetime survey, editors' recalculation; the printed conservative-rate subgroups could not be rebuilt from Fig. 4); standard rate higher with longer follow-up (B 0.046 per year, p 0.004) and lower retention (p 0.016), neither for the conservative rate. Mellor et al. (2019), alcohol, 124 estimates (71 calculated by the reviewers): 2.7% to 98.3%; nine studies with all three methods: all people with a problem 2.7–63.6%, untreated people 6.5–77.9%, remitted people 4.3–94.2% (6.4% with Table 3's values) (unweighted medians 12.4, 38.9 and 43.9, not rates); 78% of remitted people untreated (two Canadian surveys; abstinence or moderate drinking; 56.0% and 65.7% with abstinence only); 12.4% vs 32.6% of untreated people remitted (abstinence vs abstinence or moderate drinking; NESARC); 78% vs 40% of people untreated for three years in remission (any vs moderate or severe disorder; Netherlands); 36.0% vs 14.0% (remission at both 1 and 3 years vs also at 16 years; the 14.0% a reviewers' calculation; a US cohort).

risk_of_bias.note: The figures on recovery without treatment are second-hand from a review that did not appraise its 27 studies, 71 of whose 124 estimates the reviewers calculated themselves (card sc_mellor_2019: narrative-review checklist, high); the meta-analysis reports no appraisal of its cohorts and pools follow-ups of 3 to 50 years with a lifetime survey estimate (card sc_fleury_2016: AMSTAR 2 critically low); the Vietnam study rests on self-report at one interview, study-specific criteria, a window of about a year and a 95% figure without a denominator (card sc_robins_1975: JBI moderate); in the national survey, offset includes people with residual symptoms and 20% were not re-interviewed (card sc_verges_2012). A claim seen through reviews is downgraded for risk of bias (METHODS 6.3).

inconsistency.note: Estimates range from 2.7% to 98.3%, but the review shows that the range follows mostly from the denominator and the definitions, and every source finds remission common on its own terms; not downgraded, because the statement ties each figure to its definition and sample.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: each figure is given with its population (young US enlisted men in 1971–1972; US adults with alcohol dependence in 2001–2005; mostly treatment-recruited cohorts; mostly North American alcohol studies), and the statement says that no source read measured recovery without treatment for drugs other than alcohol; for the Vietnam veterans, how many were treated is not reported.

imprecision.note: Large samples behind the main figures; the Vietnam figures for dependence after return rest on small numbers (about 4 to 5 men dependent after return in the general sample) and approximate readings of a figure, stated as such.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for descriptive survey figures; the alcohol review included every numeric estimate it found, whatever its size.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim: starts low and is rated as a description of the samples. Down one for risk of bias, because the part of the question about recovery without treatment rests on second-hand, unappraised estimates (and on a meta-analysis of unappraised, mostly treatment-recruited cohorts): very low. A lenient reading would rate the Vietnam and national-survey figures alone (primary data from a near-complete random sample and a weighted national survey) as low for the narrower statement that many people no longer meet the criteria within one to three years; the rating is set by the weakest necessary link. Not upgraded (descriptive). Status replicated: the direction holds in independent samples (Vietnam veterans; the US national survey; the cohorts pooled by Fleury et al.), but the US national survey appears in four places (Vergés et al.; two of the studies pooled by Fleury et al., the lifetime estimate and Moss et al., 2010, a general-population sample from the same survey followed for three years; and Dawson et al. in Mellor et al.), which are not counted as independent of each other. Not used: the 95% remission rate as a figure (no stated denominator), Fleury et al.'s annual remission rates (inconsistent with its pooled proportions), its 14 years of use before remission (not derivable from its table) and its conservative-rate comparison by treatment at entry (not reproducible from its study values), and Mellor et al.'s medians as rates (card reporting issues). The comparison of cohorts by treatment at entry describes who entered each study, not who recovered without treatment.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether a richer, shared living space makes animals take less of a drug, and animal studies like these cannot by themselves show how surroundings shape drug use in people. In three small experiments from one laboratory (Simon Fraser University; 1978, 1979 and 1981; all three papers read here), rats living together in a large open box (8.8 m², with sawdust or wood shavings and small cages, boxes or empty cans to explore: 'Rat Park') drank less morphine solution than rats housed alone in small cages, but only under particular conditions. In 1978, 32 rats that had already had morphine solution beside water for 3 weeks were given morphine solution as their only fluid for 57 days, apart from 4 choice days. On choice days late in that period, between later 3-day cycles of no fluid, morphine only and water only, and after 2 and 5 weeks without morphine, the caged rats took more morphine per kilogram than the rats living together (on the cycle choice days, for example, 19.7 against 2.3 mg/kg in females and 6.4 against 0.8 in males), and females more than males. When morphine solution was their only fluid, however, the rats living together drank more of it: 37.2 against 26.6 g of solution a day after the first 2 weeks, or 18.6 against 13.3 mg of morphine hydrochloride per rat per day, a time base that the critical history's table leaves out. Five of the 14 females died, leaving 2 caged females, whose averages were the highest; the largest test is printed with degrees of freedom that do not fit a comparison between the 27 rats analysed; and the authors called their explanations speculative and drew no conclusion about people (Alexander et al., 1978). In 1979, 36 rats never given morphine before (9 of each sex in each housing; one caged male was accidentally killed) and never made to drink it were offered, beside water, six 5-day phases of morphine solution made sweeter and then weaker in a fixed order (0.5 mg/ml plain, then with 1%, 5% and 10% sucrose, then 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml with 10% sucrose). On the first day of plain morphine solution there was no indication of a housing effect (both F < 1.0); after that, caged rats drank more and the gap grew over the phases, though by the paper's significance marks housing was not significant for mg/kg in two of the six phases, and with 1% sucrose caged females drank less than colony females. In the last phase, the only one with printed means, caged females took 36.64 against 7.29 mg/kg in colony females, and caged males 24.09 against 1.46 (the paper's 5:1 and more than 16:1; time base not stated); females generally drank more than males. All 18 colony rats, males and females together, shared one enclosure, and the authors suggest that pregnancy and nursing may have raised colony females' fluid needs; they judged the housing effect established, at least for one strain, and drew no conclusion about people (Hadaway et al., 1979). The critical history's summary, a housing difference only with sweet, weak solutions, is narrower than the paper's own significance marks, which show a housing difference on at least one measure in every morphine phase (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In 1981, with 4 rats of each sex in each of four housing histories and sweetened solutions offered from strongest to weakest without any earlier forced drinking, males living in the colony at the time of testing drank much less morphine solution than caged males, whatever their housing before 65 days of age; early isolation raised colony males' intake only at the weakest strength; in females the results were less conclusive, and after allowing for their intake of a bitter-sweet control solution only the share of fluid taken as morphine solution still differed; and the sexes did not differ. The paper states that caged males drank 19 times as much as colony males at 0.5 mg/ml and 6 times as much at 0.3 mg/ml, per kilogram. The 19-fold figure is for males only (8 against 8), rests on 2 of that phase's 5 days (the others were lost to an equipment fault) and cannot be checked from printed values: the editors' approximate reading of the paper's own figure gives about 11-fold, and the printed table for 0.3 mg/ml gives about 5.8-fold (49.8 against 8.6 mg/kg, editors' calculation). The difference narrowed at the weakest strength, and the authors themselves suggest that longer exposure might shrink it; they still wrote that these and two earlier experiments suggest an effect 'both large and robust', and drew two conclusions, both about animal experiments: that isolated housing may strongly increase opiate intake in them, so that generalizations from them should be qualified, and that something differing between the two kinds of housing must affect a powerful control of opiate taking (Alexander et al., 1981). In all three papers, the two housing conditions drank from different devices measured in different ways: weighed bottles on the cage for caged rats, and, for the colony, drop dispensers at the end of a narrow runway (1978) or a tunnel taking one rat at a time (1979 and 1981), with drops counted and each drinker identified by camera; and in each, all the colony rats shared one enclosure, so housing was compared in a single colony (Alexander et al., 1978; Alexander et al., 1981; Hadaway et al., 1979). Groups were small, males and females lived together in Rat Park with no account of pregnancies, and the many comparisons raised the risk of chance findings (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). Two experiments designed to repeat the 1981 study with a similar but not identical procedure (4-day rather than 5-day phases, 0.25 and 0.125 rather than 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml, and rats kept in one housing from weaning), each with 10 male and 10 female rats in each housing condition, did not reproduce its result: in the first, colony rats drank slightly more of the strongest solution (3.6 against 0.0 g a day), and at the three weaker ones the differences were not significant, with colony averages higher; in the second, with the colony's intake known only as a group total and no statistical test, isolated rats drank more at three of four strengths, the direction of the original finding, but by smaller margins than the up-to-sevenfold difference Petrie gives for the 1981 rats kept in their first housing, both sexes together, without naming the measure (Petrie, 1996). The author's explanation, a change in the supplier's breeding stock, was not tested, and this study too measured intake differently in the two housing conditions. Other housing studies, summarized second-hand, point both ways: in one, rats reared in enriched or impoverished conditions did not differ in morphine intake and the enriched rats drank more cocaine solution; in another, isolated rats quickly learned to give themselves intravenous cocaine while socially housed rats did not consistently (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). Of the first, the 1979 authors note that neither group drank appreciable amounts of the bitter, unsweetened morphine solution (Hadaway et al., 1979). In a different kind of experiment, male rats offered a choice between an intravenous cocaine infusion and a sweet drink almost all came to prefer the sweet drink, also after a period of escalating cocaine intake and while under the influence of cocaine, though they still chose cocaine on about 16% of choices (about 3 infusions a day with the sampling trials), and with plain water as the alternative they preferred cocaine (Lenoir et al., 2007); earlier studies in monkeys, as those authors note, found most monkeys preferring high doses of cocaine to food. Every finding here comes from animals under laboratory conditions; how housing, poverty, opportunity or social exclusion shape drug use and drug problems in people is not shown by these designs. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: What did the 'Rat Park' studies show about environment and morphine? Less than is often said, and only in rats. In the Rat Park studies of 1978 to 1981, rats living together in a big space with things to do drank less morphine water than rats kept alone, but only in some tests; in 1978, when morphine water was almost all they had to drink, the Rat Park rats drank more. In 1979, rats that had never had morphine were offered morphine water made sweeter, then weaker, step by step; by the last step, rats kept alone drank 5 times (females) and more than 16 times (males) as much as rats living together, but on the first day of plain morphine water there was no difference. The biggest difference reported, 19 times as much in 1981, came from 8 male rats against 8 over just 2 days of measuring; the study's own graph looks closer to 11 times. The groups were small, the rats living together all shared one pen, and in all three studies the two groups drank from different machines measured in different ways. Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 study did not repeat its result. In a different kind of study, rats almost always chose a sweet drink over cocaine, but chose cocaine over plain water. None of this tested people, so it cannot say how where people live shapes their drug use. See the contested question.
population: Laboratory rats: Wistar rats in the three Rat Park experiments of 1978–1981 (1978: 32 rats, 27 analysed; 1979: 36, 9 of each sex in each housing, 8 caged males after one was accidentally killed; 1981: 32, 4 of each sex in each of four housing histories); 80 outbred Wistar rats of both sexes in two repeat experiments (Petrie, 1996); male Wistar rats in cocaine-choice experiments (Lenoir et al., 2007); no people
exposure: Housing together in a large enclosure or colony box from weaning or at testing ('Rat Park'); in the choice experiments, a sweet drink (saccharin or sucrose water) available as an alternative to cocaine
comparator: Rats housed alone in small standard cages; in the choice experiments, rats offered only the cocaine lever, or water instead of the sweet drink
outcome: Voluntary intake of oral morphine solution (sweetened or not) beside water; choice of intravenous cocaine infusions against the alternative
magnitude: Not estimable as an effect of environment. Alexander et al. (1978), choice days, mg morphine HCl/kg, caged females (n = 2), caged males (6), females living together (7), males living together (12): forced period 6.96, 4.09, 1.00, 0.26; Nichols cycles 19.7, 6.4, 2.3, 0.8; abstinence 6.2, 1.5, 1.5, 0.07 (Table 1, p. 177); housing F = 21.46 (forced period) and 26.38 (abstinence), df 1/23; Nichols cycles F = 200.90 printed with df 1/69, whereas a test between the 27 rats analysed has 23 error df; with morphine solution as the only fluid (after the first 2 weeks, sexes pooled, no variability or test), 37.2 g a day living together vs 26.6 g caged, 18.6 vs 13.3 mg morphine HCl per rat per day (p. 176), a time base missing from the critical history's table (Gage & Sumnall, 2019, PDF p. 8). Hadaway et al. (1979), last phase (0.15 mg/ml in 10% sucrose), mg morphine HCl/kg, mean ± SE: caged females 36.64 ± 2.70 (n = 9), caged males 24.09 ± 7.10 (8), colony females 7.29 ± 2.70 (9), colony males 1.46 ± 0.73 (9), printed as 5:1 (females) and more than 16:1 (males), time base not stated, the only intake means printed; first day of 0.5 mg/ml unsweetened, housing F < 1.0 on both measures; by the figures' significance marks, housing significant for mg/kg in 4 of 6 morphine phases (not with 1% or 5% sucrose) and for share of fluid in 5 of 6 (not unsweetened); the critical history's summary (Gage & Sumnall, 2019: housing difference only with 10% sucrose, largest at 0.15 mg/ml) is narrower. Alexander et al. (1981), males, 8 caged vs 8 in the colony at testing: stated ratios 19 (0.5 mg/ml; 2 of 5 days usable) and 6 (0.3 mg/ml), mg/kg (p. 572); Table 2, 0.3 mg/ml: housing at testing F = 33.64 (df 1, 12; p < 0.0001; printed without df in the critical history's table, PDF p. 9), early housing F = 0.13, interaction F = 4.32 (p = 0.06); condition means (editors' calculation) caged throughout 41.1, colony then caged 58.5, caged then colony 14.7, colony throughout 2.4 mg/kg, so 49.8 caged vs 8.6 in the colony at testing, 5.8-fold (p. 574); editors' approximate reading of Fig. 1b at 0.5 mg/ml about 58 and 44 vs about 5 mg/kg (about 11-fold), the figure's 0.3 mg/ml points lying 1 to 5 mg/kg above Table 2 (p. 573); females, after adjustment for quinine–sucrose intake, a housing difference only in the share of fluid (F = 5.53, 8.91, 6.52); sex 1 of 76 tests significant (p. 573). Petrie (1996), isolated vs colony, grams of morphine solution a day: Experiment 1, 1.0 mg/ml 0.0 vs 3.6 (colony more; F(1, 34) = 80.98 for grams), 0.5 mg/ml 0.5 vs 1.3, 0.25 mg/ml 15.7 vs 18.3, 0.125 mg/ml 30.2 vs 42.8 (no significant housing difference at these three; colony means higher; no SDs); Experiment 2 (no test), 0.3 vs 4.3, 9.4 vs 3.0, 17.4 vs 10.9, 44.4 vs 33.1; the 1981 difference between rats kept in their first housing, both sexes, described as up to sevenfold (measure not stated). Lenoir et al. (2007), male rats, intravenous cocaine (0.25 mg per infusion, study condition) vs 20 s of 0.2% saccharin: saccharin preferred from day 2 (N = 43); rats preferring cocaine 2.3% (drug-naive), 8.3% (first trained on cocaine), none of 11 (after intake escalated from 7.34 to 26.04 mg/day); cocaine chosen on about 15.6% of choices on average; with plain water as the alternative, cocaine preferred.
