risk_of_bias.note: Animal experiments without described random allocation, in which housing came with a different drinking device and a different, unblinded measurement of intake and, in the originals, all colony rats shared one enclosure: the three originals, all now read (cards sc_alexander_1978, sc_hadaway_1979 and sc_alexander_1981: SYRCLE high; in 1978 also the deaths of 5 of 14 females, selectively reported periods and measures, and a between-group test printed with degrees of freedom that do not fit; in 1979 also a mixed-sex colony analysed as 18 independent rats, a fixed order of solutions, and intake means printed for one phase only), and the repeat (card sc_petrie_1996: SYRCLE high); the choice experiments had no random allocation and excluded 15% of rats, mostly from the cocaine-only condition (card sc_lenoir_2007: SYRCLE high).

inconsistency.note: The original experiments and the direct repeat point in opposite directions, the repeat's two experiments disagree with each other in three of four morphine phases, the sex difference seen in 1978 and 1979 was not seen in 1981, and the other housing studies summarized point both ways.

indirectness.note: Preclinical evidence is always indirect: oral morphine drinking beside water, or a few intravenous cocaine infusions a day in a choice procedure, in one rat strain; cage against colony box is a narrow stand-in for an environment. Rated as worded, for animals; the statement says that nothing about people can be shown.

imprecision.note: Groups of 2 to 12 rats per sex and housing in 1978 (2 caged females after the deaths), 8 or 9 in 1979 and 4 per sex and housing history in 1981, with one colony in each experiment; the 1981 headline ratio resting on 2 days of data with no printed values, and 10 per sex and housing condition in the repeat, which gives no standard deviations and in one experiment no test.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; one published repeat attempt is known from the sources read.

grade.reasoning: Animal experiments without described random allocation start low (all three original Rat Park papers are now read, each at high risk of bias). Down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Reading the originals does not change the rating: they confirm the small groups and the different measurement in the two housing conditions, show that the 1978 amounts with morphine as the only fluid were per rat per day, and show that the 1981 19-fold figure rests on 2 days of data in 8 against 8 males, with the paper's own table giving about 6-fold at the next strength. The 1979 paper, read on 12 November (evening), does not change it either: its printed 5-fold and more-than-16-fold differences come from the last phase of a fixed sequence, after no difference on the first day of plain morphine solution, in one mixed-sex colony measured differently from the caged rats; it replaces the critical history's description of that experiment, whose summary (a difference only with sweet, weak solutions) is narrower than the paper's own significance marks. The three originals come from one laboratory, so they count as one team's experiments, not as independent replication. The relation is insufficient evidence: a housing effect on drug intake in rats is neither shown nor excluded. Status contested: the original findings and the direct repeat point in opposite directions, and a credible published critique changes how the originals should be read (METHODS 6.4), so the six-part box applies. The choice experiments of Lenoir et al. (2007) answer a different question (a sweet drink against cocaine) and are kept apart from the housing evidence; their preference is consistent within one procedure, one strain and one sex, and earlier monkey studies point the other way. The critical history misattributes Petrie's repeat to the 1979 study (card reporting issue); the statement names the 1981 study, as Petrie does. Petrie (1996) gives no dates for its experiments, so the repeat is dated by its publication.

debate.question: Do rats living together in a large, furnished space take less morphine or cocaine than rats housed alone, as the 'Rat Park' experiments reported for morphine (Alexander et al., 1978; Alexander et al., 1981; Hadaway et al., 1979), and what can such studies say about people?
debate.evidence_yes: In the 1978 experiment, after 57 days with morphine solution as their only fluid, caged rats drank more of it than rats living together on choice days late in that period, between later cycles and after 2 and 5 weeks without morphine (housing F = 21.46 and 26.38, df 1/23, both p < 0.001; F = 200.90 printed with df 1/69 for the cycle choice days), for example 19.7 against 2.3 mg/kg in females and 6.4 against 0.8 in males on the cycle choice days (Alexander et al., 1978). In 1981, without any earlier forced drinking, males living in the colony at the time of testing drank much less sweetened morphine solution than caged males, whatever their housing in early life: 8 of 9 tests at the three weaker strengths were significant, the printed table for 0.3 mg/ml gives 8.6 against 49.8 mg/kg (editors' calculation; F = 33.64, df 1 and 12, p < 0.0001), and the authors state 19-fold and 6-fold differences at 0.5 and 0.3 mg/ml (Alexander et al., 1981). In 1979, in 36 rats never given morphine before and never made to drink it, caged rats drank more than colony rats of a series of morphine solutions made sweeter and then weaker, the gap growing to 36.64 against 7.29 mg/kg in females and 24.09 against 1.46 in males in the last phase, and females generally drank more than males (Hadaway et al., 1979). In the second experiment of the repeat, isolated rats drank more of three of the four morphine solutions (for example 44.4 against 33.1 g a day at the weakest), the direction of the original finding, though without a test (Petrie, 1996). As summarized second-hand, isolated rats quickly learned to give themselves intravenous cocaine while socially housed rats did not consistently (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In choice experiments, almost every male rat came to prefer a sweet drink to intravenous cocaine, across the cocaine doses, delays and costs tested, after escalating intake and during intoxication (2.3% of drug-naive rats, 8.3% of rats first trained on cocaine and none of 11 rats with escalated intake preferred cocaine) (Lenoir et al., 2007). The critical history still calls the core message, that drug problems are more than a biological response to a drug, important (Gage & Sumnall, 2019).
debate.evidence_no: When morphine solution was their only fluid, the 1978 rats living together drank more of it than caged rats (37.2 against 26.6 g of solution a day; 18.6 against 13.3 mg per rat per day), and caged rats drank less on the cycles' morphine-only days; five of the 14 females died, leaving 2 caged females, whose averages were the highest, and the cycle-day test is printed with degrees of freedom that do not fit a comparison between rats (Alexander et al., 1978). The 1981 19-fold figure is for 8 against 8 males on 2 of 5 days, with no values printed for that phase, and the editors' approximate reading of the paper's own figure gives about 11-fold; in females the results were less conclusive and, after allowing for their intake of a bitter-sweet control solution, only the share of fluid taken as morphine solution still differed; and the difference narrowed at the weakest strength, where the authors suggest that longer exposure might shrink it (Alexander et al., 1981). In 1979, there was no indication of a housing effect on the first day of plain morphine solution, housing was not significant for mg/kg in two of the six phases, the solutions came in one fixed order, and the 18 colony rats, males and females together, shared one enclosure, so housing was compared in a single colony (Hadaway et al., 1979); in all three experiments groups were very small, males and females shared the colony and many comparisons were made (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In all three papers, the two housing conditions drank from different devices measured in different ways (Alexander et al., 1978; Alexander et al., 1981; Hadaway et al., 1979). The two experiments designed to repeat the 1981 study did not reproduce its result: in the first, with a statistical test, colony rats drank slightly more of the strongest solution (3.6 against 0.0 g a day) and the differences at the weaker ones were not significant (colony averages higher), and no difference in either experiment came near the up-to-sevenfold difference Petrie gives for the 1981 rats kept in their first housing (Petrie, 1996). As summarized second-hand, rats reared in enriched or impoverished conditions did not differ in morphine intake, and the enriched rats drank more cocaine solution (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In earlier choice studies, most monkeys preferred high doses of cocaine to food, in one study to a sucrose pellet, as Lenoir et al. (2007) note, and the rats' preference for a sweet drink was shown in one strain, one sex and one procedure with eight choices a day; with plain water as the alternative, the rats preferred cocaine (Lenoir et al., 2007).
debate.neither_can_show: None of these studies measured anything in people (Alexander et al., 1978; Alexander et al., 1981; Hadaway et al., 1979; Lenoir et al., 2007; Petrie, 1996): a cage against a colony box is a narrow stand-in for a human environment, oral morphine drinking or a few cocaine infusions a day is not human drug use, and housing, poverty, opportunity, social exclusion and access to services, which matter for people, were not studied (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). Even for rats, measuring intake by different methods in the two housing conditions, in the originals and in the repeat (Alexander et al., 1978; Alexander et al., 1981; Hadaway et al., 1979; Petrie, 1996), means that part of any difference could come from the measuring; space, company, bedding and objects changed together, as the original authors note (Alexander et al., 1978; Alexander et al., 1981), and so did the drinking device, so which of them mattered cannot be told; each original compared caged rats with a single colony, so a peculiarity of that one colony cannot be told apart from an effect of housing (Alexander et al., 1978; Alexander et al., 1981; Hadaway et al., 1979); the explanation offered for the failed repeat (a change in the rats' breeding stock) was not tested (Petrie, 1996); and no study read here allocated rats to housing at random and measured intake the same way in both groups.
debate.editors_reading: The editors' reading: the popular account, that rats in a rich environment refuse morphine, which the critical history notes is sometimes reported (Gage & Sumnall, 2019), is not what the original papers reported: rats living together did drink morphine solution, and in 1978 they drank more of it than caged rats when it was almost their only fluid (Alexander et al., 1978). The housing effect rests on three small experiments from one laboratory (Alexander et al., 1978; Alexander et al., 1981; Hadaway et al., 1979), each comparing caged rats with a single colony that drank from a different device measured in a different way; the largest printed difference in 1979 comes from the last phase of a fixed sequence, after no difference on the first day of plain morphine solution (Hadaway et al., 1979); the 19-fold figure the 1981 paper states rests on 2 days of data in 8 against 8 males, and its own table gives about 6-fold at the next strength (Alexander et al., 1981); and the one direct repeat did not reproduce the effect (Petrie, 1996). Whether housing changes drug taking in rats is therefore not settled; certainty very low. That a sweet drink can win over cocaine in a choice procedure is a separate rat finding, consistent within one procedure (plain water did not win) but contradicted by earlier monkey studies (Lenoir et al., 2007). For people, these studies can only suggest questions; the evidence in people is of other kinds (see the answers on recovery from drug and alcohol problems and on whether people choose other rewards over cocaine).
debate.what_would_settle_it: For rats: a preregistered, adequately powered replication with random allocation to colony or isolated housing and the same automated individual measurement of intake in both conditions, which neither the originals nor the repeat had (Alexander et al., 1978; Alexander et al., 1981; Hadaway et al., 1979; Petrie, 1996); several independent colonies for each housing condition, so that the colony rather than the rat is the unit compared, unlike the single colony of each original (Alexander et al., 1978; Alexander et al., 1981; Hadaway et al., 1979); strengths offered in a balanced rather than a fixed order, unlike the 1979 and 1981 studies (Alexander et al., 1981; Hadaway et al., 1979); both sexes housed so that litters cannot occur (Gage & Sumnall, 2019); blinded analysis; and more than one strain or supplier, since a change of breeding stock was proposed but not tested (Petrie, 1996). For people: longitudinal or natural-experiment studies of how housing, opportunity and social exclusion change the course of drug use, the kinds of factors the critical history names as mattering for people (Gage & Sumnall, 2019).

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether decriminalising the possession of all illegal drugs for personal use in Portugal, from cannabis to heroin and cocaine, changed drug use, drug deaths, HIV or the load on police and prisons. The law, in force from 1 July 2001, made acquiring, possessing or using up to ten days' supply an administrative offence dealt with by regional dissuasion commissions (panels of three that can refer people to treatment or impose sanctions such as fines) instead of a crime punishable by up to a year in prison; possession for supply stayed a crime. It came two years after a national drug strategy began expanding prevention, harm reduction, treatment and social reintegration (May 1999), and no study read compares Portugal with a modelled counterfactual. In national statistics compiled by two researchers who had studied the reform for years, set beside Spain and Italy where data allowed, without statistical tests (Hughes & Stevens, 2010), the share of people aged 15 to 64 who had ever used an illegal drug rose from 7.8% in 2001 (7.6% in the paper's table) to 12.0% in 2007, while use in the past year went from 3.4% to 3.7% (cannabis 3.3% to 3.6%, cocaine 0.3% to 0.6%, heroin 0.2% to 0.3%); there was no national survey before 2001, the paper does not say when in 2001 the first one was done, and past-year cannabis and cocaine use also rose in Spain and Italy. Among school students aged 15 to 16, lifetime use of any illegal drug was about 12% in 1999, 18% in 2003 and 14% in 2007 (editors' reading of a figure). Estimated problem drug use went from 7.6 to 6.8 per 1,000 people aged 15 to 64 between 2000 and 2005, within overlapping ranges that the authors say make the fall not statistically significant, and estimated injecting drug use from 3.5 to 2.0 per 1,000; both estimates are derived from numbers in treatment, which rose from 23,654 people in 1998 to 38,532 in 2008. New HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs fell from 907 in 2000 to 267 in 2008 and new AIDS cases from 506 to 108, a fall the paper says has been attributed primarily to expanded harm reduction, without saying by whom. Recorded drug-related deaths (deaths with a positive post-mortem test for an illegal drug, as the authors define this series in their later paper) went from a peak of 369 in 1999 and 280 in 2001 to about 150 a year in 2002–2004 and about 340 in 2008 (editors' readings of figures), while toxicological autopsies rose from 1,166 in 2002 to 2,805 in 2008; deaths that doctors certified as caused by drugs, a series that starts in 2001, went from about 76 in 2001 to about 9 in 2005 and about 20 in 2008 (editors' readings; Hughes & Stevens, 2012). Criminal drug arrests fell from over 14,000 people in 2000 to 5,000–5,500 a year, mostly because possession for personal use stopped counting as a crime: about 7,600 of the roughly 14,300 people arrested in 2000 were arrested for possession or use, and all police contacts for drug offences, crimes and administrative offences together, were about 10,500 to 12,000 a year after the reform against about 11,400 to 14,300 in 1998–2000 (editors' readings of a figure). The share of prisoners whose offences were drug-related fell from 44% in 1999 to 21% in 2008. Retail prices fell from 2001 (the peak year for heroin; cocaine and hash prices peaked in 2000), as measured from July 2001 by a different method; heroin and cocaine prices in 2008 were similar to those of 1998–1999. The authors state that it is impossible to say that any of these changes was the direct result of decriminalisation, and that expanded treatment and an ageing population of people who use heroin contributed. In a later critique of the two most publicised accounts, a report for the Cato Institute, a US libertarian think tank, that judged the reform a clear success and reports for an association for a drug-free Portugal (APLD) that judged it a clear failure, the same authors, who call themselves participants in the debate, found that each account rested on selected datasets and years, and argue that past-year use and doctor-certified deaths are better guides than lifetime use and toxicology-positive deaths (Hughes & Stevens, 2012; its erratum corrects only a remark on where one cited report could be found). The data end in 2008, with some series to 2009. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: What happened after Portugal stopped treating drug possession as a crime? In 2001 Portugal made having any drug for your own use, from cannabis to heroin, an offence handled by local panels that can refer people to treatment or give fines, instead of the courts; selling stayed a crime, and from 1999 the country had also been expanding treatment and other help for people who use drugs. In 2007 about 12 in 100 adults said they had ever used an illegal drug, against about 8 in 100 in 2001, but use in the past year barely changed (about 3 to 4 in 100). New HIV cases among people who use drugs fell from 907 in 2000 to 267 in 2008, and the share of prisoners held for drug-related crimes fell from 44 to 21 in 100. Deaths that doctors judged to be caused by drugs fell from about 76 in 2001 to about 20 in 2008, while deaths in which an illegal drug was found fell and then rose again as more than twice as many bodies were tested. Crime arrests for drugs fell, mostly because possession no longer counted as a crime. One famous report called the change a clear success and another a clear failure; the two researchers who compiled these figures, themselves part of the debate, found that both reports picked the figures that suited them. Nobody has shown how much of all this was the law itself. See the contested question.
population: People in Portugal, in national statistics mostly for 1998–2008: people aged 15 to 64 in the national household surveys of 2001 and 2007; school students (ESPAD, aged 15 to 16, and other school surveys); estimated numbers of people with problem drug use and of people who inject drugs; people who use drugs newly diagnosed with HIV or AIDS; deaths recorded by the National Institute of Forensic Medicine (positive toxicology test) and the National Statistics Institute (certified by doctors, from 2001); people arrested or detected for drug offences; prisoners; with Spain and Italy for some indicators
exposure: Decriminalisation of the acquisition, possession and use of all illegal drugs for personal use (up to ten days' supply), in force from 1 July 2001 under Law 30/2000: an administrative offence handled by regional dissuasion commissions instead of a crime; part of a national drug strategy that expanded prevention, harm reduction, treatment and social reintegration from May 1999
comparator: Portugal before July 2001 (late 1990s to 2001, depending on the indicator; no adult survey before 2001 and no doctor-certified death series before 2001); Spain and Italy, which had made drug use an administrative offence in 1992 and 1990, for some indicators; no modelled counterfactual
outcome: Reported drug use (lifetime, past year, past month) among adults and students; estimated problem and injecting drug use; new HIV and AIDS diagnoses among people who use drugs; drug-related deaths (toxicology-positive and doctor-certified); arrests and police contacts for drug offences; drug-related prisoners; retail prices; and what two publicised accounts claimed about these
magnitude: Hughes & Stevens (2010), Portugal, people aged 15–64: lifetime use of any illegal drug 7.8% (text; 7.6% in Table 1) in 2001 and 12.0% in 2007 (+4.4 points by Table 1); past-year 3.4% and 3.7% (+0.3); past-year cannabis 3.3% and 3.6%, cocaine 0.3% and 0.6%, heroin 0.2% and 0.3%, ecstasy 0.4% and 0.4%; Spain past-year cannabis 9.7% and 10.1%, cocaine 2.6% and 3.1%; Italy 6.2% and 14.6%, 1.1% and 2.2%. Students aged 15–16 (ESPAD), lifetime use of any illegal drug 8%, 12%, 18% and 14% in 1995, 1999, 2003 and 2007 (editors' reading). Problem drug use 7.6 (range 6.8–8.5) and 6.8 (6.2–7.4) per 1,000 aged 15–64 in 2000 and 2005; injecting 3.5 (2.3–4.6) and 2.0 (1.8–2.2); Italy, problem drug use 6.0 and 8.6 per 1,000 in 2001 and 2007. People in treatment 23,654 (1998) and 38,532 (2008). New HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs 907 (2000) and 267 (2008); AIDS 506 and 108. Recorded drug-related deaths 369 (1999); about 155, 152 and 157 in 2002–2004 and about 339 in 2008 (editors' readings of Figure 7); toxicological autopsies 1,166 (2002) and 2,805 (2008); deaths with opiates as the main substance 95% (1999) and 59% (2008). Criminal drug arrests over 14,000 (2000) and 5,000–5,500 a year after the reform; administrative detections about 6,000 a year; editors' readings of Figure 2: consumer offences about 7,600 of about 14,300 arrests in 2000; trafficking-type arrests about 4,500–6,300 a year in 1998–2000 and 5,200–5,600 in 2001–2008; all police contacts about 11,400–14,300 and 10,500–12,000 a year. Drug-related prisoners 44% (1999) and 21% (2008); prison density 119 (2001) and 101.5 (2005) per 100 places. Retail prices in euros per gram: heroin 38.50, 31.33, 49.72 and 50.27 (1998–2001) and 33.25 (2008); cocaine 45.63, 40.37, 60.31, 53.51 and 45.56. Hughes & Stevens (2012): toxicology-positive deaths (INML) 280 (2001), 216 (2006) and 314 (2007); doctor-certified drug deaths (INE) about 76 (2001), 34, 23, 20, 9 (2005), 12, 14 and 20 (2008) (editors' readings of Figure 4); adults' past-month use about 2.5% in 2001 and 2007; past-year use at 15–24 about 8.3% and 7.0%, at 25–34 about 4.9% and 7.0% (editors' readings of Figures 2 and 3); students' lifetime cannabis use (ESPAD) +60% around the reform, about 9.4% (1999) to 15.0% (2003), then about 13.0% (2007) (editors' readings of Figure 1). Neither paper gives intervals or statistical tests for these changes.

evidence.locator: Introduction, last two paragraphs (the first begins on p. 2) and footnote 1 (p. 3); The Portuguese Decriminalization and Drug Action Plan, 3rd to 6th paragraphs and footnote 3 (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: The reform made possession of all drugs, when deemed for personal use, an administrative rather than a criminal offence; possession for supply remained a crime (footnote 1). A government-appointed expert commission proposed both decriminalisation and Portugal's first national drug strategy; the strategy, with expanded resources for prevention, harm reduction, treatment, social reintegration and supply reduction, was rolled out from May 1999, and decriminalisation entered into force on 1 July 2001. Before the reform, possession, acquisition and cultivation for personal use were crimes punishable by up to 1 year in prison (in practice imprisonment for use or possession alone was rare, but criminal conviction was the norm, footnote 3); under Law 30/2000 possession and acquisition became an administrative (public order) offence sanctioned through regional dissuasion commissions (CDTs): panels of three, including lawyers, social workers and medical professionals, to which police refer people. The panels can impose a range of sanctions, including community service, fines, suspension of professional licences and bans on attending designated places, but their primary aim is to dissuade drug use and to encourage people who are dependent into treatment: they judge whether a person is dependent; for people judged dependent they can recommend treatment or education instead of a sanction, and for others they can order a provisional suspension of proceedings, attendance at a police station or at a psychological or educational service, or a fine. The law covers all illegal drugs, including cannabis, heroin and cocaine, up to ten days' supply; people found with more are charged and referred to the courts. The authors write that both of them had been involved in examining the reform for a number of years, and that two think-tank reports (their own of 2007 and one of 2009 by Greenwald) had appeared but no report had yet appeared in English peer-reviewed journals.

evidence.locator: Methods, 1st to 6th paragraphs (pp. 5–6)
evidence.extracted: Design: a review of Portuguese evaluative documents, including the annual national reports of the government drug agency (IDT) for 1998 to 2008 and the internal and external evaluations it carried out or commissioned, supplemented by interviews with 13 purposively sampled key informants in late 2007 and late 2009 (45–90 minutes; no member of the criminal justice system was willing or able to take part; the sample was not large enough to reach data saturation). The work built on the first author's research of 2002 to 2006, done in collaboration with the IDT. The authors call the absence of a control comparison the most important limitation (there is no counterfactual Portugal) and set Portuguese trends beside those of Spain and/or Italy, subject to data availability, using data reported to the EMCDDA; Italy and Spain had introduced administrative sanctions for drug use in 1990 and 1992 and made no radical change in the period. Implementation was not constant: at times between 2005 and 2008 up to 38% of the commissions, including the most frequented one, in Lisbon, were not operating. The authors state that these challenges make it impossible to attribute any changes in drug use or related harm directly to the decriminalisation, but that they can test the hypothesis that decriminalisation necessarily leads to increases in drug use and related harms.

evidence.locator: Implementation of the Decriminalization, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 6; the 3rd continues on p. 7) and 5th paragraph (p. 7); footnote 5 (p. 6)
evidence.extracted: Since 2002 the commissions opened about 6,000 cases a year (6,543 in 2008), which the authors estimate at about 2.5% of people who use drugs (from the 2007 estimate that 3.7% of people aged 15–64 used an illegal drug in the past year, about 261,968 people); 94% of those referred were male, 47% aged 16–24 and 31% aged 25–34. As fewer cases were decided between 2003 and 2006, the share of cases ending in a sanction fell from 75% in 2003 to 48% in 2006, a decline in decided cases that the agency linked to commissions not operating; the authors add that this trend has since been reversed, and by mid-2008 all commissions except Vila Real were operating again. Cases involving heroin fell from 33% (2001) to 14% (2006) and 13% (2008), and those involving cannabis rose from 53% to 70% and then fell to 64%. Provisional suspension for people judged not dependent was used in 59–68% of cases a year; provisional sanctions with treatment (for people judged dependent) fell from 31% (2002) to 18% (2008) of sanctions, and punitive sanctions rose from 3% to 15%. Only 5–6% of people were referred twice in a year; no data had been collected on prior or later offending or drug use of the people referred, which the agency said in September 2009 that it planned to start collecting.

evidence.locator: Drug-related death: Accounts compared to the available evidence, 1st to 4th paragraphs (pp. 106–108); Figure 4 (p. 107)
evidence.extracted: Portugal had not historically reported deaths directly attributable to drug intoxication, and overdose data became available only in November 2010. The main series, from the National Institute of Forensic Medicine (INML), counts deaths with a positive post-mortem toxicology test for illegal substances; it is the only series covering the years before and after the reform, it responds to recording practices such as the number of toxicological autopsies (which rose substantially from 2005 to 2009), and it shows that a drug was present, not that it caused the death, whereas the standard international classification relies on physicians' assessments of the cause. The National Statistics Institute (INE) series, made available recently and backdated to 2001, counts deaths that doctors determined under International Classification of Diseases protocols to be due to drugs; it fell from 2001, rose slightly from 2005 to 2008/9 and stayed well below its level at decriminalisation, which the authors take as support for the hypothesis that the INML rise was spurious. In the authors' view neither account grasped the full picture: the APLD account looked only at short-term patterns (such as the 2006–07 rise), and the Cato account at longer-term ones (1999 to 2005–06) without mentioning the years between, particularly 2002 to 2004, when recorded deaths were lowest. The authors say the falls are not attributable solely to the reform, expanded services being a more plausible explanation, but that, since a key goal of the reform was to ease access to treatment and harm reduction services and treatment access expanded after it, there is partial evidence that the reform may have contributed. Editors' readings of Figure 4 at 300 dpi, markers measured against the axes (approximate): INML about 318 (2000), 280 (2001), 156, 152, 157, 219, 217, 315 and 337 (2008); INE (right-hand axis, 0–80) about 76 (2001), 34, 23, 20, 9 (2005), 12, 14 and 20 (2008). risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_hughes_2010 (ROBINS-I, first pass, critical overall): national before-and-after aggregates set informally beside Spain and Italy, with no modelling or tests; the 1999 strategy that expanded treatment and harm reduction ran alongside the law and cannot be separated from it, nor can the growth of low-threshold opiate substitution, whose roll-out a footnote dates to 1990, possibly a misprint (confounding critical); several series change at the reform (possession arrests leave the criminal count; prices switch to traffickers' reports), recorded deaths follow the number of toxicological autopsies, problem-drug-use estimates follow treatment numbers, and most data come from the agency that ran the policy (measurement serious); indicators, baseline years and comparators were chosen without a protocol, some baselines at peaks (2000 for arrests, 2001 for prices). Card sc_hughes_2012 (editors' checklist, high): no systematic search, authors who are participants in the debate, the comparison with Spain and Italy restated from their own article without its caveat, and figures that cannot be reproduced from its own data. For any effect of the law these biases could change the reading entirely, so two levels.

inconsistency.note: The indicators point in different directions (lifetime use up while past-year use barely changed; toxicology-positive deaths back near the 1999 peak by 2008 while doctor-certified deaths stayed far below 2001), but the differences follow from what each indicator measures and from the rise in autopsies, as the authors argue; they are set out in the claim and are why it is contested, and are not rated down again.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: Portugal's law as implemented within its 1999 strategy, in national data up to 2008 (some series to 2009); the claim does not speak for other countries, other forms of decriminalisation or later years. That some figures are compiled second-hand from national reports is counted under risk of bias.

imprecision.note: Neither paper gives intervals or tests; the problem-drug-use ranges overlap; the doctor-certified death counts are small (about 9 to 76 a year) and, like the death and arrest figures for years without printed values, are editors' readings of figures. Not rated down separately: the claim concerns what the design can attribute, and the evidence is already at the floor.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: both papers are by the same two authors, and the two advocacy reports they discuss were not read.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence (national before-and-after statistics, and a critique that compiles further national series) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias, it is very low, the floor. The claim concerns whether the law changed outcomes, so its relation is insufficient evidence; the trends are reported in it as descriptions of the national figures, not rated as a separate claim. Counted once: the 2012 critique is by the same authors, restates the 2010 comparison with Spain and Italy and uses the same toxicology-positive death series; its new data are the doctor-certified death series (INE, from 2001) and re-presented school and adult survey figures, which enter as second-hand national statistics, while its judgements of the two advocacy accounts enter as what it argues. Status contested: credible figures point both ways on whether drug problems eased after 2001 (lifetime use rose, past-year cocaine and heroin use rose by tenths of a point and toxicology-positive deaths returned near the 1999 peak by 2008, while past-year use overall barely changed and estimated injecting, HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs, drug-related prisoners and doctor-certified deaths fell), and the critique changes the reading of the death trend and shows that both publicised accounts rested on selected data, so the six-part debate box applies. The erratum to the 2012 paper (Drug Alcohol Rev 2012;31:727, 10.1111/j.1465-3362.2012.00462.x), now read, corrects only the statement that a cited report of the US Office of National Drug Control Policy could not be found on that office's website (p. 111); nothing used here changes. Neither paper has a conflict-of-interest statement; the authors had studied the reform for years, partly in collaboration with the agency that ran it, and wrote one of the accounts in the debate.

debate.question: Did Portugal's 2001 decriminalisation of all drugs for personal use make drug problems better, as a report for the Cato Institute concluded, or worse, as reports for an association for a drug-free Portugal concluded (both as described by Hughes & Stevens, 2012), and how much of any change was the law itself (Hughes & Stevens, 2010)?
debate.evidence_yes: After 2001, past-year drug use among people aged 15 to 64 barely changed (3.4% in 2001, 3.7% in 2007), and among people aged 15 to 24 it fell (past year about 8.3% to 7.0%, past month about 5.7% to 4.1%, editors' readings of a figure) (Hughes & Stevens, 2010, 2012). Estimated injecting drug use fell from 3.5 to 2.0 per 1,000 people aged 15 to 64 between 2000 and 2005, and problem drug use from 7.6 to 6.8 (a fall within overlapping ranges), while in Italy the estimate of problem drug use rose from 6.0 to 8.6 per 1,000 between 2001 and 2007 (Hughes & Stevens, 2010). New HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs fell from 907 in 2000 to 267 in 2008 and AIDS cases from 506 to 108; the share of prisoners with drug-related offences fell from 44% in 1999 to 21% in 2008; people in treatment rose from 23,654 in 1998 to 38,532 in 2008; and the number of people detected under the new administrative system stayed at about 6,000 a year, which the authors read as no widening of formal contact with the police (Hughes & Stevens, 2010). Deaths that doctors certified as caused by drugs fell from about 76 in 2001 to about 20 in 2008 (editors' readings), and the authors argue that the later rise in toxicology-positive deaths reflects more toxicological autopsies, and that the reform may have contributed to falling deaths by easing access to treatment and harm reduction, one of its aims (Hughes & Stevens, 2012). On this evidence the authors conclude that the reform disconfirms the hypothesis that decriminalisation necessarily increases the most harmful forms of drug use (Hughes & Stevens, 2010).
debate.evidence_no: Lifetime use of any illegal drug among people aged 15 to 64 rose from 7.8% in 2001 to 12.0% in 2007, past-year cocaine use from 0.3% to 0.6% and past-year heroin use from 0.2% to 0.3%, with increases in every age group above 19 (Hughes & Stevens, 2010); past-year and past-month use rose at ages 25 to 34 (about 4.9% to 7.0% and 3.5% to 5.1%, editors' readings), and lifetime cannabis use among 16-year-old students in the longest school survey rose by 60% around the reform before falling slightly by 2007 (Hughes & Stevens, 2012). Deaths with a positive toxicology test for an illegal drug, the only death series that covers the years before and after the reform, rose from 216 in 2006 to 314 in 2007 and about 340 in 2008, close to the 1999 peak of 369 (Hughes & Stevens, 2010, 2012). In 2008 Portugal still had the third-highest rate of HIV among people who inject drugs in Europe and the fourth-highest incidence of new HIV cases (Hughes & Stevens, 2012). Several falls began before the law or are not what they seem: recorded deaths were already below the 1999 peak in 2000 and 2001, after the strategy began in May 1999 (editors' readings of a figure); treatment expanded strongly at the same time; most of the fall in criminal drug arrests is possession no longer counting as a crime; and price falls are measured from 2001 (the heroin peak, a year after the peaks for cocaine and hash) across a change of data source at the reform (Hughes & Stevens, 2010). The authors themselves dispute attributing Portugal's positive changes to decriminalisation alone and write that falls in opiate-related deaths are likely to reflect expanded treatment, particularly low-threshold opiate substitution (Hughes & Stevens, 2010), and that expanded services are a more plausible explanation for falling deaths than the reform (Hughes & Stevens, 2012). As implemented, the reform was partial: at times between 2005 and 2008 up to 38% of the dissuasion commissions, including Lisbon's, were not operating, and the share of cases ending in a sanction fell from 75% in 2003 to 48% in 2006, a fall the authors say has since been reversed (Hughes & Stevens, 2010).
debate.neither_can_show: Neither side's evidence comes from a design that can separate the law from what changed at the same time: the figures are national before-and-after statistics, set informally beside Spain and Italy, without modelling or statistical tests, while a national strategy expanded treatment and harm reduction from May 1999 and the population of people who use heroin aged (Hughes & Stevens, 2010). Several series changed at the reform itself: possession arrests left the criminal count in July 2001, price data switched from street-level police data to self-reports of traffickers and trafficker-consumers, and toxicology-positive deaths move with the number of toxicological autopsies (Hughes & Stevens, 2010, 2012). There was no national adult survey before 2001, and the doctor-certified death series starts in 2001, the reform year, so neither can show a change from the years before the reform; estimates of problem drug use rest on numbers in treatment, which rose as treatment expanded (Hughes & Stevens, 2010, 2012). Most data came from the government agency that ran the policy, the 13 interviews included no serving police or criminal justice representative, and both compilations read are by two authors who are participants in the debate; the two publicised accounts themselves have not been read here, and some figures in the critique cannot be reproduced from its own data, such as a 27–30% fall in students' lifetime cannabis use where the values it prints give falls of 36% and 27%, and a 16% fall in the other school surveys where its figure shows about 11% to 13% (editors' calculation; Hughes & Stevens, 2012). The data end in 2008, with some series to 2009.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In national statistics up to 2008, Portugal after 2001 saw a rise in the share of adults who had ever used an illegal drug (from about 8 to 12 in 100), little change in past-year use, falls in estimated injecting, in new HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs, in drug-related prisoners and in doctor-certified drug deaths, no rise in police contacts for drug offences, and a fall and then a rise in toxicology-positive deaths that tracks the number of autopsies (Hughes & Stevens, 2010, 2012). Neither a clear success nor a clear failure describes this pattern: each publicised account rested on selected surveys and years, and both contained errors identified by the critics, such as a cannabis ranking in which three EU countries were in fact lower and a 40% rise in homicides that covered all homicides, not drug-related ones (Hughes & Stevens, 2012). These figures do not fit the prediction, cited by the authors, that decriminalisation necessarily increases drug use and its harms: past-year use rose by tenths of a point, and HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs and doctor-certified deaths fell, although lifetime use rose by about half (editors' calculation) (Hughes & Stevens, 2010, 2012). But whether the law itself caused any of the changes cannot be told from them, because treatment and harm reduction expanded from 1999, recorded deaths had begun to fall before July 2001 (editors' reading of a figure), and the authors themselves say that none of the changes can be shown to be the direct result of decriminalisation (Hughes & Stevens, 2010). The evidence fits decriminalisation as one part of a package with expanded treatment; it does not show what the law alone did.
debate.what_would_settle_it: An analysis specified in advance that compares Portugal with a weighted group of European countries that did not change their law in 2001 (a synthetic control or interrupted time series), using series measured the same way before and after 2001, such as doctor-certified drug deaths, HIV diagnoses among people who inject drugs, past-year use by age from surveys with consistent methods, and treatment entries, with the expansion of services from 1999 modelled separately from the law; no such analysis was among the papers read (Hughes & Stevens, 2010, 2012). Follow-up of the people referred to the dissuasion commissions, which the government agency had not collected by 2009, would show what the commissions changed for the people who came before them (Hughes & Stevens, 2010).

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether drugs can be put in one order of harm that does not depend on who judges them and how. In the more recent of the two expert rankings read, members of the UK Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs and two invited specialists (names and number only in a web appendix, not read) met for a one-day workshop in June 2010 and, by multicriteria decision analysis, scored 20 drugs used in the UK, from alcohol and tobacco to illegal drugs and medicines, on 16 harm criteria chosen in 2009 by the government's Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs: 9 harms to the person who uses the drug and 7 harms to others. Each drug was given a group score from 0 (no harm) to 100 (the most harmful drug on that criterion), agreed in open discussion, and the criteria were then weighted, harms to others carrying 54% of the total weight and harms to the person 46%. Alcohol scored highest overall (72 of 100), ahead of heroin (55) and crack cocaine (54); magic mushrooms scored lowest (6 in the figures, 5 in the text; about 5.5 as drawn, editors' reading) (Nutt et al., 2010; funded by the Centre for Crime and Justice Studies). Alcohol's first place came from harm to others, 46 of its 72 points, against 21 for heroin and 17 for crack cocaine; on harm to the person using the drug, the panel scored crack cocaine (37), heroin (34) and methamphetamine (32) highest and alcohol fourth (about 26, editors' calculation: 72 minus 46). The paper says that most of the criteria of harm to others take account indirectly of how many people use a drug, and the heaviest single weight was economic cost to the country (12.8 of 100), which includes the costs of police and prisons. The overall scores correlated 0.70 to 0.84 with two earlier expert rankings and had essentially no relation to the drug classes of UK law (0.04). The authors showed that the order hardly moves when the weights change (heroin would overtake alcohol only if a mortality criterion gained more than 15 of 100 weight points), but they did not vary the scores themselves; the article reports neither the evidence behind each score nor individual experts' scores or their spread, shows the 320 criterion scores (16 × 20) only as unnumbered segments of stacked bars, and only two of the 16 criteria (a drug's own lethality, called drug-specific mortality, and dependence) were compared with outside data, for 5 to 12 drugs. The ranking is the panel's judgment, not a measurement. The authors list as limits that benefits were not scored, that harms depend on availability and legal status, so the results may not apply in countries with very different laws and attitudes, and that harms of drug use were not separated from harms of drug control. Replying to letters, the ranking's authors conceded that tobacco probably causes more deaths than all 19 other drugs combined, but defended its score of zero for drug-specific mortality, which the paper defines as a drug's own lethality, with deaths such as from lung cancer counted under drug-related mortality (Nutt et al., 2010), since nobody dies directly from tobacco itself; on drug-related mortality, they wrote, tobacco was second only to heroin, and they defended their decision conference as designed to minimise bias (Nutt et al., 2011). The reply's one new number, offered as further validation, is a correlation of 0.86 between five death totals from a letter and the panel's five matching scores for drug-specific mortality (Nutt et al., 2011); five pairs cannot validate a ranking: the 95% interval runs from about −0.09 to 0.99 (editors' note and calculation). In a 2007 online survey whose authors include the ranking's first author, 1501 self-selected UK residents (60% with a degree) rated 21 drugs on the nine-part scale of an earlier expert ranking from 2007; anyone who used a drug regularly, had used it or only knew someone who had could rate it, and for 12 of the 21 drugs most of those allowed to rate it had not used it themselves, for heroin 467 of 603 (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010). That earlier expert ranking, whose first author also led the 2010 one, is itself a set of judgments: two groups of UK experts scored nine kinds of harm from 0 (no risk) to 3 (extreme risk), all weighted equally and averaged with no spread reported: 29 of the 77 psychiatrists asked (specialists in drug and alcohol problems) scored 14 drugs by questionnaire, and a second panel, whose selection and total size are not reported (8 to 16 members at each of four meetings), scored 20 drugs after open discussion; the second panel, whose scores the survey was compared with, put heroin (2.77 of 3) and cocaine, crack included (2.30), first, alcohol fifth (1.85), tobacco ninth (1.62), cannabis eleventh (1.33), LSD fourteenth (1.23), ecstasy eighteenth (1.09) and khat last (0.80) (editors' calculation from its table), and its order was not significantly related to the drugs' classes under UK law (Kendall −0.18, P = 0.25; Spearman −0.26, P = 0.26), with legal alcohol and tobacco above LSD and ecstasy, both class A (Nutt et al., 2007). Across the 21 drugs, the survey's average ratings followed the 2007 experts' closely (r = 0.896), less so for pleasure (0.559) and intoxication (0.508), and they differed for some drugs: the survey rated ecstasy as more harmful than cannabis, the reverse of the experts, and for seven drugs, crack and cocaine among them, its pattern across the nine kinds of harm did not match the experts', who had scored cocaine and crack as one substance (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010; Nutt et al., 2007). A published critique argues that the overall score mixes harm per person with total harm that grows with the number of people using, so that it measures neither; that the weights are value judgments; that benefits were ignored; and that adding the criteria assumes they do not interact (Caulkins et al., 2011). A second critique, co-written by a member of the expert committee who attended both workshops behind the ranking, argues that one score cannot capture how harm depends on how much, how often, how and where a drug is used, on other drugs taken and on drug laws, and that no measure of agreement between the experts was reported (Rolles & Measham, 2011). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Can drugs be ranked by how much harm they do? Experts have tried. In 2010, a panel of UK drug experts met for one day and scored 20 drugs on 16 kinds of harm, to the person using the drug and to other people. Alcohol scored highest overall (72 out of 100), then heroin (55) and crack cocaine (54); magic mushrooms scored lowest. Most of alcohol's score (46 points) was harm to other people, which partly reflects how many people drink; for harm to the person using the drug, the panel put crack cocaine, heroin and methamphetamine first and alcohol fourth. The scores are the experts' judgment, not measurements, and only two of the 16 kinds of harm were compared in numbers with outside data. Tobacco scored zero for deaths caused directly by the drug itself, as in an overdose; deaths from diseases such as lung cancer were scored under another heading, where tobacco came second only to heroin. Replying to letters, the ranking's authors agreed that tobacco probably causes more deaths than all 19 other drugs combined. In a 2007 online survey, 1,501 people in the UK rated drugs on an earlier experts' scale, and their average ratings followed the experts' closely, though less so for pleasure and intoxication. That earlier experts' ranking was itself opinion: in 2007, 29 of 77 doctors asked who specialise in drug and alcohol problems, and a second panel, chosen in a way the paper does not describe, scored nine kinds of harm from 0 to 3, all counted equally; the panel put heroin and cocaine top, alcohol fifth and tobacco ninth of 20, above LSD and ecstasy. But anyone who knew someone who had used a drug could rate it: of the 603 people allowed to rate heroin, 467 had never used it. The ranking's lead author was one of the survey's authors. Two published critiques argue that one number mixes harm to the person with how many people use a drug, that choosing which harms count most is a matter of values, and that harm depends on how, where and under what laws a drug is used.
population: 20 drugs used in the UK (alcohol, tobacco, illegal drugs and medicines used outside medicine), scored by members of the UK Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs and two invited specialists (number not given in the article) at a one-day workshop in June 2010; for comparison, 21 drugs rated on an earlier expert scale (2007) by 1501 self-selected UK residents in an online survey in 2007, and that earlier expert ranking itself: 20 substances scored before 2007 by two UK expert groups (29 of 77 specialist psychiatrists asked, 14 substances; a second panel of 8 to 16 members per meeting, 20 substances)
exposure: Each of the 20 drugs as used in the UK, without stated amounts, forms, routes or patterns of use
comparator: The other drugs on the list, on 0–100 scales where 100 is the drug judged most harmful on each criterion and 0 is no harm
outcome: Harm as scored by the panel on 16 criteria (9 to the person using the drug, 7 to others), weighted and added into two part scores and an overall score; how far the order moves when the weights change; how closely an online survey's average ratings followed an earlier expert panel's, and that earlier panel's averaged 0-to-3 scores on nine kinds of harm
magnitude: Not a measured effect: panel scores out of 100, with no uncertainty interval for any score. Nutt et al. (2010), overall weighted scores (Figure 2): alcohol 72, heroin 55, crack cocaine 54, methamphetamine 33, cocaine 27, tobacco 26, amphetamine 23, cannabis 20, GHB 19, benzodiazepines 15, ketamine 15, methadone 14, mephedrone 13, butane 11, khat 9, anabolic steroids 10, ecstasy 9 (the figures' order, which for these three is not a ranking: the bars measure about 8.9, 9.7 and 9.1, editors' reading), LSD 7, buprenorphine 7, mushrooms 6 (5 in the Discussion; the bar measures about 5.5, editors' reading, so both are probably roundings). Part scores: harm to the person, crack cocaine 37, heroin 34, methamphetamine 32, alcohol about 26 (editors' calculation, 72 − 46; fourth); harm to others, alcohol 46, heroin 21, crack cocaine 17. Weights (of 100): harm to others 54, harm to the person 46; heaviest criteria economic cost 12.8, injury 11.5, crime 10.2, family adversities 8.9. Overall scores correlated 0.70 with the 2007 UK expert rating (15 drugs), 0.80 and 0.84 with a Dutch expert ranking, and 0.04 with UK legal classes. Input scores against outside data: drug-specific mortality r = 0.66 (12 substances) and 0.98 and 0.99 (5 substances); dependence r = 0.95 (5 drugs). Sensitivity of the order to the weights: heroin first only with more than 15 of 100 extra weight points on a mortality criterion; tobacco only with drug-specific damage weighted slightly more than 70% instead of about 4%; crack cocaine only with harm to the person weighted nearly 70% instead of 46%; the scores themselves were not varied. Weights of the two mortality criteria, both harms to the person using the drug: drug-specific mortality 5.1 and drug-related mortality 6.4, together 11.5 of 100 (editors' sum). Nutt et al. (2011), the authors' reply to letters: r = 0.86 between five death totals from a letter and the five matching scores for drug-specific mortality (editors' calculation: 95% interval about −0.09 to 0.99 by Fisher z, two-sided p about 0.06). Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, Muetzelfeldt, et al. (2010), mean perceived-harm ratings from 0 to 3 by 1501 self-selected UK residents in 2007 on the nine-parameter scale of the 2007 expert rating: correlation with the experts' ratings across 21 substances (the text says 20) r = 0.896 (editors' 95% interval about 0.76 to 0.96, Fisher z, 21 pairs); by parameter from 0.508 (intoxication) and 0.559 (pleasure), the two that missed the corrected significance level of 0.005, to 0.929 (psychological dependence); intra-class correlations of each substance's nine ratings with the experts' from 0.854 (alcohol) to below zero for seven substances (lowest crack, −0.453); the survey's order heroin, crack, cocaine, street methadone, then alcohol 5th and tobacco 9th of 21; with UK legal class, Kendall 0.234 (p = 0.18) and Spearman 0.301 (p = 0.19). For 12 of the 21 substances most of those able to rate it had not used it (heroin 467 of 603, crack 428 of 588; editors' count from Table 2); no spread or number of ratings is given for any mean. Nutt et al. (2007), the earlier expert ranking (the survey's comparison): mean scores from 0 (no risk) to 3 (extreme risk) on nine parameters weighted equally, with no spread, number of scorers per drug or count of missing scores reported; 29 of 77 specialist psychiatrists asked (14 substances, their overall means only plotted) and a second panel of 8 to 16 members per meeting at four meetings (20 substances). Second panel's overall means (editors' calculation: the mean of the three printed category means in Table 3, in the table's order and within 0.015 of the Figure 1 bars measured on a 300-dpi render): heroin 2.77, cocaine (crack included) 2.30, barbiturates 2.08, street methadone 1.94, alcohol 1.85, ketamine 1.74, benzodiazepines 1.70, amphetamine 1.66, tobacco 1.62, buprenorphine 1.58, cannabis 1.33, solvents 1.27, 4-MTA 1.27, LSD 1.23, methylphenidate 1.18, anabolic steroids 1.15, GHB 1.12, ecstasy 1.09, alkyl nitrites 0.92, khat 0.80. With UK legal class (coding not stated): Kendall −0.18 (P = 0.25), Spearman −0.26 (P = 0.26). The two groups' overall means for the 14 substances both scored are shown only as a plot, without a coefficient.

evidence.locator: Summary, Method (p. 1558); Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph (p. 1558) and 2nd paragraph (p. 1558, continuing on p. 1559); Methods › Scoring of the drugs on the criteria, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 1559)
evidence.extracted: Design: a multicriteria decision analysis built at a facilitated decision conference. The 16 harm criteria (9 harms that a drug produces in the individual, 7 harms to others in the UK and overseas, clustered as physical, psychological and social) were chosen at a special 2009 meeting of the UK Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs. In June 2010 members of the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs (ISCD) expert committee plus two external experts on legal highs (listed in a web appendix; the article gives neither names nor number) met in a 1-day interactive workshop with an independent decision-analysis facilitator, scored 20 drugs relevant to the UK on every criterion in open group discussion, and then assessed the relative importance (weights) of the criteria within and across clusters. Scores ran from 0 (no harm) to 100 (the most harmful drug on that criterion) and are treated as a ratio scale; the paper says scores are often changed from those first suggested as participants share their experiences. It also states that the criteria of harm to the individual show the extent of individual harm, whereas most criteria of harm to others take account indirectly of the numbers of people who use the drug (see quotation).
evidence.quote: most criteria listed as to others take account indirectly of the numbers of users

evidence.extracted: Only two criteria were compared quantitatively with outside data: the panel's drug-specific mortality scores against the log10 of Gable's safety ratio (ratio of an acute lethal dose to the dose commonly used for non-medical purposes) for the 12 substances in common, r = 0.66, and against mean fatality statistics from 2003 to 2007 for five substances (heroin, cocaine, amfetamines, MDMA/ecstasy, cannabis), r = 0.98 and 0.99 (substances recorded among other mentions or as sole mentions on death certificates); and the panel's dependence scores against lifetime dependence in the US survey of Anthony and co-workers for five drugs (tobacco, alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, heroin), r = 0.95. No correlation of any harm-to-others criterion with outside data is reported.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 9th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors state that the weightings affect the overall scores, are necessarily based on judgment and cannot be cross-validated with objective data. In sensitivity analyses of the weights, heroin would displace alcohol from first place only if the weight on drug-specific or drug-related mortality rose by more than 15 of 100 points; tobacco only if the weight on drug-specific damage rose from about 4% to slightly more than 70%; and crack cocaine only if the weight on harm to the individual rose from 46% to nearly 70%; extensive analyses are said to show the model to be very stable. Future work is to explore the weightings with other groups, both expert panels and the general public. No analysis that varies the scores themselves, and no uncertainty interval for any score, is reported in the article.

Each substance was scored on each parameter on a four-point scale, 0 no risk, 1 some, 2 moderate and 3 extreme risk; a category score is the mean of its three parameters, and an overall harm rating, the mean of all nine scores, was computed to aid discussion. After piloting by members of the panel of the Independent Inquiry into the Misuse of Drugs Act, a questionnaire with guidance notes (not reproduced in the article) was used by two groups: the national group of consultant psychiatrists on the Royal College of Psychiatrists' register as specialists in drug and alcohol problems (editors' paraphrase of the specialty's name), of whom 29 of the 77 asked replied and were analysed, scoring 14 substances; and a second group with a wider spread of expertise (chemistry, pharmacology, forensic science, psychiatry and other medical specialties including epidemiology, legal and police services), convened by the authors, which scored 20 substances at four meetings run on delphic principles, 8 to 16 members scoring at each: members scored independently, each parameter's scores were shown to the whole group for discussion of the reasoning behind outlying scores, members could revise their scores, and a final mean was calculated. How the second group's members were chosen, how many took part in all and who they were are not reported. Members were given recent review articles (references 5–7 and 15–18), and missing individual scores were ignored. Tobacco and alcohol were included as benchmarks, the authors adding that their scores cannot be compared directly with the other drugs' because their legality could affect their harms, especially through easier availability. Table 2: cocaine includes crack cocaine; ecstasy, 4-MTA, LSD, cocaine, heroin and street methadone were class A, and alcohol, alkyl nitrites, ketamine (when assessed), khat, solvents and tobacco not controlled.
