risk_of_bias.note: Every input is a group judgment agreed in one day of open discussion, with no documented evidence behind any of the 320 scores (16 criteria × 20 drugs, editors' arithmetic), no individual scores or spread, and no variation of the scores in the sensitivity analyses; only two criteria, both harms to the individual, were compared in numbers with outside data, for 5 to 12 drugs (card sc_nutt_2010: editors' checklist, high). The 2007 survey is a self-selected online sample with no sampling frame or response rate, mostly well educated, in which for 12 of 21 drugs most of those able to rate a drug had not used it, with no spread or numbers of ratings reported (card sc_morgan_2010c: JBI prevalence checklist, high). The two critiques and the authors' reply are arguments without data of their own, apart from the reply's one correlation over five pairs (cards sc_caulkins_2011, sc_rolles_2011 and sc_nutt_2011: editors' checklist, high), and are used for their arguments only. The 2007 expert ranking that the survey was compared with is itself a set of averaged judgments: 29 of the 77 psychiatrists asked replied, the second panel's selection and total size are not reported, nine kinds of harm were scored from 0 to 3 with equal weights, and no spread, number of scorers per drug or count of missing scores is reported (card sc_nutt_2007: editors' checklist with three domains added for expert elicitation, high; first pass).

inconsistency.note: Two expert rankings read, both led by the same first author: the 2010 ranking correlates 0.70 with the 2007 one (15 drugs in common) and 0.80 to 0.84 with a Dutch expert ranking, judgments of the same kind, not independent measurements; within the 2007 ranking, the psychiatrists' and the second panel's overall scores for the 14 drugs both scored are shown as similar, in a plot without a coefficient. A 2007 online survey, with the same first author among its authors, rated drugs on the 2007 experts' own scale and agreed with them across 21 drugs (r = 0.896), less so on pleasure and intoxication, with ecstasy and cannabis in reverse order and, for seven drugs, profiles that did not match: agreement between opinions that are not independent of each other, not between measurements, so it is not counted as consistency of evidence on harm. Later rankings on the project's list have not been read.

indirectness.note: The question is how much harm drugs do; the ranking gives one UK panel's judgment in 2010 of harm in the UK, blending harm per person with harm to others that partly tracks how many people use a drug and includes costs of police and prisons, so it does not say how harmful a drug is to a person who uses it, and the authors say the results may not apply to countries with very different laws and attitudes. The 2007 survey adds opinions on the earlier nine-part, unweighted scale, not on the 2010 criteria and weights. The 2007 expert ranking is likewise UK panels' judgment, on a coarser 0-to-3 scale with equal weights and with cocaine and crack scored as one substance.

imprecision.note: No uncertainty is reported for any score of either expert ranking, and the survey reports no spread for any mean rating; counted under risk of bias, not twice.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable.

grade.reasoning: An expert-judgment model is not randomized evidence and starts low; rated down one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, it is very low, the floor. Rated as worded: insufficient evidence for one order of harm that does not depend on who judges and how. That one UK panel, with the criteria and weights it chose, placed alcohol first overall and crack cocaine, heroin and methamphetamine first for harm to the person is reported in the statement as the panel's judgment, not rated as a measured fact. The stability of the order under large changes in the weights is real but covers the weights only; the scores were never varied (Nutt et al., 2010). The companion papers read on 13 November leave the rating at the floor. A 2007 online survey adds a second set of judgments, not measurements: self-selected raters, with the ranking's first author among the survey's authors, rated drugs on the 2007 experts' own scale and agreed with them across 21 drugs (r = 0.896), which bears on who judges, but for 12 of the 21 drugs most of those allowed to rate a drug had not used it, and whether raters knew the published expert ranking was not asked (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010). The 2007 expert ranking that the survey was compared with, read on 13 November, adds a third set of judgments, not measurements: 29 of 77 psychiatrists asked and a second panel whose selection is not reported scored nine kinds of harm from 0 to 3 with equal weights and no reported spread; by the editors' calculation from its table, the panel put heroin and cocaine, crack included, first and alcohol fifth of 20, and its order was not significantly related to UK legal classes (Nutt et al., 2007). It enters as what those panels judged, never as measured harm, and changes neither the rating, already at the floor, nor the status. The authors' reply to letters (Nutt et al., 2011) and a second critique (Rolles & Measham, 2011) are arguments; the reply's one number, a correlation of 0.86 over five pairs, cannot validate a ranking (editors' 95% interval about −0.09 to 0.99). Status contested: credible published critiques change the interpretation of the overall score, arguing that it mixes harm per person with total harm that grows with prevalence, that its weights are values and that its simple additive form assumes the criteria do not interact, which does not always hold (Caulkins et al., 2011), and that a single score cannot capture how harm depends on how, where and under which laws a drug is used (Rolles & Measham, 2011); several of these points rest on features the ranking's own paper states (most harm-to-others criteria taking account indirectly of numbers of people who use, weights as judgments, benefits not scored), and the authors' reply states that their scores for harm to others take account of how many people use each drug while those for harm to the person do not (Nutt et al., 2011), so the six-part debate box applies. The critiques enter as argument only: neither reports data of its own, and the first one's figures come from the ranking and from UK prevalence sources (Caulkins et al., 2011; Rolles & Measham, 2011).

debate.question: Can drugs be put in one order of harm, as a UK expert panel did when it scored alcohol the most harmful of 20 drugs (Nutt et al., 2010), or does a single score mix up different kinds of harm and hide value judgments, as two published critiques argue (Caulkins et al., 2011; Rolles & Measham, 2011)?
debate.evidence_yes: A UK expert panel built an explicit model: 16 harm criteria chosen in advance by a government advisory council, every drug scored on every criterion, the criteria weighted, and the result reported as part scores and weights. Alcohol came first overall (72 of 100), ahead of heroin (55) and crack cocaine (54), and the top places hardly moved when the weights were changed: heroin would overtake alcohol only with more than 15 of 100 extra weight points on a mortality criterion, and crack cocaine only if harm to the person using it carried nearly 70% of the weight instead of 46%. Where the input scores were compared with outside data they agreed (drug-specific mortality, r = 0.66 for 12 substances and 0.98 to 0.99 for 5; dependence, r = 0.95 for 5 drugs), and the overall scores correlated 0.70 to 0.84 with two earlier expert rankings from the UK and the Netherlands (Nutt et al., 2010). Different judges broadly agreed: in a 2007 online survey, 1501 self-selected UK residents rating 21 drugs on an earlier expert scale gave average ratings that followed the experts' closely across drugs (r = 0.896), with heroin, crack and cocaine at the top (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010); and in the 2007 expert ranking itself, two different groups, specialist psychiatrists scoring alone by questionnaire and a mixed panel scoring after discussion, gave similar overall scores for the 14 drugs both rated, which its authors took as a sign that the process is robust (Nutt et al., 2007). Replying to letters, the ranking's authors argued that their decision conference is designed to minimise bias and met the conditions under which a group can outperform even its best member; that tobacco's zero for drug-specific mortality reflects that nobody dies directly from tobacco itself, while they judged it the most harmful drug on drug-specific damage and second only to heroin on drug-related mortality, because harm is more than deaths; and they offered a correlation of 0.86 with five death totals as further validation (Nutt et al., 2011). The critiques themselves grant that a single measure of harmfulness can inform an individual's own decisions about drugs and that evidence should inform policy (Caulkins et al., 2011), and credit the method as engaging and credible, noting that ratings by people who use drugs gave results similar to the experts' (Rolles & Measham, 2011).
debate.evidence_no: The scores are the panel's judgments, agreed in one day of open discussion; the article gives neither the evidence behind each score nor individual scores or their spread, the scores themselves were never varied, and only two of the 16 criteria, neither of them a harm to others, were compared in numbers with outside data (Nutt et al., 2010). The overall score adds harm to the person using a drug to harm to others, most of whose criteria, by the paper's own description, take account indirectly of how many people use it, and the heaviest single weight, economic cost to the country, includes police and prison costs; the authors themselves explain that the order depends on the share given to social harms (nearly half of their criteria) and say that harms of drug use were not separated from harms of drug control (Nutt et al., 2010). A published critique argues that such a score measures neither harm per person nor total harm, illustrating with tobacco (26) and GHB (19), only a third apart although about 8.5 million people in the UK smoke and about 50,000 in England and Wales use GHB; that weights such as counting drug-specific deaths at 80% of drug-related deaths are value judgments; that benefits were ignored; that adding criteria in a simple model like this one assumes they do not interact, which does not always hold, notably for dependence and harm to the person; and that even a perfect ranking would not settle drug laws, which themselves shape harms being scored, such as crime and the cost of police and prisons (Caulkins et al., 2011). The critique's figures are read from the ranking or cited from UK sources; it adds no data of its own (Caulkins et al., 2011). A second critique, co-written by a member of the expert committee who attended both workshops behind the ranking, argues that one score cannot capture how harm depends on how much, how often, how and where a drug is used, on other drugs taken, on individual vulnerability and on drug laws; that even deaths and dependence are counted in ways shaped by society; that the experts' value judgments came with no measure of agreement between them; and that the model largely fails to separate harms of drug use from harms of drug policy (Rolles & Measham, 2011). The ranking's authors conceded, in reply to letters, that tobacco, sixth overall with 26 points (Nutt et al., 2010), probably causes more deaths than all 19 other drugs combined (Nutt et al., 2011). The survey that agreed with experts drew a self-selected, well-educated online sample in which, for 12 of the 21 drugs, most of those allowed to rate a drug had not used it (for heroin, 467 of 603); it compared only average ratings across drugs, still differed on pleasure and intoxication and on some drugs (ecstasy rated more harmful than cannabis; for seven drugs, crack and cocaine among them, the pattern across the nine harms did not match the experts'), and had the ranking's first author among its authors (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010). The expert scores it agreed with were themselves averaged opinion, from a panel whose selection and size are not reported (the 2007 ranking's other group was 29 of the 77 psychiatrists asked): nine kinds of harm were scored from 0 to 3 and weighted equally, no spread is reported for any score, cocaine and crack were scored as one substance, and the ranking's authors wrote that the scores of tobacco and alcohol cannot be compared directly with the other drugs' because their legality could affect their harms (Nutt et al., 2007).
debate.neither_can_show: None of these papers measured harm. The ranking rests on one panel's judgments, in the UK, in 2010, about drugs as used there, with no amounts, forms or routes stated (Nutt et al., 2010), and the earlier ranking on two UK groups' averaged scores, with no spread reported (Nutt et al., 2007). The survey records the opinions of a self-selected online sample in 2007 on the earlier nine-part scale, not on the 2010 criteria and weights; it cannot show whether its agreement with the experts reflects independent judgment or familiarity with the published expert ranking, which it says had drawn considerable debate in government and the media, nor how people who use each drug rate it, since ratings could not be separated by experience (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010). The critiques add arguments, not data (Caulkins et al., 2011; Rolles & Measham, 2011), and the reply adds one correlation over five pairs (Nutt et al., 2011). None can show how other panels or the public would score and weight the 2010 harms, which the authors themselves propose to test; how harm per person or per use compares between drugs, since no criterion was scored that way separately; or what the order would be in countries with other laws and markets, which the authors say their results may not fit (Nutt et al., 2010).
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). Drugs can be ranked once someone chooses which harms count and how much each matters, and the 2010 expert ranking states those choices openly; within them, its top places held under large changes in the weights (Nutt et al., 2010). It is still one panel's judgment, not a measurement: the scores were agreed without the evidence behind them being reported, were never themselves varied, and were compared in numbers with outside data for only two criteria (Nutt et al., 2010). Its best-known result, alcohol first, rests mainly on harm to others (46 of 72 points), which by the paper's own account partly tracks how many people use a drug; on harm to the person using it, the panel put crack cocaine, heroin and methamphetamine ahead of alcohol (Nutt et al., 2010). The first critique's central point, that one number mixes harm per person with total harm in a population, is borne out by the model's own structure, although no one has shown how much a different construction would change the order (Caulkins et al., 2011); the authors' reply says as much of their own scores, those for harm to others taking account of how many people use a drug and those for harm to the person not (Nutt et al., 2011). Tobacco shows what one number leaves out: the authors agree it probably causes more deaths than all 19 other drugs combined, yet it came sixth (Nutt et al., 2011); the two mortality criteria, both harms to the person using a drug, carry 11.5 of the 100 weight points between them (5.1 and 6.4, editors' sum) (Nutt et al., 2010). The reply's one number, a correlation of 0.86 over five pairs, cannot validate a ranking: with five pairs the 95% interval runs from about −0.09 to 0.99 (editors' calculation) (Nutt et al., 2011). A self-selected online survey suggests that the broad order is not peculiar to experts, since its raters' average ratings on the earlier expert scale followed the experts' across 21 drugs (r = 0.896); but this is agreement between opinions, many from raters who had not used the drug, with the ranking's first author among the survey's authors, and the two groups differed on pleasure and intoxication (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010); the expert side of that comparison was itself one UK panel's averaged scores on a 0-to-3 scale, from members whose selection is not reported, with no spread (Nutt et al., 2007). Measured against the 2007 expert ratings, the survey's raters, using the same scale, agreed more closely (r = 0.896 over 21 drugs) than the 2010 panel did on its 16 weighted criteria (0.70 over 15 drugs), a hint that how harm is scored moves the order at least as much as who scores it, though the drug sets differ and none of these judgments is independent of the others (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010; Nutt et al., 2010). The defensible reading is two rankings, not one: what this panel judged to do most harm in the UK as a whole, and what it judged to do most harm to a person who uses the drug (Nutt et al., 2010).
debate.what_would_settle_it: Several independent panels, in different countries and including people who use drugs and members of the public, as the authors propose for the weights, scoring the same drugs with individual scores recorded before discussion and their spread reported; the evidence behind each score published; harm per person who uses each drug reported separately from total harm in the population; and an analysis that varies the scores as well as the weights (Nutt et al., 2010). Each form in which a drug is used, such as crack and powder cocaine, would be scored separately, as the 2007 authors advise for any formal use of such a system (Nutt et al., 2007). Ratings by people who use drugs would need a sample drawn from a known population, each rater's own experience of each drug recorded and analysed, and agreement measured rater by rater, not only between average ratings (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt, Muetzelfeldt, et al., 2010). The critiques propose showing each kind of harm side by side for each drug, under its present legal status and under an alternative, rather than one number (Caulkins et al., 2011), and re-running the analysis for different policy regimes, such as illicit and prescribed supply, with a measure of agreement between raters, which that critique notes was missing (Rolles & Measham, 2011).

statement: In school students in grades 5 to 12 (no country given; the review presents D.A.R.E. as a US programme), in 11 controlled evaluations published in journals between 1991 and 2002 (236 to 2,878 students each, 11,505 listed in all, editors' sum; experimental and quasi-experimental designs, the review not saying which were which), the original Project D.A.R.E. (Drug Abuse Resistance Education) school curriculum compared with each study's control or comparison condition does not detectably change self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs, combined into one effect per study, measured from immediately after the programme to 10 years later: pooled d = 0.023 (95% CI −0.04 to 0.08; r = 0.011; z = 0.73, not significant), below the level usually considered small (West & O'Neal, 2004; no funding statement). In 8 of the 11 studies the interval included no difference (editors' count from Table 1); the largest, of 2,878 fifth graders, found slightly more use in the D.A.R.E. group (d = −0.117, −0.19 to −0.04), and two small studies found less (395 sixth graders, d = 0.376, 0.07 to 0.68; 236 fifth and sixth graders, smoking the only outcome, d = 0.405, 0.01 to 0.80). Four of the 11 effects, covering 4,539 of the 11,505 students listed (39%, editors' sum) and including the only 10-year follow-up, were not computed but entered as zero and footnoted as assumed. The review did not appraise its studies, names no pooling model and reports no heterogeneity; a random-effects pooling of its printed values reproduces its estimate, while a fixed-effect pooling gives d = −0.005 (−0.043 to 0.034), so the near-zero result does not depend on the model (editors' recalculation; study estimates vary more than chance would predict, I² about 54%). Many included studies analysed individual students although students were nested in schools, which the authors say tends to overestimate effectiveness and judge unlikely to change the result; ignoring the clustering also makes the pooled interval narrower than it should be (editors' note). Every study evaluated the original curriculum: D.A.R.E. was substantially revamped in 2001, and the authors found no evaluation of the new version, so this answer does not apply to it. The authors' remark that the effect would have needed to be 20 times larger to count as small overstates the gap: Cohen's small benchmarks are about 9 times the pooled values (editors' calculation). An earlier meta-analysis, as the paper describes it, found negligible effects (0.00 to 0.11) immediately after the programme. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Did the original DARE school programme stop young people using drugs? A 2004 review combined 11 studies, published from 1991 to 2002, that compared students who had the original DARE classes with students who did not. Overall, students who had DARE used alcohol, tobacco and other drugs about as much as the others, from right after the classes to 10 years later: the difference was close to zero. Two small studies found less use with DARE, and the biggest found slightly more. The review filled in four studies' results as zero and did not check how well the studies were done. It covered only the original classes: DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and the authors found no study of the new version.
population: School students in grades 5 to 12 (no country given in the review, which presents D.A.R.E. as a US programme; 236 to 2,878 per study; 11,505 listed across the 11 studies, editors' sum) in 11 controlled evaluations (experimental or quasi-experimental, not distinguished in the review) published in peer-reviewed journals from 1991 to 2002
exposure: The original Project D.A.R.E. school curriculum, before its 2001 revision; content, number of sessions and delivery not described in the review
comparator: Each study's control or comparison condition, not described in the review
outcome: Self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs, combined into one effect per study, from immediately after the programme to 10 years later
magnitude: West & O'Neal (2004): pooled r = 0.011, d = 0.023 (95% CI −0.04 to 0.08; the interval is on the d scale, editors' check), z = 0.73, not significant; positive values favour D.A.R.E. Study effects (Table 1): Becker 1992 d = −0.117 (−0.19 to −0.04; 2,878 students); Zagumny & Thompson 1997 d = 0.376 (0.07 to 0.68; 395); Ahmed 2002 d = 0.405 (0.01 to 0.80; 236; smoking only); four effects entered as assumed zeros (Ennett 1994, Rosenbaum 1994, Wysong 1994, Lynam 1999; 4,539 of 11,505 students, 39%, editors' sum); 8 of 11 intervals include zero (editors' count). Editors' recalculation from the printed d values and intervals: random-effects (DerSimonian–Laird) d = 0.023 (−0.039 to 0.085), reproducing the published estimate; fixed-effect d = −0.005 (−0.043 to 0.034); Q = 21.6 on 10 df (P about 0.02), I² about 54%. Cohen's small benchmarks (d = 0.2, r = 0.1) are about 8.7 and 9.1 times the pooled values (editors' calculation), against the paper's 20 times. No absolute difference in the share of students using any substance can be given.

evidence.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph and inclusion criteria 1 to 3, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Searches of ERIC, MEDLINE and PsycINFO in late fall 2002, plus the reference lists of retrieved articles; roughly 40 articles reviewed; 11 studies published from 1991 to 2002 met three criteria: reported in a peer-reviewed journal (dissertations, theses, books and unpublished manuscripts excluded); a control or comparison group, that is, an experimental or quasi-experimental design (the review does not say which studies were which); and assessments before and after the intervention of at least one of alcohol use, illicit drug use and tobacco use. Only effect sizes on actual substance use were taken, and two or more effects in the same outcome category were averaged; effect sizes were calculated by Rosenthal's procedures, expressed as r and as d, weighted by Shadish and Haddock's procedure, with 95% confidence intervals for each study and overall. No appraisal of the included studies is described.

risk_of_bias.note: Seen only through one brief meta-analysis that did not appraise its studies (METHODS §6.3, not appraisable): it pooled experimental and quasi-experimental evaluations without saying which were which, entered four of the 11 effects (39% of the students listed) as assumed zeros, and ignored the clustering of students in schools, which makes its interval too narrow (card sc_west_2004: AMSTAR 2, critically low confidence). The biases expected in non-randomized school comparisons and in self-reported use would, if anything, favour D.A.R.E., so they do not point to a hidden benefit.

inconsistency.note: Study estimates vary more than chance would predict (I² about 54%, editors' calculation), but most intervals include zero, the two studies that found less use are the smallest (one measured only smoking) and the largest found slightly more use with D.A.R.E.; the variation does not show a setting in which the original curriculum clearly worked, and the near-zero result holds under fixed- and random-effects pooling (editors' recalculation).

indirectness.note: Worded for the original curriculum in schools (studies published 1991–2002; no country given, though the review presents D.A.R.E. as a US programme) and for alcohol, tobacco and illegal drug use combined; no result for a single substance is given, and the claim does not apply to the curriculum revised in 2001.

imprecision.note: The pooled interval (−0.04 to 0.08) excludes effects as large as Cohen's small benchmark; that it is too narrow because clustering was ignored is counted under risk of bias, not twice.

publication_bias.note: Journal articles only; unpublished null evaluations would not change a null result, and the earlier meta-analysis that included agency reports also found negligible effects, as described.

grade.reasoning: The review admitted experimental and quasi-experimental designs without saying which studies were randomized, so the evidence cannot be treated as randomized and starts low; seen only through this review, which did not appraise its studies, it is rated down one level for risk of bias (METHODS §6.3), giving very low, the floor. Rated as worded: no detectable effect of the original curriculum on self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs combined; the pooled effect is near zero (d = 0.023) with an interval that excludes Cohen's small benchmark, and a fixed-effect pooling gives −0.005 (editors' recalculation). The very low rating reflects how little this single brief review lets anyone check (designs not reported, four effects assumed, clustering ignored), not a sign of a hidden benefit: the biases expected in such studies would favour D.A.R.E. The authors' remark that the effect would need to be 20 times larger to count as small is not adopted (about 9 times, editors' calculation). Status replicated: the review reports each study's direction, and in 8 of 11 independent evaluations the interval included no difference; the earlier meta-analysis, described in the paper but not read, agrees and is not counted. The answer does not cover the curriculum revised in 2001.

statement: In US youths aged 12.5 to 18 in a national household panel (the National Survey of Parents and Youth: three cohorts aged 9 to 18 from a probability sample of US households, interviewed at home four times between November 1999 and June 2004; 8,117 youths in the first round, with a 65% response rate, and 5,126 in the fourth), more recalled exposure to the US National Youth Anti-Drug Media Campaign compared with less recalled exposure did not detectably reduce marijuana (cannabis) use or first use, or strengthen antidrug intentions, beliefs, norms or confidence in refusing marijuana (Hornik et al., 2008). Congress appropriated nearly $1 billion for the campaign for 1998–2004; it bought advertising from September 1999 to June 2004, 64% of its rating points on TV and radio. The evaluation was mandated by Congress and paid from the campaign's appropriation, supervised by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, which also funded the authors. There was no unexposed group: 94% of youths recalled at least one antidrug ad a month, so the evaluation compared youths who recalled more with youths who recalled less, after propensity-score weighting on more than 150 candidate confounders. Self-reported marijuana use among youths aged 12.5 to 18 did not change from 2000 to 2004: lifetime use 23.6% and 23.5% (change −0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −2.9 to 2.8) and past-30-day use 7.8% and 8.2% (0.4, −1.4 to 2.2), weighted percentages whose yearly numbers of youths are not printed; of four antidrug views among youths who had not used marijuana, only an index of beliefs and attitudes rose (6.3 points, 0.4 to 12.2). At the same interview, youths who recalled more exposure held no more antidrug views (gammas −0.02 to 0.03, every interval including no association). Among youths who had not used marijuana, more exposure went, at the next round 12 to 18 months later, with fewer saying they definitely would not use it (82.3%, 78.2% and 78.4% across rising general exposure; gamma −0.07, 95% CI −0.13 to −0.01) and with weaker antidrug norms (gamma −0.05, −0.08 to −0.02, for recall of specific ads). First use by the next round was 10.7%, 11.2% and 12.5% across rising general exposure (gamma 0.07, −0.01 to 0.15, not significant when pooled), and more first use with more exposure was significant only from the third round (July 2002 to June 2003) to the fourth (gamma 0.11, 0.00 to 0.22), which the authors call barely significant. Of 80 subgroup analyses of later outcomes, 20 were significant, 19 of them unfavourable; none of the tests is reported as corrected for multiple comparisons. The authors conclude that the campaign is unlikely to have had favourable effects, and judge the support for unfavourable effects tentative, not definitive. Exposure and use were self-reported, and with no group that missed the campaign the design cannot show what would have happened without it: effects shared by everyone, spread through friends, or occurring before the first round, which began with the full launch, would be missed. As the authors describe two school surveys, these showed some fall in youth marijuana use over these years, which this survey did not, and larger falls in tobacco and alcohol use. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Did the US government's anti-drug ads stop teens using cannabis? There is no sign that they did. Between 1998 and 2004 Congress put nearly $1 billion into a national anti-drug campaign, with most of its advertising on TV and radio. A national survey interviewed thousands of US young people at home up to four times between 1999 and 2004. Almost all of them remembered seeing anti-drug ads, so there was no group without them to compare. Teen cannabis use stayed the same: about 24 in 100 teens had ever used it, in 2000 and in 2004. Teens who remembered more ads were no less likely to start using cannabis by their next interview, and fewer of them said they definitely would not use it; in one of three periods, more ads went with more first use. The authors call the evidence for a harmful effect tentative, not definitive.
population: US youths aged 12.5 to 18 at outcome measurement in the National Survey of Parents and Youth, a household panel from a stratified four-stage national probability sample (90 primary sampling units): three cohorts aged 9 to 18 interviewed at home four times, November 1999 to June 2004 (8,117, 6,516, 5,854 and 5,126 youths in rounds 1 to 4; 65% first-round response; 86% to 93% of still-eligible youths reinterviewed); association analyses restricted to youths who had not used marijuana
exposure: Recalled exposure to the National Youth Anti-Drug Media Campaign's advertising: general (how often antidrug ads were seen or heard in recent months, by medium) and specific (prompted recall of up to 4 TV and 2 radio campaign ads aired in the 2 months before the interview)
comparator: Youths recalling less exposure (general: under 4, 4 to 11, 12 or more a month; specific: under 1, 1 to 3, 4 to 11, 12 or more a month); no unexposed group; for trends, the same population in 2000
outcome: Self-reported lifetime, past-year and past-30-day marijuana use; first use of marijuana by the next round; intention not to use marijuana, and indices of antimarijuana beliefs and attitudes, social norms and self-efficacy
magnitude: Hornik et al. (2008). Trends among youths aged 12.5–18, 2000 to 2004 (weighted percentages; yearly numbers not printed): lifetime marijuana use 23.6 to 23.5 (change −0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −2.9 to 2.8); past year 17.1 to 16.7 (−0.4, −2.6 to 1.9); past 30 days 7.8 to 8.2 (0.4, −1.4 to 2.2); among youths who had not used marijuana, definitely not intending to use 86.7 to 87.5 (0.8, −1.0 to 2.6); index changes: beliefs and attitudes 6.3 (0.4 to 12.2), self-efficacy 2.4 (−3.3 to 8.2), social norms 1.2 (−5.1 to 7.3). Cross-sectional gammas −0.02 to 0.03, all intervals including 0. Lagged gammas pooled across round pairs: intention with general exposure −0.07 (−0.13 to −0.01); social norms with specific exposure −0.05 (−0.08 to −0.02); first use with general exposure 0.07 (−0.01 to 0.15) (10.7%, 11.2% and 12.5% across under 4, 4–11 and 12 or more exposures a month); first use with specific exposure printed as −0.02 (−0.13 to 0.08), although its percentages rise from 10.8% to 13.2%. First use with general exposure by round pair: 0.08 (−0.05 to 0.20), 0.01 (−0.11 to 0.13) and 0.11 (0.00 to 0.22) for rounds 1–2, 2–3 and 3–4. Subgroups: 3 of 80 cross-sectional and 20 of 80 lagged gammas significant (19 of the 20 unfavourable). No comparison with an unexposed group, so no effect of the campaign against no campaign can be given.

evidence.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 1st to 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Between 1998 and 2004 the US Congress appropriated nearly $1 billion for the National Youth Anti-Drug Media Campaign, whose goals were to help youths reject illegal drugs, to prevent them starting drugs, especially marijuana and inhalants, and to convince people who used drugs occasionally to stop. Messages ran on TV, radio, websites, magazines, cinemas and other channels; advertising was bought from September 1999 to June 2004, with an average youth expected to see 2.5 targeted ads a week, and 64% of the gross rating points bought were on TV and radio. Most ads until late 2002 did not concentrate on a specific drug; from late 2002 a Marijuana Initiative focused the ads on negative consequences of marijuana; in the final 6 months about half the ads encouraged adolescents to intervene with friends who used drugs. The campaign was supervised by the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy, most ads were made pro bono by agencies working with the Partnership for a Drug-Free America, and the evaluation, mandated by Congress, was supervised by the National Institute on Drug Abuse and carried out by Westat and the Annenberg School for Communication. The article covers September 1999 to June 2004; effects on parents are reported separately.

evidence.extracted: Exposure was self-reported recall: general exposure from how often youths had seen or heard antidrug ads in recent months, asked for each medium; specific exposure from prompted recall of up to 4 TV and 2 radio campaign ads scheduled to air in the 2 months before the interview, each played in full (recall imputed for ads not shown). Outcomes were self-reported lifetime, past-year and past-30-day marijuana use and marijuana-related intentions, beliefs and attitudes, social norms and self-efficacy; other drugs were not analysed because their use was too rare for adequate power and the campaign's drug-specific ads were almost always about marijuana. The intention measure predicted later use: among youths aged 12.5 to 18 who had never used marijuana, 9% of those who said they definitely would not use it reported use at the next round, 12 to 18 months later, against 39% of those giving any other answer. Because the campaign was national, the evaluation relied on naturally occurring differences in individual exposure, adjusted by propensity scoring on more than 150 candidate confounders; comparisons between geographic areas were considered, but the advertising agency's projected buying plans did not forecast such variation. Association analyses were restricted to youths who had not used marijuana at the current round (cross-sectional) or at the earlier round (lagged), and all analyses to youths aged 12.5 to 18 at outcome measurement.

risk_of_bias.note: A national probability sample with propensity-score weighting on more than 150 candidate confounders, lagged analyses that control for earlier outcomes, survey weights for non-response and a decision rule stated in advance (card sc_hornik_2008: ROBINS-I, moderate in every domain). The remaining problems, recalled exposure, self-reported use and a 65% first-round response, would tend to blur associations rather than hide a favourable one behind the null and unfavourable estimates observed, so they are not rated down beyond the low start.

inconsistency.note: One study; its estimates vary between pairs of rounds, but none is favourable.

indirectness.note: Worded for what was compared (more against less recalled exposure, 1999–2004, marijuana only); the effect of the campaign against no campaign is not claimed, and the statement says why it cannot be estimated.

imprecision.note: The pooled interval for first use with general exposure (−0.01 to 0.15) excludes more than a trivial favourable association, and the trend intervals exclude falls in use larger than about 3 percentage points.

publication_bias.note: A congressionally mandated evaluation, published with null and unfavourable results.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence (naturally occurring differences in recalled exposure within one national panel, with no unexposed group) starts low and is not rated down further, giving low. Rated as worded: no detectable favourable change with more recalled exposure, and no fall in use over the campaign years. Whether the campaign changed anything compared with no campaign is not rated, because almost every youth was exposed, which the statement says. The unfavourable associations at the next round are reported, not rated as a separate claim: they come from many tests not reported as corrected, appear only for some outcomes and periods (more first use only from round 3 to round 4), and the authors themselves judge their support tentative; the printed gamma for specific exposure and first use (−0.02) does not fit its rising percentages and is not used. Status single study: one national panel; the authors mention a smaller study of the campaign in two cities over 6 months that reported favourable effects, not read here.
